David Walliams' career and controversies including Britain's Got Talent and Little Britain

BBC News Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:53:28 GMT

David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.

A three-year investigation by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women for sexual purposes.

He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.

Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.

His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.

In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.

Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.

He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.

That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.

Walliams and Lucas won a string of awards for Little Britain including three Baftas and two International Emmys, and the programme was watched by 10 million people in the UK.

But in the two decades since it ended, views about the show and what is and is not acceptable to joke about have radically altered. The programme has been criticised for its use of blackface and for stereotyping and mocking characters from minority and marginalised groups.

In the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020, Little Britain was removed from streaming services including BBC iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox.

Another of the duo's shows, 2010 airport comedy Come Fly With Me, was also removed from BritBox a decade after its original broadcast, due to the show's use of racial stereotypes and using make-up to portray people from other ethnic groups.

Little Britain was restored to iPlayer in 2022 with several scenes cut out. Walliams and Lucas said they had re-edited the show to "better reflect the changes in the cultural landscape since the show was made".

Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.

Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.

In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.

Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.

In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.

Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."

He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.

Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.

Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.

Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.

He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".

The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.

Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.

Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

The Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them during the trial and following the conviction and sentencing of the disgraced comedian Russell Brand, "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".

A Met spokesperson said: "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Det Supt Andy Furphy, who led the Brand investigation, said officers were "looking at exactly what we've got" and "whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence".

Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.

On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described him as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault. The latter sentences are to run concurrently.

He was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

The head of the Metropolitan Police, Sir Mark Rowley, said on Friday that he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about him.

Asked by BBC Breakfast how the women in the case who gave evidence in the trial were coping, Furphy said: "Some have found it deeply distressing because of the amount of media attention wrapped around it.

"Even Russell Brand himself before and during trial was putting material online, but we continue to support them."

He noted how the conviction "could not have been achieved" without their "bravery, their courage, their resilience throughout the whole criminal justice process".

He continued: "It's deeply personal and quite harrowing to be a victim of rape and sexual assault, and to have to tell anybody about it, let alone police officers.

"But I'm glad they did. I'm glad they put their trust in us."

MP Dame Caroline Dinenage has re-iterated her concerns about Brand being able to post videos online in the build-up to and during his trial to his millions of followers.

"This does continue to be an issue that he has made money throughout the process on his social media platform," she told the same BBC TV programme.

"It just felt very odd that during the height of when there was a police investigation and some really serious allegations in the paper, that he was able to go online to his two and a half million followers, denying everything and putting his side of the story forward.

"That was an opportunity that his victims didn't have."

In September 2023, after the Sunday Times and Channel 4 Dispatches allegations were made against Brand, Culture, Media and Sport (CMS) Committee chair Dame Caroline wrote to social media companies Rumble, X, TikTok and Meta.

She asked if they would follow YouTube in cutting off Brand's income on their platforms. Rumble publicly refused, and X said it does not take action against accounts that have not broken its rules or the law. TikTok said he had never been monetised there.

"We know that he had used his following [online] to try and cow people into silence," added Dame Caroline.

"And the fact that they [the women] were able to come forward and tell their story and tell their truth and secure this conviction because of it is unbelievably impressive."

Australia doomed to live with stench of sandpapergate

BBC News Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:03:19 GMT

Pat Cummins has led Australia in 43 Tests since 2021

There are stories that can damage reputations, tarnish legacies and put asterisks next to achievements.

Never-ending sagas, claim and counterclaim, one word against another.

Are Pep Guardiola's trophies at Manchester City rendered worthless by financial rule breaches? Would either of the Houston Astros or Boston Red Sox have won the World Series without sign stealing? How much fake blood was spilled by Harlequins?

Now, sandpapergate has morphed into Usman Khawaja's-book-gate, opening old wounds and asking questions that have hung over Australian cricket since Cameron Bancroft hid some DIY equipment in his jockstrap in 2018.

Published on Tuesday, Khawaja's autobiography – Sabr – is only suggesting what plenty have suspected for the past eight years.

It always seemed likely that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were not the only three members of the Australia camp with knowledge of the sandpaper plot.

Careful with his words, perhaps for legal reasons, Khawaja has said enough to reignite a row that once consumed the entire nation of Australia. Crucially, the former batter has not named individuals and, in the opinion of Cricket Australia (CA), not presented enough evidence to merit a new investigation.

It was Nathan Lyon who once said Australia know how to "headbutt the line, but we won't go over it". Khawaja has headbutted the line of whistle-blowing, without taking a full toot.

This video can not be played

How sandpapergate was exposed

There are some key quotes from Khawaja, taken from the autobiography and his public statements of the past few days.

Writing in Sabr, Khawaja says: "I'm going to use the term 'we' throughout this chapter, because 'we' are team Australia – although in this book I'm not speaking on behalf of anyone but myself. This will be my recollection of events."

In a video posted on Instagram, he added: "You would have seen when I mentioned it was all of us, that's implying that whether we like it or not, we are all responsible for what happened together. As a team, we need to take that collectively. That is all."

Then, to ABC on Tuesday: "I'm not here to go on a witch hunt. All I've ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team."

Rather than directly accusing his team-mates, Khawaja is asking the Australians present in Cape Town to share the blame that was given to Smith, Warner and Bancroft. An individual can be culpable for what happened, even if they were not the one to directly rub sandpaper on the red leather.

Khawaja has also explained that much of his motivation for telling this story comes from loyalty to his childhood friend Warner.

Warner has had his say and, like Khawaja, has not named anyone else he feels should be implicated.

There are questions as to why neither man has spoken up over the past eight years. If they felt strongly, they could have come forward at any time, even if Khawaja is proved correct in his claim he was not interviewed in the original investigation.

Then again, there was the issue of squad harmony, loyalty to their friends and protecting their places in the Australia team. Warner may yet reveal more in the future, ditto for Smith and Bancroft.

This latest evidence has done little to shift views that were entrenched before Khawaja put pen to paper. Darren Lehmann, Australia coach at the time, has stuck to his story of denial, as has Mitchell Starc. Chadd Sayers, another seamer in the 2018 squad, has come out in support of Khawaja and Warner.

So far, so much stalemate.

Josh Hazlewood (313), Nathan Lyon (577), Mitchell Starc (460) and Pat Cummins 328) have taken almost 1,700 Test wickets between them

It leaves the ball in the court of the other Australian players involved, the coaching staff and CA.

On Tuesday, CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said, with a straight face, he did not see "any compelling reason" to reopen the investigation into the ball-tampering saga.

What evidence could compel Greenberg to act? Even if Khawaja has not directly pointed the finger at anyone else in the dressing room that day, surely CA should be curious about the claims that are currently causing so much reputational damage, especially when Khawaja and Warner have called into question the rigour of the original investigation.

The Cape Town files have never been made public. In 2021, David Saker, an Australia assistant coach in 2018, called for them to be released. Now, Saker is not named but is among the staff Khawaja has implicated in the book by claiming a member of the backroom team encouraged Bancroft. That allegation alone surely merits further scrutiny by CA.

Of the players in the Australia XI on that Saturday at Newlands, three were punished; now Khawaja has accepted his share of responsibility, making four.

Tim Paine inherited the captaincy, a reign that ended in his own scandal. Mitchell Marsh remains an active player and is about to skipper Australia in the limited-overs series against England. Marsh will speak on Thursday. His brother Shaun was also in the team in Cape Town. That makes seven.

Then there are the four bowlers, possibly the greatest four-man attack ever assembled.

Starc, with more Test wickets than any other left-arm bowler in history. Lyon, the most successful orthodox finger-spinner in Test cricket. Josh Hazlewood, the reincarnation of Glenn McGrath. Pat Cummins, the clean-cut current Australia captain, an Ashes and World Cup-winning leader.

That they are still Australia's first-choice bowling unit is testament to their talent, longevity and desire. They remain as a quartet, hunting prizes that have previously eluded them over the coming year – an away Test series win in India, winning the Ashes in England.

As it stands, they are adhering to a joint-statement made in 2021 that they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field".

The plausibility of elite bowlers not knowing a ball has been tampered with is up for debate. The quartet point to the fact the on-field umpires on the day did not see any reason to change the ball at the time. In contrast, Khawaja said the effects of sandpaper could leave swirls on the leather.

For Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon, champion bowlers, the insinuation hangs over them. It is hard to prove a negative. Perhaps the off-ramp is for the foursome to themselves call for a reopening of the investigation? It could clear their names.

As it stands, Australian cricket is stuck in a sandpaper limbo, a halfway house full of historical scandal, innuendo and unanswered questions. According to former captain Michael Clarke, further inaction would leave supporters unable to "trust what's real".

Perhaps there is another scenario, the unpalatable prospect of those at the top having no desire to open the door for fear of what might lie behind it. It is worth remembering that the past two Australia captains have lost the job in disgrace: Smith for sandpaper, Paine for sexting.

Is that worse than the status quo? Sandpaper is the stench Australian cricket cannot shake.

French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104

BBC News Tue, 10 Nov 2026 13:23:54 GMT

One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104. Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.

After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of Ruillé-sur-Loir.

With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.

President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.

"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.

Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France, Solange Alexandre, née Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.

"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917. The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.

In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany. She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.

"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.

Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's – a Tunisian-born French army veteran called Saïd Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.

Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.

"There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.

In 1943 she met her first husband Guy Déliot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.

The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.

Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy. There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian.

"Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.

After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).

Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.

Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the Légion d'Honneur, saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy.

Finally in 2024 she relented.

On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour. I am very proud – even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."

Divorced after five days: 'My sham husband made me believe he loved me'

BBC News Tue, 10 Nov 2026 06:13:46 GMT

Five days after her Islamic wedding, Jane received a text message which turned her life upside down.

"I divorce you and have divorced you," wrote her new husband.

Jane - whose real name the BBC has agreed not to publish - said she had met him on the Muslim marriage website Muzz 10 months earlier.

At the time, she believed he was called Adam and that he lived in Manchester.

"It's very hard for me. I thought I was getting into a marriage and instead I got into my worst nightmare," she said.

"It's just crazy. I don't understand why people do this kind of stuff for sex."

Jane said they spent six months chatting online together and on video calls before agreeing to meet in person.

She told the BBC she believed their relationship to be genuine and did not question what was happening when he subsequently proposed.

"He made me believe that he loved me and that he wanted to build a life with me, so I had no reason to really doubt him," she said.

She later discovered Adam's real name was different and that he was already married.

Adam's lawyers said he rejected Jane's allegations in their entirety.

On 2 June, Jane - a convert to Islam - went to Brierfield in Lancashire for a nikah - an Islamic marriage contract or ceremony under Sharia law.

Such contracts, however, are not the same as a civil legal marriage and are not legally recognised as marriage in England and Wales.

Jane said she wanted to get married in her home city of Glasgow, surrounded by friends and family, but said her future husband objected to a wedding in Scotland.

She now looks back on this moment as a warning sign.

"In Scotland, they asked for legal marriage and a nikah to be done at the same time," she explained.

"He said 'Why do they need to see my ID? I mean, nikah is very simple and they don't need to see my ID at all'.

"And so he was really upset about that."

Jane said the ceremony in Brierfield took place in the presence of two imams who acted as witnesses and the couple then spent two nights at a hotel.

Just five days after the wedding, however, Jane received the message informing her that their marriage was over.

Jane said she was left feeling shocked and confused, describing it as a "sham marriage".

Jane believes her "shocking" experience amounted to emotional and sexual exploitation.

The BBC understands he remains married to another woman, both legally and religiously.

In a detailed response through his lawyers, he said the allegations were part of a sustained campaign against him, were unsupported by evidence, and were false.

They told the BBC he had not deceived Jane about his previous marriage because he had not mentioned it.

He had also not hidden his identity during the ceremony with Jane because he provided his driving licence.

The BBC has seen a copy of Jane's Islamic marriage certificate provided to her by the mosque, which contains missing and incorrect details.

Mufti Adeel Zaman, the imam who conducted the ceremony, said the marriage had been between two consenting adults who appeared happy and that he did not consider it his responsibility to ask further questions.

"We are deeply saddened by the circumstances that have arisen," he told the BBC.

"Our intention throughout has been to provide appropriate support and assistance while remaining fair to all parties and limiting our comments to matters of which we have direct knowledge."

He acknowledged that mistakes had been made over checking identification but said he had helped uncover the true identity of the man that Jane had married.

The Lancashire Council of Mosques, which has been involved in mediation following the breakdown of the marriage, said those conducting such ceremonies had a responsibility to carry out appropriate checks.

New Beginnings, a group based in Oldham, Greater Manchester, that provides services to people who have converted to Islam, said it had encountered cases involving people who sought to deceive others within the Muslim community.

"We know about these charlatans in our community, the Muslim community, and people they're out there to deceive," said founder Bilal Brown.

He said relationships or marriages that seem rushed or where extended family are not involved are clear warning signs that all may not be well.

Converts to Islam could be particularly vulnerable in such circumstances, he added.

Saima Afzal, a former assistant police and crime commissioner for Lancashire, told BBC North West Tonight the lack of legal recognition afforded to Islamic marriages could be a problem for some women.

"There is the nikah loophole that you hear about quite a lot around: 'Well, we can't do them for bigamy because nikah is not legally recognised in the UK'," she said.

"Putting that to one side about nikah, let's look at the behaviours here.

"So you've got trickery, manipulation and ensnaring really a woman.

"So it's deception."

An independent review presented to Parliament in 2018 found that a significant number of Islamic marriages were not followed by civil marriages, leaving people without the protections associated with legally recognised marriages.

Police Scotland said no criminality had been established in Scotland.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed it had been asked to investigate a complaint made by Jane.

Muzz said the man had been permanently blocked from its platform.

Its chief executive Shahzad Younas said: "We ask users to declare if they are married (legally or otherwise).

"If they are we block them from the app during sign-up."

He said the company carried out email, telephone number, device and selfie validation as part of its standard checks, while identity verification was optional.

Profiles indicate which checks have and have not been completed.

Jane said she wanted her case to help prevent other women from experiencing similar situations.

"It's an issue in the community," she added. "If I can help any other vulnerable woman like I was, it's a win."

The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills

BBC News Tue, 10 Nov 2026 00:08:28 GMT

A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E. ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.

Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.

But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."

There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"

Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".

"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.

Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.

But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.

With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.

The alternative is to build.

Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.

Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.

All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.

And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.

And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.

I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".

Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.

Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.

"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.

Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.

Foreign investment, then - just not from China.

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.

And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.

If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

Correcting quantum computer errors may be more complicated than expected

New Scientist November 10, 2026

Quantum computers will not become useful until researchers perfect methods for correcting errors that these devices naturally make. Quantum error-correction (QEC) techniques have advanced rapidly in recent years, but several studies now suggest that the landscape of errors they must tackle is unexpectedly complex, which poses new challenges for making quantum computers practical.

The idea of QEC dates back to the very inception of quantum computing and the first investigations of how quantum computers could be put to work. At that time, no one had built a quantum computer, so researchers relied on mathematical theory to work out how well errors could be corrected, and which computations this error correction would allow the computers to reliably complete. Now, quantum computers do exist and data about their errors is fast accumulating. Increasingly, researchers are finding there are some types of errors that the earlier investigations had overlooked, and they could threaten quantum computers’ progress.

Google showcases way to fix quantum computer errors more efficiently

Quantum computers are made from building blocks called qubits, and qubits make errors because they are sensitive to interactions with their environment. One long-standing assumption about these errors – the Markov assumption – has been that they are memoryless: errors that a qubit makes at different points in time are uncorrelated.

Advertisement

Memory effects are detrimental for the useful operation of quantum computers because they mean that making a qubit repeat the same operation at different times may lead to different results based on what its environment “remembers”, says Lorenza Viola at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. It is as if multiplying a number by 2 gives one value right now and a different value later. The Markov assumption posits that this happens either never or in a small number of cases, which would allow quantum computers to run longer programs. But troublingly, the assumption seems to be incorrect. Memory effects keep appearing in experiments.

Recently, Ioan Pop at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and Stuttgart University in Germany and his colleagues developed a measurement method that uncovered very long-lived defects – spurious quantum states that arise from material imperfections, stray molecules or several other sources – in a superconducting qubit’s environment, each of which could act as a memory. “We are concretely showing how this long-lived environment can break one of the assumptions of error correction,” he says.

Free newsletter

Earlier this year, Rami Barends at Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH in Germany and his colleagues studied a different type of superconducting qubit and found similar violations of the Markov assumption.

The assumption has been challenged at the level of whole quantum computers, too. In 2025, John Fidel Kam at the Agency for Science, Technology and Research in Singapore, Kavan Modi at the Singapore University of Technology and Design, Muhammad Usman at Monash University in Australia and their colleagues analysed a key error-correction experiment with Google’s Willow quantum computer. They found that some of the errors that were difficult to correct or account for matched a theoretical model in which the Markov assumption didn’t hold. The qubits’ environment was non-Markovian.

Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated

In another analysis, Gregory Quiroz at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland and his colleagues discovered that a model including non-Markovian effects represented an IBM quantum computer that they accessed through the cloud seven times better than the noise models commonly used in studies of error-correction. IBM and Google did not respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

Working with colleagues, Viola has found that the parts of a qubit’s environment that can “remember” can additionally act as quantum systems in their own right and “respond” to a qubit. This introduces a new kind of error – another effect that QEC approaches currently do not account for.

This work is preliminary, but Viola says that as quantum computers are rapidly improving, previously irrelevant effects could become increasingly important. Modi thinks it is too early to sound the alarm, but he says that there are currently no guarantees, experimental or theoretical, that the problem will not worsen as quantum computers grow in qubit number.

Will the backlash against AI data centres hit quantum computing too?

“There is a chance that error correction does not work because correlated noise [memory effects] has not been accounted for,” he says. “We don’t fully know where it breaks down, partly because complex noise is hard to describe.”

There are mathematical theorems suggesting that a quantum computer could reach fault-tolerance – a mode of operation where errors do not stymie it – even when there are memory effects and errors are correlated in time or space. But just how strong those correlations can be before they become a problem is another open question, says Viola. Amit Hagar at Indiana University Bloomington says that the situation isn’t necessarily black and white, and standard error-correction methods could end up working, but only for computations of a certain length or complexity. This would undermine the promise of a quantum computer as a machine that can run arbitrarily long computations. For any firm that is trying to build one, the burden of proof now shifts to their researchers, he says. “They were basing their promise on a theorem, which was conditional, and currently the condition may not work,” says Hagar.

Determining how useful different quantum computers are has been a long running challenge – now researchers appear to have the answer

In Usman’s view, the future is rather open because the programs researchers use for quantum error-correction are themselves evolving alongside quantum computing hardware. Until recently, QEC programs that date back to the 1990s were the gold standard, but a whole new class of codes known as QLDPC have now gained traction, and how well they work in the face of correlated errors is not yet clear, he says. “There is a lot more to investigate and study before we make any claim about whether error correction is going to work or not,” he says.

“Error correction codes can adapt to non-Markovian errors. They will have to adapt to that,” says Pop. The measurement technique that he and his colleagues developed recently could play a part here because it may enable other teams to identify memory effects in their devices and devise strategies for avoiding them, says his colleague Nicolas Gosling at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. Correlated errors could also be mitigated by adjusting conventional computer algorithms that control quantum computers and read their output, says Kam.

So, there are several ways for tackling this neglected class of errors. The researchers who study them say that they haven’t necessarily uncovered an unsolvable problem – as long as it’s taken seriously. “It was not on the radar of many people until now,” says Pop.

What terrifying sleep paralysis demons reveal about the mind-body connection

New Scientist November 10, 2026

Years ago, I woke to see a darkly cloaked figure towering over me. I thought it was going to kill me, but I couldn’t move. I wasn’t dreaming. I could see my room and feel my body beneath my sheets. I was consciously aware, yet hallucinating a figure that didn’t exist.

I was experiencing sleep paralysis, a phenomenon that affects approximately 30 per cent of people worldwide. Episodes are usually benign, but for roughly 1 per cent of people, they reoccur weekly, raising the risk of insomnia. Even isolated instances can leave a lasting impression. I still think about my experience today. While I know the figure wasn’t real, the fear it instilled in me was.

In his latest book, The Phantom Mind: Insights from the borderlands of sleep, Baland Jalal reveals how and why sleep paralysis can take hold. A neuroscientist at Harvard University, his research has brought us closer to understanding what affects the appearance of so-called “sleep paralysis demons” and how we can potentially prevent these frightening experiences. Jalal sat down with New Scientist to discuss what all this tells us about the mind-body connection.

Advertisement

Epic dreaming is leaving people exhausted and distressed

Grace Wade: I am curious – have you experienced sleep paralysis?

Baland Jalal: I have. I had my first episode when I was about 18 or 19. I was sleeping and suddenly realised: I am awake, yet I can’t move. I can’t speak. I felt this looming presence, this shadow-like creature approaching me. And then it strangled me. It pressed on my chest, and I saw my legs flying up and down. I was sure I was going to die. But eventually, I managed to wrestle myself out of it. It was a horrifying, but also life-changing, experience because this was the trigger for me to become a scientist.

That sounds awful. What happens in the brain during this phenomenon?

Sleep paralysis emerges out of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when we have our most vivid dreams. During REM sleep, we are completely paralysed from head to toe so that we cannot act out our dreams. What can happen is that the outer layer of the brain can suddenly activate and jolt you awake while you are still in REM paralysis.

We know what can trigger this. Deep in the brain, you have the limbic structures, the emotional department of the brain. If you are aroused during the day – you have a lot of anxiety, a lot of stress – that part of the brain is hyperactive. When you go to sleep, it will stay activated and sort of tickle the outer layers of your brain, and you jolt awake. Now, if the emotional part of the brain wakes you when you are supposed to be in REM sleep, you have sleep paralysis, because you can’t move.

Free newsletter

But why do people see or hear things that aren’t there?

Sleep paralysis is really being awake and asleep at the same time. And what happens in REM sleep? All these parts of the brain are turning on and off, and that creates a surreal dream world.

For example, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the rational part of the brain, shuts down during REM sleep. It puts the world together in a logical way, and for that reason, dreams are bizarre. The cingulate cortex, which has to do with conflict monitoring and empathy, is hyperactivated during dreams. It is why we can create theory of mind, meaning we can project agency and intentions onto other beings in our dreams.

The temporoparietal junction, which creates a sense of body image, also takes a hit during REM. So your sense of self is all fluid. And then the emotional part of the brain, the limbic structures, is about 30 per cent more active in REM than when awake. That explains why dreams are so emotional, so intense.

Now you have sleep paralysis, where you start waking up, yet these elements of the REM dream are spilling into waking reality.

How do we know this?

In terms of the brain regions that turn on or off during REM sleep, that comes from brain-imaging studies. In terms of why we see monsters during sleep paralysis, that is all theoretical. It would be interesting to conduct brain-imaging studies of people while they see [them] to find the exact neural pathways that light up. You might think that isn’t important, but I think it could be. It might show us the pathways governing extreme dread, religious fear and mysterious experiences.

Why haven’t we done that? I imagine capturing sleep paralysis with a brain scanner would be challenging.

I don’t think it would be that challenging. You would have people that are already predisposed to sleep paralysis and then disrupt them during REM sleep with a scanner on.

I think the reason it hasn’t been done is because, in most cases, sleep paralysis is benign. It would be hard to get grant money.

In your book, you suggest that sleep paralysis is a unique window into consciousness. What do you mean by that?

You have the dreaming brain, with all these different parts being shut down or hyperactivated, and then it blends with the waking brain, where you have some conscious awareness. I think that gives us a potential window into understanding aspects of consciousness.

The ability to choose is a key aspect of conscious experience. If you were able to communicate with someone in sleep paralysis and ask them to choose, say, Pepsi or Coca-Cola, they would be able to. Compare this with sleepwalking. From the outside, that person might look conscious, but they aren’t because they cannot choose.

Sleep paralysis has shown us that mixed states of consciousness are possible and that you can have some self-agency in these states. I think one of the most important insights is that your own mind can potentially trigger an event that seems comparable to trauma.

We also know that if you have a certain cultural idea about sleep paralysis, it becomes more common and it seems to last much longer. That is a big insight of the mind-body connection.

Dream engineers are developing technologies that can help you sleep more soundly and use your nighttime hours to your advantage – but there could also be a dark side

Your research has focused on the role beliefs and expectations play in sleep paralysis. Tell me about those findings.

After my sleep-paralysis episode as a teenager, I decided to become a scientist and study it. I went to Egypt, got into The American University in Cairo. I am originally from Denmark, where we have very secular views. Everything is as you see it. Egypt, on the other hand, is a very superstitious place. So I thought, how would sleep paralysis differ in these two cultures? And it differed quite severely.

My colleague, David Hinton at Harvard, and I surveyed hundreds of people in Denmark and Egypt, asking them whether they experienced sleep paralysis and, if so, what it was like. About 90 per cent of people in Denmark said it is just your brain. It is stress. It is physiology. Nothing supernatural about that. The people in Egypt were completely different. They would say it is a genie – evil genies, not the nice blue one from Aladdin – and they feared it intensely. About 50 per cent of people who had sleep paralysis [in Egypt] thought they might die from it.

And this seemed to influence their experience of sleep paralysis. So, people in Egypt would say their episodes last much longer [than people in Denmark]. It was also twice as common in Egypt than in Denmark. We think that has to do with how the idea spreads from person to person.

I was once told that you can only experience sleep paralysis after learning about it from someone else. Then, boom! I had my first episode.

That isn’t the only way, but it definitely becomes more common, which has to do with a phenomenon called priming. This is how it works. Let’s say you have this girl who has never heard about sleep paralysis. Then, her grandmother warns her of these monsters that come at night.

Now what happens? She goes to bed and the emotional core of her brain is hyper-alert, which is this perfect disaster for sleep paralysis, because you are so likely to jolt out of REM. Then, in REM, she feels something holding her down, which is just her brain paralysing her. When she tries to move and can’t, she panics. Then her dream imagery will create these vivid hallucinations. She wakes up terrified, tells her friend and the scenario starts all over. It keeps spreading.

This is a personal question, but what form does your sleep paralysis demon take?

It has evolved. My first encounter was a shadowy sense of presence. It was the most terrifying episode ever.

When I was in Egypt, it was during the Libyan revolution, and Muammar Gaddafi [the former Libyan prime minister] was on the news all the time. One day, I was sleeping and it was Gaddafi hovering over me. That was very spooky. Later, as a PhD student in England, I would go to these castle-like hotels to give talks, and they seemed so haunted. I would have terrifying episodes there.

So it isn’t only cultural beliefs that shape sleep paralysis, but also environment?

Absolutely. Terrifying castles? Terrifying sleep paralysis. Somebody who doesn’t know the neuroscience of sleep paralysis would think it is a haunted hotel. We have data from people reporting that if they have a poster on their wall, suddenly that would morph into a dangerous face, or a little glass on their table would morph into a skull. So the environment primes the experience, for sure.

How we feel about a night’s sleep can have a bigger impact on mood and grogginess than actual hours of rest. Here’s how to change your mindset to feel more energised

If our beliefs and expectations are partly to blame for sleep paralysis, could they also help us manage it?

Absolutely. I developed four steps people can do during sleep paralysis. It is very simple. First is a cognitive reappraisal, which is a fancy way of saying “reinterpret the whole thing”. Remember, it is just the brain playing tricks on you. Then, you do emotional distancing. Since you know it is the brain, it makes no sense to be scared. I may have those emotions, but I am going to distance myself from them.

The third step is key: you meditate on something positive, your mother’s face or God or the sunset, whatever is positive for you. That can make the frontal parietal part of the brain, the part that has to do with attention, bias the brain toward positive emotions. Number four is that you will still have paralysis. You can’t avoid those physiological symptoms, so ignore them.

We did a study with six people in Italy who had sleep paralysis frequently. Their episodes decreased by about 50 per cent after using this for eight weeks.

This is very promising, but very preliminary. We are now working on a follow-up study of this therapy.

Why is treating sleep paralysis important, given we know people aren’t actually being attacked by a monster?

Because of the pervasive nature of the experience, the way it spreads, the way it can harm people psychologically. Even having a few episodes a year can be destructive. And a small percentage of people have several episodes a month. That is when it is really pernicious and pathological. You just can’t get rid of it, and it is causing insomnia.

Have you tried this technique yourself?

A few times. It seemed to work. Sleep paralysis has evolved for me from being terrorised by this shadow-like creature to now [when] I can take control. I have learned to have my prefrontal cortex kick in and regulate some of the fear structures.

What is the electrification target at COP31 and can countries meet it?

New Scientist November 10, 2026

One of the key items being discussed at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, this week is a voluntary global target to increase electricity’s share of total final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035. This 35 by 35 target is based on analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) on what is needed to keep the 1.5°C global warming target within reach.

Currently, electricity is estimated to make up just 23.4 per cent of the energy delivered to consumers, known as final energy – a figure that has increased by only 6.7 percentage points since 2000. This means that hitting the target will require the rate of electrification to quadruple compared with the first quarter of the 21st century and triple compared with the rate between 2020 and 2025.

Judit Hecke at New Climate Institute, a German think tank, says such an acceleration is possible but “the challenge is getting policies, investment and infrastructure moving at the same pace”.

Advertisement

Progress on renewable energy has been encouraging, with renewables making up a higher proportion of overall electricity production year after year, and renewable capacity additions have been setting new records each year. In 2024, the most recent IRENA data, nearly 32 per cent of global electricity production came from renewable sources compared with just 18 per cent in 2000.

Renewable energy capacity has increased from 0.8 terawatts in 2000 to 5.2 terawatts in 2025. But this is a long way from the COP28 pledge for UN member states to reach 11 terawatts of renewable capacity by 2030.

However, Hecke points out that the electrification target includes electricity regardless of how it is generated, meaning that a country could make progress while still heavily relying on coal and gas in the power sector.

Electrification, renewables and energy efficiency should be looked at together as the “three pillars of the energy transition”, says Hecke. “At COP31, governments should back the target as part of this wider transition and set out how they will deliver it nationally.”

Solar energy is going to power the world much sooner than you think

Jan Rosenow at the University of Oxford says the 35 by 35 target is “broadly the right level of ambition” and it is achievable now that electric vehicles, electrical industrial heat and heat pumps are often the cheapest options.

“Most new electricity generation built today is renewables and batteries. And electric technologies are so much more efficient that they cut fossil fuel use even on today’s grids, [which] are getting cleaner every year,” he says.

The share of energy supplied by electricity varies widely from sector to sector, with transport a long way behind buildings and industrial applications.

Politics is also a big constraining factor, with many governments seemingly unwilling to commit to ambitious targets. The US has withdrawn from the global climate framework entirely and will be the only major economy absent from COP31 negotiations this week.

Meanwhile, there are question marks about countries that have voiced support for the 35 by 35 target, like the UK, which has also set a legally binding target to meet net-zero emissions by 2050. This week, it has been reported that the UK government is expected to weaken its electric vehicle targets.

The Lancet Countdown for 2026, an annual report on the links between climate change and health, showed that global preparedness for the transition to a net-zero emissions economy fell from 0.48 in 2024 to 0.38 in 2025, with 1 being the highest preparedness score achievable.

The researchers said that the drop in the preparedness score, which is based on a country’s capacity for the transition compared with its dependence on fossil fuels, indicates that the gap between climate ambition and delivery has widened.

Last month, the UN Emissions Gap report acknowledged that it is now impossible to meet the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, but there is still hope that we could stay under 2°C of warming if countries cut emissions sharply.

In a statement to New Scientist, IRENA said achieving 35 per cent electrification by 2035 won’t be sufficient to meet the temperature objectives on its own and renewables are a key component.

“What matters now is the speed and scale of action. Faster emissions reductions can help limit the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and reduce the associated climate risks,” the agency said.

A science fiction novel has finally won the Booker prize. It’s about time

New Scientist November 10, 2026

Back in June, our science fiction columnist Emily H. Wilson made a bold claim: M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything was not only “the best science-fiction book of the year so far”, but also a “wholly original… work of genius”.

Not only has Emily been proved right, but perhaps she didn’t go quite far enough. This story of an alien invasion won the Booker prize last night, making it – in the Booker judges’ opinion, at least – not just the best science fiction book of the year so far, but the best novel in any genre of the year.

These two new sci-fi novels really impressed us

It’s about time. Back in 2009, the great Kim Stanley Robinson – another writer of genius, in my opinion – wrote a piece for New Scientist in which he argued that “three or four of the last 10 Booker prizes should have gone to science fiction novels the juries hadn’t read”. With remarkable prescience, Robinson even tipped Harrison’s Signs of Life as one of those books.

Advertisement

There has been a long-running reluctance in the literary world to allow science fiction (often abbreviated to SF) into the starry ranks of so-called “literary” fiction. As Harrison himself told the BBC’s Front Row last month, he has “been working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic… Why shouldn’t a well written SF be considered to be literary fiction?”.

His win is being trumpeted today as the first time a science fiction novel has won the Booker prize. I’d quibble a little with that – how about Margaret Atwood’s The Testaments, the sequel to The Handmaid’s Tale, set in a dystopian version of the US, which was 2019’s winner? She’d likely quibble with me in return: Atwood has a lot to say about the difference between science fiction and speculative fiction, defining her Gilead stories firmly as the latter.

Free newsletter

But this very unwillingness to define a novel as science fiction speaks to that long-running literary snobbery. As the late, great Ursula K. Le Guin put it, reviewing Atwood’s The Year of the Flood back in 2009: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.”

Whether or not Harrison is the first science fiction author to win the Booker, it’s definitely the case that, as Booker Prize Foundation chief executive Gaby Wood put it in the prize announcement: “Many past Booker Prize authors have borrowed facets of science fiction in their work, but M. John Harrison is the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world.”

And this means, I hope, that our days of looking down on science fiction are over. Harrison’s brilliant book tells the story of Phillip Tennent, a beachcomber who lives with his grandmother on the Kent coast, in the wake of the invasion of mysterious shapeshifting entities called the iGhetti. It’s “the politics of now seen through the lens of the future”, said the Booker’s chair of judges, Mary Beard – an apt description of all the very best science fiction out there, whether that’s Le Guin’s masterpiece The Dispossessed, Octavia Butler’s terrifyingly prescient Parable of the Sower, Robinson’s masterpiece Red Mars or Cixin Liu’s own tale of an alien invasion, The Three-Body Problem.

We asked New Scientist staff to pick their favourite science fiction books. Here are the results, ranging from 19th-century classics to modern day offerings, and from Octavia E. Butler to Iain M. Banks

“The literature that best expresses our time, that speaks to our time, is science fiction. How could it be otherwise? Our world is a science fiction,” wrote Robinson in 2009. In these strange and fluid times, of climate change, artificial intelligence and shifting political sands, that is only more true today.

Newly described insect may live its whole life on a spider’s web

New Scientist November 10, 2026

This minuscule bug lives dangerously, possibly spending its whole life cycle on a spider’s web.

The insect species – which is new to science – is a variety of web-loving true bug. These tiny, carnivorous insects nimbly crawl along silk threads, largely ignored by their comparatively immense arachnid hosts.

Since the 2020s, Haoyang Xiong at China Agricultural University in Beijing and his colleagues have been studying web-loving bugs in China.

Advertisement

New-to-science spider builds trap that flings ants into the air

“They are rare, they occur in low numbers and their behaviour is quite unusual,” says Xiong. Web-loving bugs are scattered across most tropical regions but nearly 80 per cent of the species are each known from only a single location, he says.

During fieldwork in Fujian province in September 2025, Xiong found tiny, millimetre-long insects – barely bigger than grains of table salt – living in the tangled homes of funnel web spiders. He collected them and brought them into the lab for identification and further study.

After comparing the physical features of the tiny reddish bugs to the few known web-loving bug species, Xiong and his team determined they belonged to an undescribed species, which they named Heissophila sinica. The bugs are smaller than their closest relatives, which live predominantly in South-East Asia.

Free newsletter

Web-loving bugs capitalise on an ephemeral microhabitat made by spiders and a few other silk-weaving arthropods. In H. sinica, the size difference between the spider and the bugs may keep them from being targeted as food.

“They do not avoid the [spider] at all,” says Xiong. “On the contrary, they like to follow it about and circle around it, for reasons we do not yet understand.”

The bugs feed on the scraps left after the spider eats, and they also eat up web-dwelling mites – some of which are spider parasites.

“When the spider moults, [the bugs] gather round and drink the spider’s body fluids,” Xiong says. He and his colleagues aren’t yet sure whether the bugs mostly help or hinder the spiders. Another option is that they have largely do neither, which would make the bugs commensal organisms.

A carnivorous caterpillar species camouflages itself with dead insects so it can live safely alongside spiders, stalking their webs and stealing their prey

The insects may live their entire lives on the spider’s web. The team has found eggs, juveniles and adults on the web simultaneously. It’s still unclear precisely how the bugs manage to climb around on the silk without becoming stuck, but Xiong says it may come down to the insects’ unusual feet, which have just two simple claws and lack many of the other structures found in other insects’ feet.

Randall Schuh at the American Museum of Natural History in New York lauds the research team for the fieldwork efforts and for documenting the natural history of such bizarre and diminutive insects.

“None of this [work] is straightforward, including finding the spiders and their burrows or observing these tiny bugs under what are oftentimes less than ideal conditions,” he says.

Xiong and his colleagues plan to increase their efforts collecting web-loving bugs in China and neighbouring regions to gather genetic data to help them better understand the evolution of these mysterious spider web tenants.

How neutrinos are beginning to reveal the secrets of our galaxy

New Scientist November 10, 2026

The day before this year’s Nobel prize in physics was announced, I was quoted in The New York Times as saying the question of why neutrinos are non-trinary is one of the most pressing scientific issues facing my field. What a happy coincidence that the next day, the Nobel committee announced the prize had been given to Francis Halzen for his leadership on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. I joked on social media that I was somehow responsible for the committee noticing this important experiment in Antarctica, which studies neutrinos that come from deep space, often looking for how they provide information that other signals – light, gravitational waves – cannot by themselves.

Record-breaking, fast-spinning magnet could help uncover new physics

Regular readers of this column know that I love to talk about these subatomic particles because they have the distinct property of being non-trinary. There are three flavours of neutrino and, as they travel through space, they oscillate between these identities. Neutrinos refuse the notion of a fixed identity. We understand these oscillations to be related to their mass. But we actually still don’t understand how they get their mass.

Despite this mystery, we do know plenty about where neutrinos are made. One place is in stars, including our own sun. The nuclear fusion processes that make all the light we get from stars also make neutrinos as a by-product. Those same phenomena also play a role in stellar deaths, like the fantastical explosions we call supernovae. In fact, next year we will be celebrating the 40th anniversary of our first time connecting observed neutrinos with such an explosion.

Advertisement

The first supernova detected in 1987 – designated Supernova 1987A – was a brilliant collapse of a former blue supergiant star. It was the closest supernova to our solar system in centuries, and we witnessed it across the electromagnetic spectrum: optical, infrared, ultraviolet and even in the X-ray. But one of the most interesting things about 1987A’s discovery is that hours before the light became visible, three different neutrino detectors on Earth noticed an influx of these ghostly particles.

In other words, neutrinos were our first messenger from the stellar death that occurred 168,000 light years away. The reason the neutrinos arrived first is down to how deeply antisocial they are. Neutrinos pass by other matter like it’s not even there. So, while the light particles – made in stars alongside neutrinos – were trying to escape the plasmas and atoms they ran into, the neutrinos were streaming freely out of the collapsing star into the cosmos.

In the 39 years since 1987A’s neutrinos helped us place bounds on the mass of neutrinos, and also how many neutrino flavours there are, neutrino astrophysics has become a new vista on the universe.

In the years after 1987A, Halzen led the group that conceptualised IceCube to use those neutrinos as a lens on the cosmos. Over the past few decades, thousands of scientists have worked together to make this concept into a reality in Antarctica and used the instrument to do some truly fascinating science. For example, Naoko Kurahashi Neilson at Drexel University in Pennsylvania led the effort to make a complete map of the Milky Way using only neutrinos. It took almost a decade, but, in 2023, IceCube unveiled a groundbreaking new atlas of our home galaxy. The image is very different from what we get with light: it’s not symmetric and is full of neutrino blobs that are begging us to figure them out. The asymmetry is especially tantalising to me because that’s usually an indicator that something interesting is happening – but what?

These days, Neilson is leading a group within IceCube that is trying to understand what neutrinos can tell us about the galactic centre, especially any details about what is accelerating particles in the region to relativistic speeds. In September, the group shared new research about the challenges of matching neutrino sources with the most high-energy light sources we know, on the assumption that the neutrinos and the light are coming from the same place. The hope is that we can establish what exactly is sending these energetic and mysterious particles out into the void. From my point of view, they’re showing that our galaxy is one of the best naturally occurring particle physics experiments out there.

Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated

Global carbon emissions set to fall in 2026 due to Iran energy shock

Carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to drop this year for the first time in five years.

The slowdown has been partly attributed to the energy shock triggered by the US and Israel’s war on Iran. The conflict, which began in February, led to a jump in oil prices after the Strait of Hormuz, the main trade route for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas, was blockaded by Iran in response.

This is still affecting petrol prices and household gas bills, and has seen countries around the world turn to alternative fuel types to boost energy security.

Advertisement

Solar energy is going to power the world much sooner than you think

Around 38.2 gigatonnes of CO2 are expected to be emitted in 2026 globally, according to the latest annual Global Carbon Budget – put together by more than 140 researchers.

This is a 0.4 per cent decrease on the previous year, largely due to a projected 1.9 per cent fall in emissions from oil. The drop in oil use was partly offset by a 0.6 per cent increase in emissions from coal.

Robbie Andrew at climate research group CICERO in Oslo, Norway, one of the report authors, says financial pressures due to the energy shock are likely to have caused the drop in emissions this year, which may turn out to be a “blip”.

“On the assumption that there are no further crises, then you’d expect that emissions would bounce back,” says Andrew.

The two biggest dips in emissions in the 21st century have been attributed to the covid-19 pandemic, which saw emissions drop by around 6 per cent in 2020, and the global financial crisis, which saw emissions drop around 2 per cent in 2009.

The future outlook depends on how long the energy shock lasts, says Andrew, with governments forced to look at the economic case for continuing to subsidise fossil fuels.

The rollout of renewable energy also played a part in bringing down carbon emissions. Electric vehicles and solar and wind power are predicted to offset 64 to 79 per cent of increasing emissions from demand growth through to 2028.

In China, the world’s biggest emitter of CO2, emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9 per cent in 2026 as the country continues to make strides with expanding renewable energy and electric vehicles.

“What’s keeping emissions down is the renewable energy, and the price of oil actually suppresses this even more,” says Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia, UK, who also worked on the report.

“So, that’s encouraging in a way, but it does mean that if the price of oil rebounds to pre-Iran [conflict] levels, most likely the emissions will rebound as well until we have enough further acceleration in renewable energy to really bring the emissions down durably.”
