Cold therapy may be worse than doing nothing for post-exercise recovery

New Scientist November 09, 2026

Plunging into an ice bath after a workout may be worse for your muscle recovery than doing nothing. Cold therapy is a popular intervention after rigorous exercise, like marathons, to relieve soreness and dampen the inflammation that can impair muscle recovery. But in a new study, adults who had ice baths after intense leg exercise showed markers of muscle damage for longer than those who just rested.

“Ice baths have long been considered a go-to recovery strategy in sport, so many people might expect them to outperform doing nothing,” says Freya Bayne at the University of East London. But emerging studies suggest that cold therapies slow muscle-protein synthesis by restricting blood flow and reducing the supply of nutrients to the muscles. “The [latest] study contributes to a growing conversation that recovery strategies should be selected based on the desired outcome, rather than assuming one approach works for everything,” she says.

Cold-water swimming has benefits for the brain as well as the body

The use of cold therapy – from ice baths and cold showers to open-water swimming – dates back centuries. Some studies suggest that cold therapy, particularly if it involves open-water swimming, benefits our mental health. But other claims, such as those made by Wim Hof around ice baths improving athletic performance and immune health, lack good scientific evidence.

Advertisement

Focusing on muscle recovery and soreness, Bayne and her colleagues compared cold therapy with other post-exercise interventions.

Forty adults who regularly strength-train had the strength of their quadriceps measured via a machine that also controls movement. While seated, the participants pushed against the machine as hard as possible while it kept their knee in a fixed position. They then performed a high-intensity knee-extension exercise using the same leg. This involved them trying to straighten their knee as much as possible while the machine pushed it back towards a bent position, causing the quadriceps to lengthen.

Free newsletter

Similar movements occur when lowering into a squat or running downhill. These can cause small tears to muscle fibres, which trigger an inflammatory response and lead to muscle soreness. This discomfort usually kicks in within hours of doing a new or particularly intense workout, peaking between 24 and 72 hours, and fading after a week.

Straight after exercising, the participants’ muscle strength was measured again, revealing a loss of 36 per cent, on average. They were then randomly assigned to one of four recovery strategies: cold-water immersion at 9°C (48°F) for 15 minutes, hot-water immersion at 42°C (108°F) for 30 minutes, hot-air exposure at 30°C (86°F) for 30 minutes, or passive rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. Cold-water immersion is typically a short treatment to reduce the risk of hypothermia, which is why it was offered for just 15 minutes.

After 72 hours, those who simply rested had recovered strength to a similar extent as those in the hot-water and hot-air groups, with all three groups regaining around 89 per cent of their maximum muscle strength. The cold-water group recovered about 82 per cent of their maximum strength.

Less than 4 minutes of vigorous exercise a day could halve your dementia risk

Self-reported pain and muscle soreness significantly increased in all groups at 24 hours after exercise, with none of the groups reporting a significant reduction by 72 hours. The cold-water group did report less pain at 24 hours relative to the other groups, but this had increased by 48 hours, suggesting the cold-water therapy had only temporarily masked pain.

Blood samples showed that levels of creatine kinase-MM, an enzyme in skeletal muscle cells that enters the bloodstream when muscles are damaged, returned to normal levels faster in the hot-water group than in the control and hot-air groups. In the cold-water group, levels remained 25 per cent above normal, even after 72 hours.

It is possible that changes to the interventions, such as repeating them or applying heat or cold therapies more locally to the affected area, would also change the results, says Bayne.

There are huge benefits to ringing the changes when it comes to exercise, finds committed runner Grace Wade when she analyses the science

Ken Nosaka at Edith Cowan University in Western Australia says that much of the evidence supporting cold therapies is anecdotal. “It is interesting that the authors found that none of the thermal recovery strategies were effective in alleviating pain and muscle soreness, but importantly none of them had negative effects,” he adds.

But it remains to be seen whether each recovery strategy has longer-term benefits, or whether different types of exercise would have different outcomes. “Athletes and recreational exercisers experience muscle fatigue and recovery demands in many different contexts,” says Bayne.

Mike Tipton at the University of Portsmouth, UK, says the findings shouldn’t stop athletes using ice baths altogether. “[It] may assist with repeated bouts of continuous activity in the heat as well as blunt perceived muscle soreness and fatigue during multi-day events where rapid recovery is required,” he says.

Cold-water exposure can be dangerous due to risks of cold-water shock and hypothermia. Swimming in water below 15˚C (59˚F) should always be done with a partner, a float, a bright hat and a full understanding of the potential risks and how to mitigate them. For more on water safety for cold-water swimming, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution has resources available.

A true paleo diet would include a lot more insects

New Scientist November 09, 2026

There is a cliché in journalism where you say that something or other “is having a moment”. In 2024, Sabrina Carpenter released Espresso and suddenly she was having a moment. Right now, the cast of Celebrity Traitors are all having a collective moment.

For much of the 21st century, entomophagy – the eating of insects – has been having a moment. The first edible insect farm opened in the US in 2014, and many have followed its example. Insects are high in protein and there is evidence that farming them produces fewer greenhouse gases than conventional meats (alongside other environmental benefits). Magazines like New Scientist have run countless stories about edible insects. Insect-based food companies have launched to enormous buzz (sorry, not sorry).

Yet entomophagy hasn’t really taken off (again, not sorry). While edible insects are commonplace in many cultures, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, nowadays they are falling out of favour. In Europe and the US, they have long been viewed with disgust.

Advertisement

The overlooked power of diet for improving your mental health

Western culture reflects this. Try to think of an example of a fictional character eating insects. Did your mind instantly go to the vampire’s familiar Renfield in Dracula, endlessly chowing down on creepy-crawlies while also serving his evil master? Or maybe the, er, let’s go with “problematic” dinner sequence in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom?

The thing is, this cultural belief that insects are gross is just that: cultural. There are insects you absolutely shouldn’t eat because they carry diseases or are poisonous, but many others are safe and nutritious. As I said, plenty of societies use insects as food.

How far back does this practice extend? When we talk about prehistoric foods, we often focus on large mammals like deer or mammoths, or cereals like wheat and barley, or – if you go back a few million years – grasses and sedges. We don’t often talk about Neanderthals or Homo erectus munching on crickets. But maybe we should.

Our evidence about prehistoric entomophagy is partial and scattered. That is partly because archaeologists haven’t often actively searched for it, says Lisa-Marie Shillito, an archaeologist at Durham University in the UK. “We don’t always recognise things that we’re not looking for,” she says. Insect remains are often found on archaeological sites, but often “people just assume it’s contamination or pests”.

Some of the best evidence comes from fossilised human faeces, known as coprolites, which can contain bits of insect exoskeleton and other traces. Unfortunately, “they’re not routinely collected in the same way that other artefacts are”, says Shillito. “They can be surprisingly hard to recognise” and may be mistaken for lumps of clay. Only a handful of researchers specialise in coprolites, including Shillito. “I’m kind of known, I guess, as being the expert in ancient poo.”

Shillito has now brought together a lot of evidence about insect-eating in prehistory in a synthesis paper published in World Archaeology on 27 October.

The first thing to note, Shillito says, is the practice is “really geographically widespread”. Some of the best evidence comes from the Americas, where coprolites have been more routinely studied. Shillito highlights Paisley caves in Oregon, which has evidence of human presence from around 14,300 years ago: one of the oldest such sites in the Americas. In 2020, she and her colleagues studied coprolites from the caves and found evidence that people were eating, among other things, insects.

Specifically, “big juicy ones”, says Shillito. These included ten-lined June beetles (Polyphylla decemlineata), which grow to almost 3 centimetres in length. The team also found the remains of Jerusalem crickets, which is an inaptly named group since they aren’t crickets and don’t come from Jerusalem. They are related to the oversized wētā insects of New Zealand, albeit not quite as large. “If you’re hunting and gathering, they’re quite meaty-looking things that you might just pick up and eat,” says Shillito.

A more subtle piece of evidence comes from the Bonneville Estates Rockshelter in Nevada. A coprolite from this site contained the eggs of parasitic worms called acanthocephalans. These parasites use insects and other arthropods as intermediate hosts – so the person who was infected may well have eaten insects.

On the other side of the world, at Cloggs cave in Australia, researchers have found evidence of Aboriginal Australians eating bogong moths (Agrotis infusa). These moths migrate in huge numbers every year, and it seems the Indigenous peoples took advantage of this. A grindstone from the site had the remains of ground and cooked bogong moths from about 2000 years ago.

There is also evidence that people were using bees as a food source thousands of years ago. In Nigeria around 3500 years ago, farmers and foragers lived alongside each other. A 2021 study of pottery vessels from the Nok culture found that many of them had telltale lipids. This reveals the people were eating honey or other items from beehives, perhaps including bee larvae. Likewise, in Egypt there are pottery vessels with traces of beeswax from at least 8000 years ago.

So far, all these examples have been from the relatively recent past: the last 20,000 years. But our species has been around for 300,000 years, at least, and human evolution spans 7 million years or more. Were our more distant ancestors eating insects too?

The first thing to say is that non-human primates, which are our closest living relatives, absolutely eat insects. A 2012 review found it was a common behaviour and that non-human primates tended to go for insects with a high protein-to-fat ratio – suggesting that insects are a significant source of protein for them. This hints, though of course doesn’t prove, that the most recent ancestor we share with apes also ate insects.

There is some evidence that this behaviour was carried through. In studies published in 2001 and 2008, two researchers – Lucinda Backwell at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa and Francesco d’Errico at the University of Bordeaux in France – described bone tools found at sites in South Africa. They argued that the pattern of wear on the bones was consistent with digging into termite mounds. The tools are over 1 million years old and may have been used by Paranthropus, extinct hominins related to our genus, Homo.

Likewise, in a 2014 study in the Journal of Human Evolution, researchers compiled isotopic data from early Homo specimens, and from older Australopithecus. The mix of carbon isotopes found in the remains gives us a broad-strokes picture of what the hominins ate. It seems they were eating at least some animal material, and at least some of that may have been insects.

Some readers may also remember an intriguing study published in 2025. It re-examined isotopic data from the bones of Neanderthals. Because living organisms tend to accumulate the heavy isotope nitrogen-15, and lose the lighter one nitrogen-14, organisms higher up the food chain tend to have more nitrogen-15 than those at the bottom. Neanderthals have sky-high levels of nitrogen-15.

We have an unprecedented choice of food, yet our diets are worse than ever, says palaeoanthropologist Daniel Lieberman. So what can evolution tell us about how to eat better?

One interpretation is that Neanderthals ate meat and little else: you could conclude they were “hyper-carnivores”. However, this doesn’t make a lot of sense, partly because eating just meat is dangerously unhealthy, and partly because there is plenty of evidence from other sources that Neanderthals had varied diets. So instead, researchers have suggested that Neanderthals sometimes ate the maggots that were feasting on rotting meat.

One of the authors of that study is Julie Lesnik at Wayne State University in Detroit, Michigan. In her 2019 book Edible Insects and Human Evolution, Lesnik argues that insects are both abundant and relatively low risk, making them an ideal food source. She suggests that mothers could have safely gathered insects while also carrying their babies. Of course, that assumes women weren’t hunting large animals alongside the men, an assumption that looks decidedly shaky – but that aside, it seems a reasonable hypothesis.

Nevertheless, there is a huge amount we still don’t know about insects in prehistoric diets. “How important were they?” asks Shillito. “How did that change over time, and why, in different parts of the world?”

Insects were probably seasonal foods in many places, Shillito suggests. “They’re not around all the time.” This may help to explain why it is tricky to find hard evidence of entomophagy in the archaeological record. “We’ve got this tantalising evidence,” says Shillito. Now, she wants to look more systematically.

The obvious takeaway from all this is that everybody banging on about the so-called paleo diet needs to rethink. Less red meat, more grasshoppers and beetles. It’s (probably) what our ancestors did!

Your body changes as you age and so should your diet – here’s how

Finally, let’s go back to where we started. In the past 20 years there has been a lot of coverage of the environmental and food-security benefits of eating insects. Yet, insect products aren’t supermarket staples, at least not where I live. If the wheel is turning, it’s only turning slowly.

That leads me to a book chapter by the entomologist Friedrich Simon Bodenheimer. He begins: “It has been known for many centuries that insects are eaten as delicacies in many parts of the world. Reports have come down from antiquity of insects, especially locusts, being eaten by primitive peoples. Honey has been known as a prized food from time immemorial. Yet entomophagy, apart from honey consumption, has always been regarded as a curiosity or as barbarism.”

Bodenheimer goes on to say that he began examining the subject “largely out of curiosity”, only to be taken aback by the sheer scale of entomophagy. “It is actually astonishing that the real and basic importance of insects as food for early and primitive man has been so long ignored.”

Savvy readers may have twigged from archaic terms like “barbarism” and “primitive man” what the punchline is going to be. Yes, this chapter is old: Bodenheimer published it in 1951.

We keep rediscovering the fact that humans have routinely eaten insects, and we keep being surprised by it. At some point, we should stop being surprised.

Embark on a captivating journey through time across southern France, from Bordeaux to Montpellier, exploring key Neanderthal and Upper Palaeolithic caves and sites accompanied by experts in ancient humans.

X chromosome gene may reduce autism rates in women and girls

New Scientist November 09, 2026

A single gene on the X chromosome may help explain why autism is less common in women and girls. The gene, ZFX, has powerful effects on a set of genes that contribute to the risk of autism, and is expressed more in women than in men.

“It’s about the fact that ZFX has a relationship with these other autism-associated genes,” says Rebecca Andersen, a neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts. This one gene can keep other genes turned on when they might otherwise be deactivated, she says, reducing the chances that girls will develop autism.

Autism is a developmental condition. Autistic people have a variety of traits that can include difficulties with socialising and communicating, unusually high sensory sensitivity that can cause them to become overwhelmed, and restricted behaviours and interests.

Advertisement

A revolutionary new understanding of autism in girls

Many studies have found that autism is more common in males than in females: up to four times as common. “That specific number is contested,” says Andersen, partly because we now know that autism presents differently in females, including subtler effects on socialising. Furthermore, women and girls with autism often “mask” or “camouflage” their autistic traits, enabling them to pass as neurotypical at the cost of their mental health. This means females often go undiagnosed, or are diagnosed later in life, skewing the figures.

Nevertheless, many autism researchers believe there is a “female protective effect”: something about being female makes people less likely to be autistic. Notably, women diagnosed with autism tend to have more autism-linked mutations than men diagnosed with autism. This suggests there is a requirement for a “greater genetic load in females in order to manifest with autism at all, or to manifest to a degree that would be diagnosed”, says Andersen.

Understanding this requires understanding the genetics of autism. “We’ve long known that there’s a very strong genetic component to autism,” says Andersen. “There have been a lot of large-scale sequencing studies that have identified hundreds of different genes that are implicated in autism,” she says. “It’s been really perplexing to understand how so many different genes could all be relevant for autism.”

Free newsletter

To figure out how these genes work together, Andersen and her colleagues grew neural progenitor cells – which develop into neurons – in culture. They then targeted each of 20 genes, all known to be associated with autism. Rather than deleting or mutating the genes, they used a version of the CRISPR gene-editing technology to break down the RNA produced when the genes were expressed. Reduced expression of these genes is thought to increase the chances of developing autism. “We could target the RNA for degradation and have very rapid changes in expression levels of those genes,” says Andersen.

To their surprise, the researchers found that reducing the expression of any one of these genes tended to also significantly reduce the expression of most of the others. “Across almost all of our perturbations, they just looked very similar to one another, and in particular, how much they affected the other autism-associated genes,” says Andersen. “It seemed to make sense that they would have to converge in some way, in order to be related to autism, but we didn’t necessarily expect to find such a strong degree of convergence.”

What if the idea of the autism spectrum is completely wrong?

The researchers then built a model of the interactions between the genes. This enabled them to identify a core of 70 genes, all of which strongly regulate the 20 autism-associated genes, and also regulate each other. Andersen calls these genes the “central hub”.

“This provides strong evidence that apparently distinct genetic causes of autism may converge on common pathways,” says Louise Gallagher at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Having identified these core genes, the team then identified a set of 82 genes that were expressed less when the autism-related genes were suppressed, and which are known to be more heavily expressed in female brains compared with male. This led the researchers to ZFX, which is found on the X chromosome. Females have two X chromosomes, but males have one X and a smaller Y chromosome. This means females have two copies of ZFX – and unusually for genes on the X chromosomes, both copies are expressed.

Simon Baron-Cohen’s influential research helped pin autism as a particularly male condition. As studies increasingly broaden our view of autism, has his perspective changed?

“We found that ZFX was very related to many of these different autism-associated genes,” says Andersen. This means ZFX could act as a buffer. A girl could have a lot of mutations that reduce the expression of autism-associated genes and thus increase her probability of autism – only for the ZFX to increase the expression of those genes and reduce her chances of autism.

“That’s very interesting and biologically plausible,” says Gallagher. However, the claim rests on the team’s model of the interactions between the genes. “The paper doesn’t show that increasing ZFX expression rescues the consequences of the variants.” That would require additional experiments.

“It’s also unlikely that something as complex as the female protective effect will be attributable to a single gene,” says Gallagher. “It could be related to other sex-linked genetic mechanisms, hormonal influences and broader differences in developmental biology.”

Wool levy: Sheep farmers to vote on proposal early next year

New Zealand Herald November 10, 2026

Farmers once paid a wool levy, and there are hopes it can be reinstated. Photo / Alan Gibson

By Penny Miles of RNZ

Sheep farmers will vote early next year on a proposed wool levy to invest in work that grows demand and value for New Zealand’s wool clip.

Beef and Lamb NZ (B+LNZ) and a new group, the New Zealand Wool Collective, made the announcement, with work now underway to encourage farmers to vote in favour.

Additional funds from industry and government would also be sought for specific projects.

“It varies by scale; the amount we’re looking at is 2-3 cents per kilogram,” Ross McIsaac, chief executive of New Zealand Wool Collective, said.

“It’s hard to define an average farm, but for a farm that maybe has 2000 sheep and produces about 10 tonnes of wool, you’re looking at about $200 to $300 per year.”

The Wool Collective was formed in a merger earlier this year, taking over from the Campaign for Wool NZ and Wool Impact.

“It builds on the consolidation of the work being done by Wool Impact and Campaign for Wool NZ and the innovation and investment being made by individual wool businesses across the sector,” McIsaac said.

“Momentum behind wool is evident in price lifts, brand activity and consumer interest.

“That momentum needs to be sustained and built on.

“We’ve worked with commercial wool businesses, with input from growers and brands using wool, to refine a programme of work that addresses foundational sector needs that underpin demand, while leaving commercial activity to individual businesses.

“This is the work that no one business or grower can do alone.”

Farmers paid a wool levy for many years to promote the sector, build markets and fund research and development.

But in 2003, wool growers voted the NZ Wool Board out, ending the levy, and since then, attempts at reinstatement have failed.

“Being part of B+LNZ would allow us to deliver dedicated wool work in a cost-effective way without doubling up on administration and overheads,” he said.

“It’s about securing the long-term financial backing needed to realise greater value for growers, industry participants and the wider wool sector.”

B+LNZ chairwoman Kate Acland said the levy proposal was a positive step forward to build profitability for sheep farmers.

“As a sheep farmer, keeping the wool part of our businesses profitable will be a critical part of our ongoing financial sustainability.

“Although values have increased recently, there are some great opportunities to do more.

“Collective investment in key areas will help grow and sustain stronger wool prices at the farmgate.

“With funding for New Zealand Wool Collective coming to an end in late 2027, a grower levy will be essential to continue building on the work that is underway.

“It would also fund wool-specific activities behind the farm gate, ensuring wool is considered as part of the whole-farm system.

“Bringing wool-focused work into B+LNZ is a positive and practical step - it provides the most cost-effective way to undertake this work.”

Money collected would be invested across both the strong and fine wool sectors.

If approved, the wool levy would likely start to be collected in December 2027 or early 2028.

PGG Wrightson national auction manager Dave Burridge said since the levy was done away with, there had been 25 years of poor returns for wool growers.

“It’s the old saying of, you do nothing, you’ll get nothing.”

Industry good practices had declined – with less resourcing for shearing and woolhandling training – and promotional spending was below what was needed to compete with synthetic fibres, he said.

He was pleased to see a levy proposal put back on the table.

“If growers were to get in behind, and industry, to put a fund together that all contribute, not just some but everyone’s contributing, I think we’ll get some real go forward.”

Brown said he had only nice things to say about Weenink, telling Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast she had been a tireless doorknocker during the campaign so would have heard a range of views.

“People are brutally honest at the doorstep.”

He said it was a “sad day” when the Opposition leader was claiming conspiracy theories around the campaign to split votes on the right, pointing out Prime Minister Christopher Luxon had urged people to give National both votes.

Did New Zealand just witness a first-past-the-post election under MMP?

There was a time when elections were determined by results in a handful of marginal electorates. Since the introduction of MMP in 1996, however, overall voter support for individual parties has been the deciding factor.

This year, the old days seem to have returned. The outcome could well hinge on a small number of close-run seats – just like pre-proportional elections used to.

Put aside any questions about who will hold the balance of power when final results are announced on November 27.

Deeper down, the tectonic plates of New Zealand politics are drifting.

The next Parliament is going to be the largest in history. While it generally numbers between 120 and 123 MPs, the overhangs created on the left and right are so large it could have as many as 131.

This will be the sixth overhang since MMP was adopted, but two things set this one apart: its size and its impact.

The discrepancy between the parties’ share of the vote and their share of all parliamentary seats will be distorted. That means it will affect the formation of the next Government.

Rotorua designer Kharl WiRepa’s jail sentence reduced by eight months on appeal

New Zealand Herald November 10, 2026

Kharl WiRepa appears in the Rotorua District Court for sentencing after admitting he ripped off Miss Rotorua pageant contestants who had raised money for charity. Photo / Kelly Makiha

Rotorua fashion designer Kharl WiRepa has had his three-year jail sentence reduced by eight months on appeal.

WiRepa was jailed in August after admitting he ripped off Miss Rotorua beauty pageant contestants who raised money for charity. WiRepa, who ran the pageant, instead spent the money on himself.

He also admitted other dishonesty charges, including running into Farmers wearing a Spider-Man mask and gloves, with plastic bags on his feet, and filling a bag with fragrance packs valued between $500 and $5000.

The fraud charges involved spending nearly $10,000 given to him by others. More than $6300 was from nine Miss Rotorua contestants who had raised money for charities and $3200 was from a person who thought WiRepa was booking him a trip to attend London Fashion Week.

WiRepa spent the money on himself or made cash withdrawals.

At sentencing in the Rotorua District Court, WiRepa was described in a pre-sentencing report as “self-centred” and someone who blamed others when things went wrong.

The former reality television star, who was the main character in the show Gowns and Geysers, appealed on the grounds that three years’ jail was “manifestly excessive”.

Justice Laura O’Gorman agreed with WiRepa’s lawyer, Douglas Hall, that the sentencing starting point set by Judge Thomas Ingram was too high.

She also agreed WiRepa should have been given more reductions for addressing his methamphetamine addiction.

Justice O’Gorman separated WiRepa’s “crime spree” into two sections of offending.

She described the first as “deceptive dishonesty” involving two fraud charges – the offending against Miss Rotorua contestants and ripping off the would-be fashion week traveller.

The other three charges were described as “physical dishonesty” and involved shoplifting $767.75 worth of food and alcohol from Woolworths and two burglary charges relating to a Tutanekai St building and Farmers Rotorua.

The two fraud charges relate to offending in 2024 while the other three charges were for incidents between December 2024 and January 2025.

At sentencing, Judge Ingram gave each set of offending a starting point of two and a half years, taking the overall starting point to five years’ jail.

She gave a reduction of 20% (or one year off) for WiRepa’s guilty plea and a further 20% for a legal term called “totality”, which took all matters into account. The end sentence was three years, made up of two 18-month cumulative sentences.

Hall told the High Court at the November 2 appeal hearing that Judge Ingram’s starting point of five years was too high.

Hall argued the starting point for the physical dishonesty should have been 23 months and a 10-month uplift should have been given, allowing for totality.

Hall argued even the police asked for a starting point at sentencing lower than what Judge Ingram adopted.

Hall tried to get the sentence reduced by five to six months more based on WiRepa spending 13 months on electronically monitored bail. He also asked the High Court to acknowledge WiRepa’s rehabilitation work.

A letter from Mana Enhancing Stop Charitable Trust dated June this year outlined therapy sessions WiRepa attended before he went to jail.

WiRepa told Justice O’Gorman he had abstained from drugs since January 14, 2025.

Justice O’Gorman agreed with the Crown’s lawyer, Briana Cardon, that no discounts could be given for his time spent on electronically monitored bail because he breached it several times.

These were listed in the appeal decision. They included him being caught absent from his address on February 13, 2025 – two days after being granted electronically monitored bail. He was arrested the next day and held in custody.

He was granted electronically monitored bail again on May 9 but deviated on an approved absence on May 27.

He was readmitted to electronically monitored bail the next day. He deviated and misused an approved absence on January 24 and was caught on an “unapproved absence” on February 8 and remanded in custody.

He was granted electronically monitored bail on March 9 and was compliant until August 18 when he was sentenced.

Cardon argued WiRepa could have been given an uplift of three months for his prior dishonesty offending but wasn’t.

His prior offending included 18 fraud-related convictions for benefit fraud between 2013 and 2016 when he claimed nearly $12,000 he wasn’t entitled to.

Justice O’Gorman disagreed with Judge Ingram’s approach and instead sentenced WiRepa on all dishonesty offending, saying it was part of a “spree”.

She referred to a sentencing report that said WiRepa was “feeling that his life was spiralling out of control when he was living a chaotic lifestyle fuelled by drug use, antisocial peers, financial hardship and homelessness”.

Justice O’Gorman gave a starting point of 30 months for the physical dishonesty charges, uplifted it by 10 months for the deceptive dishonesty offending (two fraud charges) and maintained the 20% reduction for guilty pleas. She granted WiRepa a further 10% reduction for his rehabilitation efforts.

“In my view, Mr WiRepa deserves credit for his ongoing effort at addressing his drug addiction issues, which I accept have causatively contributed to his offending.”

She didn’t uplift the sentence for his previous fraud convictions because they were more than eight years old, or his offending on bail.

Justice O’Gorman said the end sentence of 28 months’ jail was not in range to offer WiRepa home detention, which reflected the seriousness of his offending.

WiRepa will become eligible for parole after serving a third of his prison sentence.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 30 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Parliamentary Service working on extra chairs and offices for increased number of MPs

New Zealand Herald November 10, 2026

On current numbers, up to 131 MPs could be sitting in the Chamber following the election, brought on by a record overhang result. Photo / RNZ, Diego Opatowski

By Tuwhenuaroa Natanahira of RNZ

The chief executive of the Parliamentary Service is confident there will be enough room to accommodate the increased number of MPs and their staff coming into Parliament.

On current numbers, up to 131 MPs could be sitting in the Chamber following the election, brought on by a record overhang result.

Clerk of the House of Representatives Dr David Wilson told the Spinoff that currently the debating chamber had enough chairs to seat 124 MPs – including the Speaker of the House – and work was being done to accommodate more by altering the seating arrangement.

In a statement, Parliamentary Service chief executive Rafael Gonzalez-Montero said planning for a larger Parliament had been going on for “some time”.

“Now that the election results have confirmed an increase to the number of members we are looking at several options.

“We are confident we will be able to accommodate all members within the Chamber.”

Gonzalez-Montero said office accommodation for members and their staff would be “stretched” for a short time, but the new Members’ Building was only a few months away from “practical completion”.

That building – located behind Parliament – was due to be ready to occupy next April and had capacity to accommodate about 30 backbench MPs.

“All members should be in fit-for-purpose accommodation from that point,” Gonzalez-Montero said.

Following the 2023 election, 123 MPs sat in the Chamber – a record number at the time. That decreased to 122 following the resignation of National MP Judith Collins.

Collins held the seat of Papakura and stepped down in May and Parliament voted against holding a byelection because it was too close to the election.

The election result also meant high-ranking National Party MPs such as Chris Bishop, Paul Goldsmith, Nicola Willis and Gerry Brownlee – Speaker of the House and an MP for 30 years – would likely not make it back into Parliament.

Only resigning or retiring MPs were permitted to give a valedictory speech, meaning none of them would get the chance to give a valedictory statement.

Asked if there would be special allowances for valedictories, Wilson said in a statement that normally only MPs were allowed to speak in the House, but the House could suspend its own rules or temporarily alter them.

“It could do so to allow former members to address the House.”

Wilson said no such arrangements could be made until the next Parliament opened and members sworn in.

– RNZ

Nearly 2000 patients spent more than 12 hours at Christchurch Hospital’s Emergency Department (ED) in the first six months of 2026, a nearly 70% increase on the same period last year.

Figures released to the Herald under the Official Information Act (OIA) show 1997 patients remained in ED for more than 12 hours between January and June, compared with 1178 in 2025.

Health New Zealand said Christchurch Hospital faced sustained high occupancy, increasingly complex patient needs and pressure on inpatient services, despite a slight drop in ED presentations.

For Christchurch resident Laura Xavier, the reality of a lengthy ED stay became clear when her husband suffered a serious injury recently.

Marcello Giuseppe was working in gardening when his finger became caught in a lawnmower, leaving a deep cut reaching the bone and a fracture.

He drove himself to Christchurch Hospital before 11am, with his clothing covered in blood.

Xavier, who was four months pregnant at the time, left work to join him.

She said her husband was assessed quickly by a triage nurse, but the subsequent wait and treatment took more than 13 hours.

Nurses cleaned and dressed the wound and administered a tetanus vaccination, but an X-ray was not completed until about 4pm.

An emergency doctor treated the injury and stitched his finger about 6pm.

“He was initially listed in a serious condition,” Xavier said.

“You would think he would have been prioritised.”

About 7pm, Giuseppe believed he was ready to go home but was told he needed to be assessed by an orthopaedic specialist.

“From about 7pm until after midnight, we just sat there in the hospital, doing nothing, waiting for the orthopaedic specialist to come and see him,” Xavier said.

She described the department as “extremely crowded” earlier in the day, with patients on stretchers and in wheelchairs waiting in corridors.

“There was hardly anywhere to sit.”

Xavier said that when the specialist arrived, her husband’s medical records could not be found, and a new record had to be created.

Giuseppe was admitted overnight for further assessment by an orthopaedic surgeon the next morning.

He was discharged the next day without needing another procedure.

Xavier described the experience as “frustrating”, particularly the delays and what she considered poor communication between staff.

“Despite that, the nurses who looked after us were all fantastic,” she said.

The experience left her concerned about needing emergency care again, particularly now that she has a baby.

“Children can deteriorate very quickly when they’re sick,” she said.

“If I had a sick child and it took me as long to get help as it took my husband, I’d be screwed. The child could die in my arms.”

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

The OIA figures show the number of patients spending more than six hours in Christchurch Hospital ED rose 24%, from 13,585 in the first half of 2025 to 16,847 in the same period this year.

That increase came despite overall ED presentations falling slightly, from 72,092 to 71,134.

June recorded the highest monthly figure for stays exceeding 12 hours so far this year, with 569 patients, compared with 302 in June last year.

The number of patients who left before being seen by a clinician also increased, from 899 to 1076.

The data, covering January 2023 to June 2026, show prolonged stays were also common in earlier years, with 2217 patients spending more than 12 hours in ED during the first half of 2024.

Health NZ acting group director operations for Canterbury Rebecca Hickmott said Christchurch Hospital had faced sustained high occupancy, increasingly complex patient needs and ongoing demand for inpatient services.

“Emergency departments are dynamic environments, with pressure changing from hour to hour,” she said.

Hickmott acknowledged presentations were lower in the first six months of 2026 compared with the same period last year.

“ED presentation numbers are only one factor affecting how long patients spend in ED,” she said.

Hickmott said the hospital had faced an unprecedented winter surge in influenza and other respiratory illnesses, adding further pressure to emergency and inpatient services.

To manage demand, Health NZ introduced 24 additional flex beds, extra evening and weekend urgent care clinics at three Christchurch general practices, 750 additional urgent care telehealth vouchers and more medical staff for evening shifts at Christchurch Children’s Emergency Care.

Hickmott said about 76% of Christchurch Hospital ED presentations were completed within six hours during the first half of 2026.

The Government’s target is for 95% of ED patients to be admitted, discharged or transferred within six hours by 2030.

Apology over cult conference and church convention clash

New Zealand Herald November 10, 2026

Christchurch Town Hall management has apologised to anti-cult conference organisers. Photo / RNZ, Nate McKinnon

By Jean Edwards of RNZ

Christchurch Town Hall management has apologised to anti-cult conference organisers for failing to disclose during the booking process that an evangelical church was holding a convention in the building at the same time.

The Decult conference, held over Labour Weekend, was aimed at improving support services for cult leavers and raising public awareness about the physical, psychological and spiritual harm caused by coercive high-control groups.

Revival Centres Church members from Australia and New Zealand also came together for a “weekend of encouragement” on the theme “The Joy Set Before Us”.

Revival Centres is a strict Pentecostal church founded in Melbourne with assemblies across New Zealand and globally, although some former members have described it as a “doomsday cult” founded on abuse.

A New Zealand Revival Centres spokesperson rejected any suggestion the church was a cult.

Decult trustee and MC Mark Darbyshire, who left a Revival Fellowship 10 years ago, said it was a bizarre coincidence that was confronting for some conference attendees.

“I couldn’t believe it, partly because it seems like I can never quite escape this Revival movement – it’s still always around me – and partly as a trustee of Decult I was concerned about the experience of our attendees and the religious trauma that might be triggered by seeing an evangelical group there.

“It was a bit of a shock for me to realise that the group I was born into, which I consider to be a cult, was actually going to be downstairs.

“Hearing worship songs and speaking in tongues can be really triggering when you’ve been impacted by fundamentalist Pentecostal Christianity.”

Former Geelong Revival Centre member Ryan Carey sat on a Decult panel in the Limes Room as the church group met downstairs in the Avon Room.

Livestream footage of the Revival Centres convention showed a song leader suggesting attendees sing louder.

“Apparently we’ve had a few complaints upstairs with the noise, let’s just ratchet it up a bit more,” the man said.

Melbourne-based principal pastor Simon Longfield later joked about someone being kicked out of the church, saying “This is good deculting, isn’t it?”.

Dunedin Revival Centres Church pastor Graeme McKinstry said he discovered the Decult conference was being held at the Town Hall after reading an RNZ story days before the convention.

“We weren’t concerned by them, they were concerned by us.

“We don’t see ourselves as a cult. Allegations are easy to make. I’ve no doubt that some people would take offence to some of the things we believe, that’s true of anything. We don’t control people’s lives.

“I’ve been a pastor for many, many years. If I felt there was anything untoward, I certainly wouldn’t be involved in it.”

McKinstry said his church had not been connected to the Geelong Revival Centre for more than 50 years.

“We would see them as very autocratic and authoritarian. The only similarity is that we share a similar name.

“Some people are determined to draw connections that frankly don’t exist.”

Decult organisers said Venues Ōtautahi advised them early in the planning process that another group was hosting an event at the Town Hall but they were not told who it was until the day before the conference, leaving little time for risk mitigation.

Decult director Anke Richter said organisers had a duty of care to inform guests about the Revival Centres gathering, given a speaker, trustee and some attendees had experienced harm associated with the church.

She said they were not suggesting Venues Ōtautahi should have refused the Revival booking but a failure to disclose the information when requested meant they did not have time to consider additional safeguards.

“Our primary concern is that we were not given critical information despite repeatedly asking Venues Ōtautahi for it. Safety and wellbeing are fundamental to a trauma-informed event and being told only 16 hours before opening left us with little time to prepare for that.

“It was our duty of care to inform our guests, reassure them and apply appropriate measures. For some cult survivors, hearing worship songs can be deeply distressing and triggering. Some attendees chose not to come because of this.

“We are not questioning the other group’s right to be there, we are questioning the lack of transparency and communication that prevented us from properly supporting our attendees.”

Venues Ōtautahi chief executive Caroline Harvie-Teare confirmed that staff did not detail the type of event being held at the same time as the Decult conference, despite organisers asking for information “some time ago”.

“That’s on us. That is an error. If we had taken the time to actually dig into the event types – and while I can’t talk to the conflicting perspectives of those events – we should have identified that risk and acknowledged that for our client,” she said.

“We have apologised to them for that oversight. Obviously it’s not good enough, there are sensitivities associated with those events and the people attending them. I can appreciate and understand why they were frustrated and, more so, upset for those who were negatively affected.”

While there was security and wristbands for event attendees, Harvie-Teare said Venues Ōtautahi would better assess event management risks and share broad information about bookings in future.

Just the word “Fatherland”, with its three staccato syllables, has the rattle of sabres behind it. “I don’t have a strong connection to the word fatherland. I would probably rather say ‘motherland’,” says German actor Sandra Huller. “But these words are quite stained where we live. You can’t use them. They are not innocent any more. Although I think, for the film, ‘fatherland’ has a double meaning.”

Fatherland is the name given by Polish filmmaker Pawel Pawlikowski to his concise, complex and utterly compelling film about a postwar journey taken by Thomas Mann, the great German novelist who won the Nobel Prize for literature in 1929, around a newly divided Germany. In Frankfurt, Mann will receive an award commemorating Goethe’s 200th birthday; on the other side of the line that will soon be a wall, he will visit Weimar.

With him is his middle-aged daughter Erika (Huller) – journalist, cabaret entrepreneur, rally driver and a bold and brilliant character in her own right – who acts as her father’s assistant. This is the double meaning Huller has observed: Erika is living in her own private fatherland, the habitat of the great man of letters.

Hanns Zischler plays Thomas Mann, whom both sides of Germany want to claim as their own, with the weary dignity of a man on an obligatory civilising mission. Mann and his wife left for the United States in 1933, where Thomas was offered citizenship and the questionable comforts of exile. Erika later joined them.

When we meet them, Thomas has lived in California for 16 years. “They don’t know where their home actually is any more,” says Huller, whose performance has generated glowing reviews and Oscars buzz (her previous best actress nomination was for 2023’s Anatomy of a Fall). “And that doesn’t only mean the place where you live, but it means the language that you’re using. It has been abused by a fascist regime. It can’t be understood the way it was understood before.”

Pawlikowski is Polish; his previous film, Cold War (2018), was also set in this peculiar period of flux, but in his home country. He came across the story of the Mann tour when a publisher sent him a new biography of the author, suggesting he could turn it into a biopic.

“I didn’t want to,” says Pawlikowski emphatically. “But in that biography, I discovered this moment in 1949, where he came back to Germany. He was trying to be bigger than the situation and to fight and argue for a ‘good Germany’, which he hoped could be resurrected. Instead, he was being forced to choose between communism – which was Stalinism at that time – and American capitalism.”

Pawlikowski didn’t want to stick with the facts. The real journey itself took months, while he compresses it into five days. Erika wasn’t really there; Mann went to Germany with his wife, Katia. “I was very imprecise, let’s say,” Pawlikowski says. “We took huge liberties with what happened when.” News reaches the Manns of family members who are ill or dying, events that really happened in other years altogether.

“I wanted to combine the kind of intimate family story – very focused, very narrow, claustrophobic in a way – with a big historical vista. That was one interesting thing. How do you bring these two things together? And that led to all sorts of formal solutions as well.”

2:04

Fatherland: Official trailer

Sandra Huller in Fatherland. The film that navigates a 'stained' German history

Those solutions include Lukasz Zal’s luminous black and white photography, which evokes the period; his use of the square aspect ratio, which makes every scene feel confined, and a frequently static camera trained on those square sets, suggesting nothing so much as a series of dioramas showing how things were in postwar Germany. “It helps me to limit what we see and to force people to look very precisely in a certain place and the details that are there,” Pawlikowski says. “Not to show everything, but using out-of-frame sounds and context so people fill in the space that is not shown.”

On tour, Erika proves an ideal helpmeet. She filters the poison pen letters from the mail at the hotel, makes tea, battles border guards at each checkpoint and drives the car. She also fends off the fans. “Erika has been chosen as the favourite child, which is not always a good thing,” says Huller. “It means you don’t want to lose this position, so you have to do a little work to stay connected.” Her louche brother, Klaus (August Diehl), craves his father’s love in vain.

Erika Mann was a famous adventurer; she is still well-known in Germany. “There were some discussions around this movie where people were asking me if she was losing her freedom in deciding to follow her father, but I don’t think so,” says Huller. “I think it was a very deliberate decision. She had such a rich life, she could do whatever she wanted.”

Reading the letters they sent to each other, she says, revealed to her the strength of their bond. “They had a way of talking that I admire very much, because they wouldn’t lie to each other regarding their opinions. They don’t hold back with critique, don’t shy away from conflict. And at the same time, they would forgive each other everything.”

Overall, the family was a tangled web. After his death, Mann’s diaries revealed his lifelong attraction to men. Erika was gay but married twice; her first husband, Gustaf Gründgens (Joachim Meyerhoff), was an actor who toadied to Hitler’s right-hand man, Hermann Göring, and thus thrived under the Nazis, while her second was her lifelong friend W. H. Auden, the English poet, who married her so she could stay in Britain.

Klaus and Erika, meanwhile, were so devoted they described themselves as twins. Klaus was an aspiring writer, which set him on a collision course with his father; he also had a serious drug habit. His best-known work is the novel Mephisto, which was banned in Germany because it centred on an actor – clearly based on his sister’s husband – who became the Nazis’ patsy. “It’s also about jealousy,” says Diehl.

Diehl sees Thomas Mann as representative of the end of an old German culture. “The culture that was destroyed by the war, before Germany was aware of being the most evil nation in the world. It’s hard for us to imagine.” If he really tries, he says, he feels his use of the language change gears. “There was a different way of talking. When you read letters from before the war, just from normal people, they’re close to literature. And the war destroyed that language.”

He used to love Klaus Mann’s writing as a teenager, he says, but now he sees the seeds of that destroyed language in the way he wrote, “although you feel he’s doing that on purpose, to be different from his father”. Choosing to be a writer when his father was such a giant, he says, was choosing to have a complicated life. “He was destroyed by family, but also by the war. By what happened to Germany. He’s a writer who hates his mother tongue, so he’s screwed.”

But all of culture was poisoned, it seems. There is a gimlet-sharp scene in Fatherland where Wagner’s grandsons urge Mann – who loved Wagner’s music – to lend his public support to the reconstruction of the Bayreuth opera house. “It should be razed to the ground,” he snaps back. Even outdoor pursuits like mountaineering were tarnished. “We can’t even look at the Alps any more!” says Diehl. “It is crazy what a movement like National Socialism destroys, along with its catastrophes. Many, many, many things.” Even Thomas Mann could not recover them.

Fatherland is in cinemas from November 12.

The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counter-terrorism policing investigations.

Israeli opposition hurries to seize control as new Knesset is sworn in

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 19:59:33 GMT

Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has mandate to try to form a government – with Netanyahu waiting if he fails

Opposition lawmakers have wasted no time after Israel’s new Knesset was sworn in, deploying their majority to seize control of the legislature from Benjamin Netanyhau and his allies.

Although they are still too divided to form a government, the opposition requested a vote for a new speaker, who sets the Knesset’s agenda. Once Netanyahu loyalist Amir Ohana has been replaced, the six opposition parties will be able to work on key legislation even if they broker a coalition.

Priorities include setting up a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks and introducing term limits for Israel’s prime ministers, which could block Netanyahu from taking power again. He has ruled Israel for 19 of the last 30 years.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, now has the presidential mandate to try to form a government. If he fails to broker a deal within six weeks, a second candidate – probably Netanyahu – will get a second chance. Further failure is likely to lead to another election.

Netanyahu responded to the swearing in of the new Knesset on Tuesday with a racist attack on two Palestinian-led opposition parties, whose voters were key to unseating his coalition, calling their lawmakers “terror supporters”.

Eisenkot denounced his speech as a “delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful” exploitation of a state occasion, that showed the prime minister was unfit for office.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, and Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish-Israeli former police chief who ran on the slate of Islamist Ra’am party, both walked out of Netanyahu’s speech in protest.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the country’s population. Netanyahu put attacks on these voters and their parties at the heart of his campaign, and since polling day has promoted groundless accusations of fraud in their communities in a bid to undermine results.

Election officials say there was no evidence of irregularities that affected the election outcome or compromised its integrity.

A period of prolonged, difficult coalition negotiations or even a new round of elections would extend Netanyahu’s hold on power as caretaker prime minister. But if the fractured opposition can make progress on key legislation, his grip on the state would be weakened.

Eisenkot’s Yashar party submitted a series of bills to the Knesset moments after the swearing in, with backing from other opposition parties.

In addition to term limits and the 7 October inquiry, legislation includes several bills designed to revoke the “judicial overhaul” pursued by Netanyahu, which weakened the power of Israel’s judiciary and the attorney general.

Ohana has tabled the vote on a new speaker to replace him for next Tuesday, the latest date possible. The opposition have also nominated candidates to take over key defence and finance committees.

Eisenkot has admitted the path to power is “extraordinarily complex”, because of incompatible election promises made by different parties, but described ousting Netanyahu as a national emergency that could require breaking promises.

At the swearing-in ceremony, the president, Isaac Herzog, warned lawmakers they should do everything in their power to avoid a second election.

“Reach out a hand for compromise, even between ⁠rivals … Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability and experience found in every part of this House.“

The Guardian view on David Walliams: allegations about abuse of power and sexual misconduct deserve publication

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 19:20:14 GMT

The judge took the suicide risk seriously while defending investigative journalism and the right of women to tell their stories

The Guardian and ITV News investigation into David Walliams has exposed difficult dilemmas for journalism. Last week, the high court helped clarify how to navigate them. The court heard that women had described to the Guardian how Mr Walliams, one of Britain’s most successful comedians and children’s authors, used his fame to prey on them for sex when they were young adults or teenagers. Publishing their claims carried a serious risk that Mr Walliams might take his own life. But this is a story of great public interest, and those women deserve to be heard. Some of them told the Guardian that they have lived with the effects of his alleged conduct for years.

For months, the Guardian and ITV News weighed concerns for him and his family against the women’s right to tell their stories. Both organisations wanted the court to scrutinise the evidence and rule on publication. If they then decided to proceed, Mr Walliams and his carers would be given time to prepare before publication.

Mr Justice Nicklin refused the injunction sought by Mr Walliams to prevent publication of the claims – all of which he denies – that he groomed fans he met when they were as young as 15, and harassed women in the workplace for years. The hospital, the judge said, was responsible for Mr Walliams’ immediate safety and could reduce the risk to his life; protecting him did not require suppressing public-interest journalism.

The court has clarified the role of journalism in a democracy. It did not give journalists carte blanche to publish stories without considering the potential consequences. Editors must continually assess the public interest and allow those responsible for a person’s care time to take protective steps. Both duties should be integral to the editorial process, as they were in this case.

But the judgment did provide an endorsement of the importance of public-interest-driven journalism. Had Mr Walliams won the case, he would have silenced the media and all his accusers. The consequences for journalism and society would have been seismic: courts could have been required to stop otherwise lawful reporting because of the danger it posed to its subject. Even if editors and reporters pressed ahead, the prospect of a costly court battle could be enough to keep a story from seeing the light of day.

Having assessed all the medical evidence, Mr Justice Nicklin rejected Mr Walliams’ demand that he be protected under the Human Rights Act’s article 2, which protects the right to life, and article 3, which prohibits torture and inhumane and degrading treatment. His judgment establishes an important legal precedent about why reporting individual cases matters. By “illuminat[ing] the operation of power”, the court reasoned, journalism shows readers how alleged sexual misconduct was practised in ways that a general discussion in public cannot.

The Guardian first exposed Mr Walliams’ inappropriate conduct on the hit TV show Britain’s Got Talent in 2022. He was dropped as a judge after a decade. Last December, HarperCollins dropped him after an investigation into alleged inappropriate behaviour towards young women, and in September the company announced that it would no longer publish any of his works.

The allegations in this latest investigation were put to Mr Walliams in May. He has now been sectioned under the Mental Health Act after two suicide attempts. The welfare of Mr Walliams and his family deserved to be taken seriously. So did the prospect that an injunction would silence the sources who had courageously come forward. If Mr Walliams had won the case, this would have had a chilling effect on responsible investigative journalism – and been a sweeping new restriction on the media.

The Guardian view on rough sleeping: Burnham’s laudable target is in danger of being missed

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 19:19:25 GMT

Energetic mayors and councils can help street homeless people to rebuild their lives. But the underlying affordability crisis needs tackling too

Bringing an end to rough sleeping was among Andy Burnham’s first pledges after entering Downing Street – as it was when he became mayor of Manchester. With temperatures dropping, and frosts expected, winter night shelters across the UK are up and running. But an ongoing acute shortage of suitable housing and the latest tranche of early prisoner releases mean ministers know that the prime minister’s laudable target is in danger of being missed.

The official figures are shocking. There were 8,748 rough sleepers in England in June, an increase of about 1,000 since January (Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland collect data separately). These are among the most vulnerable people in society, both in terms of past experiences and future prospects, including drastically curtailed life expectancy. The complex and sometimes chaotic situations of people who end up on the streets, most of whom are men, mean that helping them is challenging. Family breakdown, substance misuse, mental health difficulties and prison are among the many adverse life experiences that rough sleepers are disproportionately likely to face.

But the problems of councils and charities are made far worse by the fact that this visibly distressed group is only the tip of the homelessness iceberg. While rough sleepers are the most obvious victims of the UK’s homelessness crisis – which is national in the sense that it affects all four nations, but varies enormously between places – they are a small minority of the total number who cannot find or afford to rent (let alone buy) their own home. The latest count of families in temporary accommodation such as B&Bs and hostels in England, in March, was 135,600 – 90% more than a decade ago.

Mr Burnham’s personal commitment to rough sleepers has seen a big increase in funding, to almost £900m next year. This ought to enable councils, and charities providing local services, to make plans that go beyond the expansion of winter shelters, or hostel places, to meet the immediate goal of getting “everyone in for Christmas”. People with mental health, addiction or other issues need support and treatment that goes further than a roof over their heads. The spike in rough sleeping is a reflection of housing affordability problems, but also of a lack of the other services that enable fragile, vulnerable people to manage their lives.

Manchester’s “A Bed Every Night” scheme saw rough sleeper numbers fall, then climb back up – partly because it could not keep pace with the pressures pushing people on to the streets. Helping people to rebuild their lives takes sustained effort. Charities rightly warn that prison releases add to councils’ burdens. Probation and housing services must work together: freeing people from jail to sleep on the street is the act of a dysfunctional system. But no scheme, council or charity can find homes for people if those homes don’t exist, or are priced beyond their reach. That requires a mix of more social housing, rent controls and housing allowances that meet reasonable costs. It also means confronting policies that generate homelessness.

UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 18:49:36 GMT

António Guterres calls for ‘clear next steps’ as countries face pressure to agree concrete measures

Turkey and Australia, the co-hosts of crucial climate talks, must urgently move from discussing the end of fossil fuels to delivering it, the UN chief has said.

“It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” António Guterres said, in a dramatic intervention on the second day of the conference on Tuesday.

“Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it.”

The two countries hosting Cop31 are significant exporters of fossil fuels. Early on Tuesday, the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was extolling his country’s oilfields even as he prepared for his appearance at the summit on Wednesday.

Guterres said the talks should end with “clear next steps” to advance a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels presented to delegates on Tuesday by Brazil, which presided over last year’s talks.

During a presentation with the Brazilians, Guterres – who will step down as UN secretary general at the end of this year and has made the climate crisis a central part of his agenda, often intervening on issues with dramatic language – was energetically backed by the former US secretary of state and climate envoy John Kerry, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, and his predecessor, the Mexican diplomat Patricia Espinosa. He was met by rapturous applause as he left the stage.

Brazil announced at the close of last year’s Cop30 climate summit that it would produce the roadmap. Previewing it last week, the country said an exit from fossil fuels would boost economies and help pull people out of poverty.

Kerry said the roadmap had come “at a critical moment” but “words in conversation don’t cut a single ton of emissions – action does”.

There is growing pressure on this Cop to deliver after several years in which the summits have been criticised for a lack of progress. It took 28 years of annual UN Cop negotiations for the first mention of a transition away from fossil fuels to be included in a final decision, at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023.

Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, attended this year’s Cop for the first time since 2021,. “Cops have become greenwashed circuses. That is the reality,” she told reporters.

The drama came on the eve of a two-day leaders’ summit at which more than 90 world leaders, including the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, his Australian counterpart, Anthony Albanese, and the newly elected Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were expected to speak and join negotiations.

Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate thinktank E3G and a Cop veteran, described the presentation of the roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels as “an incredible display of collective firepower”.

“There’s clearly now an expectation that the presidencies [of Australia and Turkey] will pick up the baton from Brazil in some way,” he said. “But it won’t be agreed by consensus here. It took us 28 Cop meetings to get the need to transition away from fossil fuels into a Cop decision.

“This is what we are getting down to and it will be interesting to see how this hybrid presidency responds to this. This is the challenge to this presidency and how they pick up this baton and keep this discussion going.”

A spokesperson for Australia’s climate minister, Chris Bowen, said: “Our message had been clear: countries working together is not only the best way, it is the only way of dealing with climate change and the other crises that countries are facing.

“Before us is the opportunity to make our nations more prosperous, our energy system more secure and the climate more safe.”

The Turkish hosts were approached for comment.

The second day of the conference also saw more than 700 groups, ranging from trade unions to disability advocates, urging diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.

Organisations from 88 countries demanded a mechanism at Cop31 to turn promises of a just transition into action. Known as the Belém-Antalya Mechanism (BAM), it would seek to support issues including human rights, gender equality and good jobs, while respecting Indigenous rights.

Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, said: “Workers and communities, especially in the global south, welcomed and celebrated the Cop30 decision to develop a just transition mechanism – or BAM – which has the promise of delivering real support and action for just transition on the ground.

“However, in pre-Cop, governments of the global north have once again exposed their determination to pour cold water over this promise, by limiting what a mechanism can do and delaying the process of its operationalisation.”

On Tuesday, with 100,000 people attending the talks, many delegates were stuck in traffic for hours. Tram services were crammed with attenders, while some bus journeys took more than three hours.

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 18:41:49 GMT

Kevin Sinfield says collaboration with clubs will be key

England need to find a talented understudy for their injured star wing Manny Feyi-Waboso, and are poised to invite Gloucester’s Will Joseph to audition for a ­leading role against Japan on Saturday. The latter was a travelling reserve for last ­weekend’s Australia game and appears set for a Test recall four years after being given his debut by the current Brave ­Blossoms head coach, Eddie Jones.

The 24-year-old Joseph, whose brother Jonathan was a regular in England’s midfield for years, has been in outstanding club form and, as things stand, seems likely to ­feature in some capacity with injuries ­forcing Steve Borthwick to reconsider the backline blend that prospered against the Wallabies.

With Feyi-Waboso, Seb Atkinson and George Furbank all sidelined on Saturday, a number of spaces need filling in the matchday 23 and ­England’s assistant coach Kevin ­Sinfield believes Joseph, who can operate at both centre and wing, has the talent to seize any opportunity that comes his way. “What a player he is,” said Sinfield, who was knighted earlier this year for his contributions to rugby and Motor Neurone Disease charity fundraising.

“I’ve been really impressed with him in training … having only worked with Will for a little while he’s made a huge mark on everybody. He beats people, he’s got great balance and he’s a good defender with ­unbelievable power and speed off the mark. He’s a good jackaller, he breaks the line … he’s a special player. Some of the bits he’s done in training have been ‘wow’ moments. He can play.”

Joseph’s only previous cap came in the closing minutes of England’s Test victory against the Wallabies in ­Brisbane in 2022 when he was a 20-year-old apprentice and Jones was the head coach. The ­scintillating try he scored for Gloucester at Exeter earlier this season, however, was a striking reminder of his talent and he has also been impressing his teammate Alex Coles on Bagshot’s training pitch. “He rounded someone on the wing in five metres of space and even Henry Pollock, who was on the ­defensive side against him, celebrated his try because it was that good,” Coles said.

There are plenty of other back-three contenders lurking in England’s squad, including Cadan Murley, Joe Marchant, Noah Caluori and Tobias Elliott, but Joseph’s positional ­versatility could also boost his cause when it comes to picking a final World Cup squad next year.

That said the uber-talented Feyi-Waboso remains England’s most lethal attacking weapon, with ­Sinfield describing his performance against Australia, before he came off with an ankle injury at half-time, as “world class”. “He’s our Jason ­Robinson,” said Sinfield, referencing his fellow cross-code legend.

“He’s frustrated but what a last game it was for him. We can’t ask somebody to come in and play like Manny, but we can ask them to come in and bring the best of ­themselves. That’s what we’ll be doing this week. We would like whoever comes in to play with a lot of ­courage, back ­themselves and, when they’re put in space, to try and take the ­opportunities that they’re given.”

Woman jailed for posing as man to dupe partner into sex found guilty of similar deception

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 18:08:29 GMT

Jury finds Blade Silvano, who presented herself as a male army veteran, guilty of six counts of sexual assault

A woman serving a prison sentence for sexual assault after pretending to be a man and duping a woman into a physical relationship has been found guilty of tricking another woman into a similar abusive partnership.

In both cases, Blade Silvano, 44, met the women on an online dating site and falsely claimed she was a man who had served in the armed forces before meeting them in person and sexually assaulting them.

Both women said Silvano tricked them into believing she was male and neither had any idea they were being deceived.

Silvano was jailed in 2023 in Cambridge after a jury heard she carried out the deception using a blindfold, sex toy and a “wholly fake persona”. Silvano and her victim even became engaged as a man and woman.

On Tuesday, a jury at Caernarfon crown court in north Wales found her guilty of six counts of sexual assault by penetration between November 2022 and the following June after being told she had carried out the same sort of deception on another woman.

Using the alias “Hunter”, Silvano began messaging the victim on the Plenty of Fish site before meeting her for sex, always keeping the lights very low and not allowing herself to be touched intimately.

Silvano claimed to be a captain and surgeon in the army and on one occasion claimed “his” condom had broken as they had sex. Silvano assured the alleged victim it was “very unlikely” she would get pregnant and told her: “Trust me, I’m a doctor.”

The jury was told the woman noticed her partner sounded a “little feminine” and began to have doubts about their “odd” sex life.

Eventually, the victim received a call from Silvano’s long-term partner, a woman, who said the person she’d known as “Hunter” was female, the court heard.

The victim told police she felt sick when she learned of the deception, saying: “I thought it was some sort of joke.” In court, she said: “I believed I was in a relationship with a straight, heterosexual man. I would never go out with a woman.”

Philip Clemo, prosecuting, told the jury Silvano was a gifted con artist and suggested she was inspired by the myth of Zeus turning into a bull.

The Cambridgeshire offences took place in 2016 and 2017. Using the fake name Blade Mendez, Silvano presented herself as a male army veteran throughout a two-year relationship.

She would send the victim photos of herself apparently shaving her face and would pretend to urinate standing up.

Silvano, of Shropshire, would not allow the victim to touch her genitals, claiming to be “body conscious due to injuries sustained in the army”. Silvano and the woman got engaged and she was encouraged to try on wedding dresses and book a registrar.

The victim accidentally uncovered Silvano’s deception after coming across her on Facebook in September 2018 “in a completely different living situation”. Silvano was found guilty of two counts of assault by penetration.

Silvano will be sentenced for the six sexual assaults next month. Judge Jones ordered a pre-sentence report so that the risk she posed could be assessed.
