Growth at all costs is not a sustainable policy

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:52:52 GMT

The key task should be to ensure that essential services improve the wellbeing of individuals and local communities, writes Peter Riddle. Plus letters from Sheila Triggs and Stephen Smith

A key lesson for the UK from the US midterm elections is that a different approach to managing the economy is essential if Labour hopes to retain power in two years’ time. Voters in the UK will judge Andy Burnham’s government just as harshly as American voters have judged Donald Trump if they too feel the economy is not working for them.

Meeting the rising costs of food, utilities, transport and housing has become a daily challenge for millions of people. The pain of rising costs is compounded by a collapse in the quality and reliability of many vital public services and a sense that many people feel that their community life has become more fractious, fragile and unsafe.

Burnham, on becoming prime minister, discredited the previous 40 years of neoliberal economics because it had not delivered perceptible benefits for much of the population. In his quest to replace these outdated orthodoxies with a different kind of economics, he would do well to read the work of Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal, referred to in your editorial (The Guardian view on Labour’s growth obsession: a different economics is possible, 3 November).

The pursuit of economic growth can swiftly be sabotaged by unpredictable global forces and events beyond a nation’s control and risks repeating the errors of the past. Burnham’s strategy of focusing on small fixes that will give people breathing space has been generally welcomed.

Williams and Johal build on that approach by proposing a more forensic and wide-ranging strategy. They argue that the key task of government should be to ensure that essential services, such as health, education, housing, transport and welfare, all contribute to improving the collective wealth and wellbeing of individuals and local communities.

For several decades voters have felt that successive governments have dismissed their concerns and failed to address those things that have most impact on their daily lives. The question remains as to whether Burnham’s government has the courage to do things differently. Peter Riddle Wirksworth, Derbyshire

Thank you for the editorial challenging Labour’s obsession with economic growth, which addresses the need for a more equitable distribution of wealth.

However, we must go further and address the lack of our depleted planet’s resources to allow for endless growth. Growth demands the seeking of new frontiers to extract more coal, oil, gas, timber, minerals and food. More than we need. This is intrinsically colonial, maintaining the global south as a source for the expansion of wealth in the west. It is also exacerbated by the vast resources being wasted on wars and the world’s military budget.

The urgent need, essential to avert climate disaster, is to reduce the world’s consumption of energy and material goods in a way that is globally just. Sheila Triggs Orpington, Kent

Your editorial on Labour’s obsession with growth was helpful in its reminder that redistribution is the forgotten instrument of such change. Such a reminder is also very timely, however, because the many environmental crises require a radical change in our culture in order for us to turn away from the impossibility of never-ending increases in mankind’s material claims upon the planet.

There will be no meaningful attempt to address these crises as long as the priority always remains the expansion of the human footprint, with all that implies for planetary health. If the insane momentum of “growth” towards inevitable collapse eventually ceases (it is slowing now in many western countries), the insanity of the inequalities of our current world must also be recognised. Radical redistribution is the only social alternative that can offer hope. Stephen Smith Glasgow

A proper leftwing take on taking back control

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:52:42 GMT

Mark Bergfeld suggests the quest for a better quality of life deserves as much political recognition as climbing a career ladder

Gaby Hinsliff’s portrait of Claire Ainsley and her latest book Control: How We Lost It and How to Take It Back (‘The world is out of control’: how political strategist Claire Ainsley is challenging the left to take it back, 3 November) leaves a crucial question unanswered: can working people exercise control collectively over those in power?

Reviewing her earlier book The New Working Class for the Global Labour Journal in 2020, I argued that she treated working-class people primarily as voters to be won over rather than people capable of organising to change society.

Instead of thinking through how one could expand the current government’s focus on collective workers’ rights, Ainsley focuses on giving tax breaks to those who sign up for courses and have the ambition to move up the career ladder.

For a cleaner, care worker or security guard, control should mean having a say over working hours, workloads and pay. The ambition to spend time with your children, work safely and earn a decent living deserves as much political recognition as the ambition to climb a career ladder. Strong trade unions, collective bargaining and democratic participation at work should be central to the left’s answer. Mark Bergfeld Brussels, Belgium

Compassion is the antidote to the politics of cruelty

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:52:36 GMT

Readers respond to an article by John Harris in which he argues that around the world virtues such as kindness and compassion are gathering dust

John Harris’s powerful article exposes the growing assault on empathy in politics (From the US midterms to the hard right in Britain, empathy has become a dirty word in politics, 3 November). But why has empathy become such a threatening quality? Perhaps because extinguishing it completes the work of aggressive neoliberalism by severing the last thread of the social contract: our sense of responsibility for one another. If we can persuade ourselves that people are to blame for their own suffering, and that helping them merely enables dependency, we can abandon them without guilt.

We founded Compassion in Politics in the aftermath of Brexit and Trump’s first election because we feared precisely this erosion of compassion from public life. Yet evolutionary science tells a different story about human nature. Our capacity for compassion is innate. It is one of the qualities that enabled our species to survive through cooperation and mutual care. Crucially, it is not fixed. The cultures and institutions we create can nurture it or suppress it.

That is why defending compassion is not enough. We must actively build political institutions and a culture that bring out the best in human nature. We now have more than 60 MPs working with us across party lines, and our movement is spreading internationally. Compassion is the antidote to the politics of cruelty, and we must all urgently spread it. Jennifer Nadel Co-founder and CEO, Compassion in Politics; director of compassionate politics, Centre for Compassion and Altruism Research and Education, Stanford University

As John Harris points out, the hard right have indeed been fighting a culture war against all things empathetic, woke or ethical. However, his conclusion that “all over the world, compassion, kindness and other such virtues gather a thick layer of dust, like old hymn books in a long-deserted church”, while poetic, does overstate the effects of this culture war.

We know from science that empathy is partly influenced by genetics, from polling and surveys that between 60% and 80% try to be other-centred at least some of the time, and from our own lived experience (like the Guardian’s Kindness of Strangers series) that people can be surprisingly kind too – even in 2026.

And we also learned from the US midterm results that just because a lot of rich men say a thing is true on their social media channels, that does not mean all the people can be fooled all the time. Comfortingly, it’s looking like it will take more than a few billionaires to dislodge the tendency for compassion and kindness from the human experience. Rob Harrison Editor, Ethical Consumer Magazine

“Comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable” is a sound principle for most serious public addresses. As a research professor in engineering and technology, Methodist local preacher and former parliamentary candidate, I am familiar with the weak sensibilities of most audiences and church congregations.

I have learned that a powerful, uncomfortable truth should be the cornerstone, because this is the nature of the evolving creation of which we are a part. There is no other hiding place, but because there seems to be a kind of unity and wisdom in all of this we can recognise and find some comfort.

But we, the media and our politicians need to be far more realistic, humble, and probably less demanding. Kindness and goodness, yes, but empathy needs to be very carefully used, because it is extremely difficult to be in another’s shoes. Barry Jones Malvern, Worcestershire

Mauricio Pochettino interested in leaving USMNT job for Manchester United

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:40:40 GMT

United expected to sack Michael Carrick after awful start

US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is interested in a move to Manchester United, multiple sources told the Guardian, with those same sources characterizing the interest as mutual.

United are expected to sack their head coach, Michael Carrick, after a disastrous start to their season which leaves them at risk of relegation from the Premier League, their worst opening to a campaign in four decades.

Securing Pochettino’s services is far from simple or inexpensive. The Argentinian’s contract contains a release clause in the neighborhood of $10m (£7.5m), multiple sources familiar with the deal told the Guardian this week, a figure that grows should United choose to retain Pochettino’s staff, including his longtime assistant and confidant Jesús Pérez, who has worked with Pochettino for 16 years. The Athletic first reported the details of Pochettino’s buyout.

Pochettino was brought on by the US in 2024 and guided the USMNT to a last-16 finish at the 2026 World Cup, by most accounts a disappointment. US Soccer brought him back through 2030, with both sides expressing a mutual belief and commitment towards not only brightening the fortunes of the US men but also overhauling the federation’s approach towards youth development.

“Every time we sign a contract, it’s to go to the last day of the contract,” Pochettino told reporters after his contract renewal. “If we sign a four-year contract, we need to think to arrive there. And we signed the contract because we really believe that we are going to be four years there. Because if not, it’s bad. If we don’t believe in that process, if we don’t believe in that journey, why sign [for] four years? Only to be sure that we are going to receive a salary at the end of the month? That is not nice. It’s not the way that we think. We really signed that contract because we really believe that we can arrive to the end.”

Pochettino, who has been linked with a host of high-profile club openings since his arrival in the United States, tempered those remarks by adding another: “In life, nothing is sure. Less in football.”

The USMNT are days from a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches against Haiti in Cincinnati and Miami, their first competitive fixtures of the 2030 qualifying cycle. Pochettino is scheduled to address reporters on Friday afternoon.

Pochettino has repeatedly expressed his interest in returning to the Premier League during his time with the US. As recently as September, he spoke to Sky Sports about the idea of winning the league and “building a project with the possibility of winning”. In late 2025 he said much the same, telling the BBC he believed the league was the best in the world and adding “of course I am missing it. I am so happy in America but am thinking but also thinking one day to come back.”

Beyond his stated interest, Pochettino is also widely known as a coach who enjoys the day-to-day responsibilities of coaching and he’s widely regarded as an excellent man-manager who thrives in the daily rhythm of life at a club. He maintains a home in London and speaks glowingly of the UK and the football culture that permeates it. In short, there are no shortage of reasons for him to leave the US.

Most federations have contingency plans developed for the departure of a head coach and the US federation is no exception, especially given the repeated interest in Pochettino over the years. Prior to bringing the Argentine on board, US Soccer reached out to or spoke to several other high-profile candidates, most notably former Liverpool and current Germany boss Jürgen Klopp.

In the nearer term, several domestic candidates could fit the bill – current U-23 head coach Steve Cherundolo being one. In some respects, there is no better time for Pochettino to depart; doing so now would allow an incoming coach the majority of a four-year cycle to work with and the federation itself would earn millions just months after Pochettino could’ve departed for free.

That feels highly unlikely. Pochettino enjoys an unusually close relationship with his assistants, in particular his second-in-command, Jesús Pérez. UK social media ban expansion for under-16s could cover YouTube Kids

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:30:15 GMT

Regulations under consideration could affect up to 150 platforms, including LegoPlay, Spotify and eBay, sources say

A substantial expansion of the social media ban for under-16s could inadvertently lead to a ban on YouTube Kids and other sites that had been thought exempt, sources briefed on the government’s proposals have said.

One source close to the talks said the regulations now under consideration meant up to 150 platforms, including games platforms such as Lego Play, could be covered by the ban, which is set to come into force in March.

The regulations will be sent for cabinet signoff this week, and the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, is expected to lay them in parliament in December.

Ministers are understood to be keen for a catch-all approach that limits ban workarounds. Critics of Australia’s social media prohibition say teenagers have switched to new platforms or found innovative ways of messaging using other seemingly innocuous sites.

Tech companies, industry groups and MPs have been briefed that the government’s working proposal focuses on recommender systems and user-generated content.

Spotify – which has some user-generated content and shows recommended music or podcasts – could technically be in scope if those proposals are enacted, though the music streaming site has sought reassurances that it would not face a ban because it is not primarily a social platform.

One industry source said: “We all share the goal of keeping teenagers safe online. Proposals have to be workable, and a situation where eBay, Lego, YouTube Kids and Spotify aren’t clear whether they comply is unsustainable. Detailed guidelines can’t come soon enough.”

Another said: “The whole internet has a recommender system. The regulation is just too broad. But they want to make it really broad and legally airtight so they can be prepared for any eventuality.”

Companies are expected to be briefed on the final proposal in the coming days by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) and No 10.

When the ban was announced by Keir Starmer in June, the government said it would ensure the ban did not include educational services, e-commerce platforms or music streaming, saying there would be “a narrowly defined list of exemptions to the definitions which will be kept under review”.

But tech companies are understood to be telling the government that removing the recommender algorithm would make it impossible for their sites to function.

The regulations do not require primary legislation in the House of Commons, and will be tabled as an addition to the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act.

Ministers are also looking at a second tranche of regulations in the spring which could cover e-commerce platforms such as Vinted, eBay and Depop. MPs and campaigners have raised concerns with Nandy that teenagers and groomers can find innovative ways to communicate on platforms that allow unknown or anonymous user messaging, such as those websites.

After Nandy confirmed in interviews on Sunday that the government was looking to bring Vinted and other e-commerce platforms in scope, officials held a panicked call with retailers on Tuesday where several are understood to have strongly contested the plans.

Another industry figure said it would be illogical for the government to continue to allow messaging apps such as WhatsApp and iMessage – but ban platforms such as Vinted and eBay because they had messaging capabilities.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

after newsletter promotion

The minister for online safety, Ian Murray, also confirmed to MPs last week that the government was looking at those sites for the next tranche of regulations which examines “features and functions” and is expected next spring.

“Platforms that might have been out of scope are perhaps being brought into scope by having new functionalities that we might think are different from the social media platforms we are seeking to regulate. For example, Spotify has introduced stranger conversation functionality to its platform,” he said.

Murray told MPs that platforms which redesigned their services to remove harmful or addictive functions would have a route to removing themselves from the banned list.

“The way back is to comply with the regulations and fall out of scope. That is an easy thing to say but not an easy thing to deliver, but that is the principle with which we will go forward on this,” he said.

He said platforms such as YouTube Kids and Lego Play would need to demonstrate they did not have harmful algorithms.

“Are there ways in which you can stop the harms being created by the algorithms, the recommender systems, the commenting systems or the conversations that can be had with strangers?

“If you have created a service that complies with all the regulations, is it then available to under-16s? I would say that, currently, the government’s position is that, yes, there has to be an off ramp.”

Tech industry bodies have told the government that platforms such as YouTube Kids cease to function without the recommender system, making it impossible for them to comply with the “off ramp”.

DCMS has been approached to comment.

Call it tough love, with the love removed: it’s Kemi’s war on benefits claimants

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:04:29 GMT

The Tory leader outlines her £36bn welfare cuts, again, to an audience of an age and a wealth that they don’t need to work

Call it tough love. Only without any of the love bit. Let’s face it. There comes a time in every Conservative politician’s life when you have to say enough is enough. That it’s just not fair on the rest of us. Now, MPs might just have enjoyed a five-day mini-recess, but they deserve every minute’s free time they get. Because they clearly work far harder than everyone else. But on a Tuesday morning it sticks in the throat to think of people lying around at home, being paid to have disabilities that exist mainly in their imaginations, while you have to give a speech in central London.

The thing is, we just haven’t been ambitious enough for people on welfare payments. Let me introduce you to KemiWorld. Think of the double amputee who ran a marathon. Though try not to think of the cost to the NHS of the prosthetics. Welfare is very much a one-way balance sheet as far as Kemi Badenoch. The point is that most disabled people just sit at home and moan. They need to get out more. Let’s face it, if a double amputee can run a marathon then it ought to be a doddle for a single amputee to run a double marathon. Just get out there and do it.

Too many people just think of welfare benefits as an excuse to sit indoors and watch TV all day. So, diddums has bad anxiety and suffers from panic attacks. Frankly, I’m not surprised. I’d be having panic attacks if I was as useless as you. Just get out there and do something.

Find a job, even if there aren’t any jobs to find. Leave the house and start walking. And don’t come back until you’ve pulled yourself together. Take a leaf out of the tech bros’ book. Most of them have ADHD of some sort. So, rather than complaining, use your spare time to establish a billion-pound startup. It’s not that hard. All you need is an idea. And you’re not going to have one if you spend all day on your arse.

Tuesday morning saw Kemi and the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, in Westminster explaining their plans to cut £36.1bn from the welfare budget. The £0.1bn is there to make sure you don’t think the Tories have just plucked some random numbers from thin air, which of course they have. This way we can all pretend it’s fully costed down to the last 50p.

It’s also possible that somewhere in the back of your mind you will remember Kemi and Helen talking about £36bn in savings at the Conservative party conference last month. You may well have wisely zoned out and missed the announcement. Which is why the Tories have popped back for another go. One that is almost certainly doomed to fail, as no one takes the costings of an opposition party particularly seriously. So don’t be surprised if there’s yet another press conference before Christmas, to re-announce the re-announcement. Third time lucky.

Still, it’s not hard to see why Kemi increasingly enjoys a presser. She’s taken to having them almost as often as Nigel Farage. For one thing, it’s about the only way she can get any attention. For another, it’s a chance to highlight the gap between her and her shadow cabinet. Her approval ratings continue to poll considerably higher than those of the Tory party itself. Mostly because her team are a bunch of deadbeats. Twenty or so semi-sentient beings in search of a personality. None more so than Whately. More of her later.

There were whoops and cheers from a surprisingly large audience as Kemi approached the lectern. They were all – there is no kind way of saying this – of an age and a wealth that apparently had no better place to be at 10.30am on a working day. Credit where credit is due. At least they hadn’t stayed in bed like the benefits claimants.

For Kemi and the audience, though, it was all common sense. A token nod to compassion – people who were terminally ill and well past retirement age would still get benefits – but for everyone else there would be a rude wake-up call. Why waste time saying a last goodbye to your family when you could be doing a productive day’s work instead. Sentimentality was the Labour way. And who, now she had come to think about it, really needed two legs anyway? Bipedalism was overrated.

Then came the charisma vacuum that is Helen. Like so many Tory MPs, she has been on quite the journey. When she was first elected to parliament, she was a wetter than wet Cameroon. Well on the left of the Tory party. Since then, she has slid to the right. She talks these days of getting people back to work, but you can’t help wondering if the only job she is really interested in is her own.

Helen was there to talk us through the numbers. Though not the ones that really counted. Such as how the welfare bill almost doubled under the Tories. It turns out, it’s far easier to cut the bill when you are in opposition. And for Whately, all benefit claimants were just debit sums in the ledger. There was no understanding that – as in the Netherlands, where there had been great success in funding measures to get young people into work – it might be an idea to invest in opportunities.

Nor was there any acknowledgment that cutting benefits by up to £10,000 per household might create further costs. That people might lose their homes, forcing councils to accommodate them in bed and breakfasts. Claims by charities that these changes would lead to a massive surge in child poverty were dismissed by Kemi. Just attention-seeking from charities that would say that, wouldn’t they?

The questions from the media slipped by easily enough. Kemi refrained from having a go at Ed Miliband and Lucy Powell about their fatal attraction to Russell Brand more than a decade ago, and she did say she wouldn’t be cutting benefits for people from the EU with settled status. So there is a heart there, somewhere.

Historians uncover more questions for insurers over their role in the slave trade

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:17:46 GMT

Academics are slowly piecing together the financial networks behind the transatlantic trafficking of ‘human cargo’

While the UK government is considering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, Lloyd’s of London said it was “deeply sorry” six years ago. The historic insurance marketplace said it was deeply sorry for the “significant role” it played in the trafficking of enslaved people and for the enormous suffering caused. It has since installed a commemorative plaque at its London headquarters.

Perhaps more consequential was the research that followed. Through an independent collaboration with Johns Hopkins University in the US, researchers Alexandre White and Pyar Seth examined Lloyd’s archives.

The resulting Underwriting Souls project laid bare how merchant insurers – some linked through predecessor businesses to major insurers operating today – underwrote ships carrying enslaved people across the Atlantic and, in some cases, the enslaved people themselves as “human cargo”. But historians interviewed for a podcast by specialist news title InsuranceERM say the full extent of the insurance industry’s involvement is still far from understood.

White, now an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge, said part of the problem was the fragmented surviving evidence. Risk books, the ledgers in which individual underwriters recorded their business, are particularly rare and provide only a snapshot of an underwriter’s activity.

“There could be tons,” White said when asked how much more evidence remains to be uncovered. “It’s possible we’ll find more. It’s possible much has been destroyed … or lost to time.”

White said researchers were nevertheless getting “a much clearer sense of the scale and importance of insurance to slavery”, with work in London, Liverpool and Bristol helping to piece together the financial networks that supported it.

One place where researchers are breaking new ground is Liverpool, through the Connector Project, a £1m initiative funded by the Lloyd’s Register Foundation – an independent charity that is separate from Lloyd’s of London but has historical links to enslavement – and facilitated by National Museums Liverpool. Its first pilot study, Overwriting Underwriting, is already piecing together fresh evidence about the role of insurers.

Lucy Moynihan, a PhD student and research associate on the project, has been examining the 1797 risk book of John Gladstone, the enslaver and merchant who later became the first chair of the Liverpool Underwriters’ Association.

Moynihan said previous histories had overlooked Gladstone’s role as an underwriter in the trafficking of enslaved people. Her research has identified voyages in his risk book connected to enslavement, adding underwriting information missing from existing datasets.

Central to the research is reconstructing the networks behind this business. Malik Al Nasir, an academic, author and Connector Project manager, said Liverpool’s merchants, shipowners, bankers and underwriters were often connected through their families and commercial interests. Because the merchants acted as underwriters, evidence can also sit in private family and business collections. Moynihan said private archives had a responsibility to “do a review of what they have” and give the public access to their records.

Al Nasir’s own research, which has involved sourcing material from disparate repositories and even eBay because of gaps in established archives, led him to a letter referring to insurance for the sloop Speedwell, which he says does not appear in the widely used Slave Voyages database.

“If I can just find randomly from one letter one slave ship that’s not mentioned on the Slave Voyages database, then there must be many others as well,” he said.

Historians also believe more remains to be uncovered about what happened after Britain outlawed the transatlantic slave trade in 1807. “British insurers are pretty openly still involved with the insurance of foreign slave voyages after 1807,” said Hannah Farber, an associate professor at Columbia University in New York City.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

As enforcement tightened, Farber said that involvement became harder to trace, with financiers finding more covert ways to take on the risks of slave voyages without formally underwriting them.

“It’s a lot easier to stop slave ships than it is to stop slave insurance,” she said.

Farber believes there is still substantial work to be done connecting the financial centres of London, Liverpool and New York with Brazil and Cuba, where enslavement remained legal later into the 19th century. “There’s so much more to learn about insurance in the slave trade,” she added.

White said the records also revealed that enslaved people were reduced to financial assets within the insurance system. “African lives at this time could still provide value not just from their bodies, not just from their labour, but also in their death,” he said.

After its apology Lloyd’s of London said it was committing £52m, including £12m for Inclusive Futures initiatives to help Black and ethnically diverse individuals participate and progress “from the classroom to the boardroom”. It also pledged to earmark £40m towards profit-making investments in the African Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, which has programmes in the Caribbean.

Lloyd’s efforts to address its historical support for the slave trade were criticised as “completely inadequate” at the time by the academic Kehinde Andrews. The race equality thinktank the Runnymede Trust welcomed Lloyd’s work to acknowledge its history but said it needed to do more to address issues such its ethnic pay gap.

A deeper examination of the research and what it means for insurers can be found in the InsuranceERM podcast episode, Why insurance’s reckoning with the transatlantic slave trade is far from over, released on 10 November.

Joshua Geer is news editor at InsuranceERM

Welcome Break Rotherham: is this really Britain’s best motorway service station?

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:09:16 GMT

It is modelled on a Yorkshire village and came top in a new survey, with 99% of visitors praising it. But with its branches of Burger King, Pret and Krispy Kreme, what makes it a cut above?

Name: Welcome Break Rotherham.

Age: Opened last year.

Appearance: A gleaming temple of unlimited possibility.

Steady on, you’re talking about a service station, right? Absolutely not, my good fellow. I’m talking about the service station, a miraculous wonderland designed to restore vitality, banish fatigue, straighten the spine, brighten the eyes …

So it’s good, then. Good?! Such meagre praise barely does justice to this palace of abundance. Welcome Break Rotherham is not just good. It is officially Britain’s best motorway service station.

What’s in it? Why, Burger King, Pret, Krispy Kreme and Chopstix Noodle Bar among others.

You could be describing any motorway service station. Listen, you can’t argue with the data. Transport Focus, the independent watchdog for transport users, asked almost 40,000 people what they thought of the quality of their service stations, and 99% of Welcome Break Rotherham visitors said they were fairly or very satisfied.

I suppose being fairly satisfied in a food court is about as good as one can expect. Clearly, you haven’t been. This is no ordinary food court. Welcome Break Rotherham aims to look and feel like a Yorkshire village, with street names, a village square, a fountain, faux stonework shopfronts and a red telephone box containing a defibrillator.

OK, fine, that does sound charming. I’ve barely touched the surface. There is also a children’s soft play area, a gaming room, an outdoor exercise area and a dog exercise enclosure. If you’re a HGV driver, you can also use the station’s gym.

Wow. Yes, suck it Rugby.

Pardon? Why does Rugby have to suck it? Because Moto Rugby is a two-time winner, and the expectation was that it would breeze to a third win. But it got cocky and complacent, and was taken out by a newcomer.

What’s in Moto Rugby? It has a Burger King, Pret, Krispy Kreme and Costa.

Not even a Chopstix? I know. Losers.

Out of interest, are all the service stations ranked? You want to know which was the worst one, don’t you?

Do I ever. The answer is Roadchef Watford Gap Northbound, which came 122 out of 122 service stations, thanks to its miserable lineup that includes McDonald’s, Costa, Krispy Kreme and Chozen Noodle.

Disgusting. Hey, isn’t Gloucester services supposed to be good? What? No. If we don’t mention that place, it means it doesn’t exist.

It didn’t want to take part, did it? You’re right, and it probably would have won. But still, all hail Welcome Break Rotherham, officially the best of those that were judged.

Do say: “Let’s go and visit Welcome Break Rotherham!”

Don’t say: “Or genuinely any other service station.”

The decision to sack Sage was made on Sunday evening after Palace slumped to a 3-1 defeat against Liverpool. It was their fourth successive loss in the Premier League and left them bottom of the table for the first time since 2017.

Despite reports on Monday that the Frenchman had been dismissed, there has been no announcement, and it is understood negotiations are continuing over compensation for his three-year contract. However, Yannick Cahuzac’s sacking by Lens on Tuesday after they were embarrassed 9-1 by Como in a record-equalling Champions League defeat last week, before losing 2-1 against Marseille in Ligue 1, has opened the possibility of a swift return across the Channel.

The Lens owner and president, Joseph Oughourlian, has remained in close contact with Sage since he left to pursue what the 47-year-old described as his dream move to the Premier League. After winning the French Cup and finishing as runners-up in Ligue 1 under Sage, Oughourlian is thought to favour reappointing him in an attempt to get their season back on track. That would mean Palace could avoid paying compensation, having already spent more than £4m to buy Sage out of his contract when he replaced Oliver Glasner in the summer.

Cahuzac was promoted from his role as assistant to replace Dino Toppmöller when the German was sacked in mid-September after just four matches. But he has been under growing pressure, with supporters unfurling a banner before the defeat by Marseille that called the players a “disgrace”.

Sage remained hopeful that he would be given more time to turn things around at Palace but there have been few signs of improvement since a 5-0 thrashing by arch-rivals Brighton last month. Some players are understood to have questioned his training methods, although several others are said to have sent him messages of support since the Liverpool defeat.

Thomas Frank is the leading contender to take over, with the former Tottenham and Brentford manager having indicated that he is looking for a new challenge. He held talks with Palace in the summer before they turned to Sage. Sean Dyche and Vítor Pereira are potential alternatives, while Eddie Howe is believed to have rejected an initial approach in recent weeks.

Jamie Oliver is a global chef and campaigner with a 27-year television and publishing career. He is working to improve people’s relationship with food and, through his Ministry of Food, aims to teach more than 1 million people to cook by 2030. Jamie lives in Essex with his wife, Jools, and their children. His latest book, 20 Minute Meals: Real Fast Food, is published by Penguin.

Honestly, I just want to have a lovely time with the people who matter most. Being together and having a giggle is all the Christmas joy I need. If you want to twist my arm, I wouldn’t say no to a bottle of Glenmorangie whisky and some nice socks.

Glenmorangie 12-year-old the Original, 70cl

We go for the double: a KellyBronze turkey and a lovely goose. And all the usual trimmings, of course – you’ve got to go all out come Christmas. But the most important thing, certainly in my wife’s eyes, is the gravy. And she’s right. That’s why I make my get-ahead gravy every year, without fail.

Whole turkey

I love a Pump Street bakery panettone and will always get a chocolate bar for Jools – she’s obsessed. Grasmere Gingerbread is legendary; buy a tin, and you’ll be hooked. And I love to dip into the online provisions store at Coombeshead farm for all those Christmas easy eats such as pork pies, cured meat, jams and condiments.

Gingerbread, 12 pieces

A big question, and dependent on the time of day, whether I’m snacking alone or entertaining. Alone, it’s got to be the unbeatable combo of Westcombe cheddar with salt and vinegar Hula Hoops. For a crowd, a baked cheese with tear ’n’ share bread is always a winner. I’d go for a British cheese such as Tunworth or Baron Bigod.

Baron Bigod cheese, 250g

You can’t go wrong with a good whisky – I was given a membership to the Scotch Malt Whisky Society one year, and it was a joy. That would be a great present for someone, actually. I’m also weaning myself back on to negronis – Vault does a very special vermouth using local British-grown botanicals. Delicious.

Vault red vermouth, 75cl

For more, read our guide to the best whisky

I’m a strong advocate of Hill St chocolates, outrageously good handmade chocolates from bean to bar. I’d recommend getting a mixed box so you can try a bit of everything. And if you’re talking guilty pleasures, for me it’s gotta be a mint Aero.

Gourmet chocolate selection box, 500g

I’m really into good vinegar at the moment, like an apple cider vinegar – I like Willy’s. I decant mine into a spray bottle to add an extra layer to my spuds as they roast. I will also be splurging by being luxurious with my time – I plan to radically chill out this Christmas.

Willy’s organic apple cider vinegar, 1l

This is firmly Jools’s domain. I just do what I’m told. She likes to choose the loneliest, saddest-looking tree available and give it a lot of love, and I love her for that.

I think a good bottle of new-season extra virgin olive oil is a really thoughtful and useful gift. It’s not cheap, but it’s something people often don’t buy for themselves. Just a few drips when you’re plating up can totally transform everything from soups to salads, pasta to fish. My favourites are Capezzana and Fèlsina.

Police receive further criminal allegations against Russell Brand

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:57:34 GMT

Met says several people have been in contact since start of disgraced comedian’s rape and sexual assault trial

Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Police have received further criminal allegations against Russell Brand since the start of his trial.

The Metropolitan police said several people had been in contact during and since the conclusion of the 51-year-old’s rape and sexual assault case.

The force said those who had been in contact had either provided further information or reported potential criminal allegations.

A spokesperson said: “Several people have contacted the investigation team during and since the trial to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation. Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing inquiries.”

The judge in Brand’s trial, Mr Justice Bennathan, praised the bravery of the women who had come forward with evidence that led to his conviction.

But the way the victims were questioned by the disgraced comedian’s legal representative, Ian Winter KC, has been criticised in recent days.

Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, described the cross-examination as “depressing”, saying she believed the courts had “long gone past that sort of culture”.

Powell, who is also the education secretary, said that she regretted a meeting the former party leader Ed Miliband had with Brand in 2015 when she was Labour’s campaign chief.

Brand was jailed for 10 and a half years on Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others, including at their workplaces.

Powell was asked on LBC radio about Brand’s defence in court, during which Winter suggested he must be innocent because none of his victims had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”. Winter also said the anal rape of a 21-year-old woman was a “short and momentary failure” where “he did not respect her consent”.

Asked if that was reminiscent of the attitude of the 1950s, Powell said she had been shocked at some of what took place in the courtroom, while praising the judge’s words. “I found reading some of that incredibly sort of depressing. I thought we’d long gone past that sort of culture and that phase of things.

“And the judge’s remarks were also incredibly powerful in sentencing: that it doesn’t matter what you wear, how you behaved, how drunk you are, you know, you have the right to give your consent or not give your consent. And if it’s not given, then that is rape and that is a sexual offence, pure and simple.”

The BBC’s director general, Matt Brittin, wrote to the corporation’s staff to say that he wanted to ensure any concerns raised about workplace culture were heard “at the highest level”. His intervention followed criticism that Brand’s troubling behaviour had not been challenged properly during his time at the broadcaster.

Brittin said in his email that there had been valid criticism levelled at the media industry over its workplace culture after Brand’s conviction and recent allegations of antisemitism at the BBC.

Brand, who had stints as a presenter on BBC 6 Music and Radio 2 in 2006 and 2007, once joked on air about exposing himself to a woman moments before his show was broadcast. He also described one BBC boss, who has since left the broadcaster, as “incredibly tolerant” of his behaviour.

Brittin said the BBC and the wider media industry had made progress in improving culture, but that there was “still more to do to engage with staff and represent their views and concerns at the highest level”.

after newsletter promotion

Brittin said he was looking at changes to improve culture that could be made immediately and as part of the next BBC charter being discussed with ministers.

The BBC published a review in 2025 that found some staff had felt unable to speak out because of Brand’s status and power. The corporation repeated its apology this week.

After the treatment of some of Brand’s accusers during his trial, Powell said the government had taken steps in guidance to challenge myths about rape and victim-blaming in court. “But clearly, a lot more needs to be done because I think many of us were really shocked that that could still take place in a courtroom today,” she said.

At sentencing, the judge criticised Brand, saying the women had been subjected to additional suffering because of the conduct in court “on your instructions”.

“Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent,” he said.

Powell said she and Miliband regretted that he had done an interview with Brand in 2015 during the hype around Revolution, Brand’s book on politics. At the time the interview took place, Brand had resigned from his BBC Radio 2 show for leaving a series of lewd messages on actor Andrew Sachs’ answerphone about his granddaughter.

“It was a long time ago, obviously, and had I or Ed Miliband or anybody at the time had any sense at all that this was someone who was a sexual predator, who was involved in these sorts of crimes,” she told Sky News, anyone who was involved in promoting him would “look back and really regret that, knowing today what we now know”.

Asked about her role in setting up the interview, Powell said she had not understood the full extent of his sexual conduct that was already in the public domain – such as in his autobiography. “If there was any suggestion at all we were dealing with someone who was a known sexual predator at the time then, of course, no one would have done that.

“But as I say, he was a well-known public figure. Lots of people, from Hollywood to the BBC to many others, gave this person a very, very powerful platform.”

Yabba dabba doo! Could these bulging, Flintstones-style towers be the future of eco-building?

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:25:29 GMT

Ruggedly good-looking and greener than bricks and concrete, Petra Heights are made of three-metre slabs of rough rock. Could they herald a new stone age? Our writer fires up his Flintmobile

There’s been a geological eruption on London’s Finchley Road. Great chunks of pink basalt and igneous larvikite appear to have exploded from the railway cutting, shooting skywards to form teetering towers. Anyone trying to find Finchley Road & Frognal station need wonder no more: just look for the multistorey Stonehenge.

Countless apartment towers have sprouted above London’s stations in recent years, a result of public transport-oriented policies, but none have looked like the Flintstones were in charge.

“This is one of those stations where people are always scratching their heads trying to find it,” says architect Amin Taha, standing at the foot of his rocky megalith, an unmissable landmark next to the Overground entrance. “We’re unlikely to start building church spires or grand civic buildings with clocktowers again, so we wanted to make something people could point to and say, ‘It’s next to that building.’”

They might add that the towers, called Petra Heights, look like they’ve been assembled by a giant child, with building blocks chiselled straight from the quarry. The igneous rock that holds up these flats has been stacked with deceptive simplicity. Each slab weighs about three tonnes but they look like rustic Jenga blocks, their faces left with marks from drills and saws where they were prised from the bedrock. “Quarries normally expect architects to want everything absolutely clean cut,” says Taha. “But we just use it as it comes, saving the cost and waste of cutting. And the beauty is, you never quite know what the finished result will look like.” If only more clients were so brave.

Building a trio of six- to 10-storey towers out of solid stone may sound like an expensive proposition, but Taha says it is not only cheaper but saves a huge amount of carbon emissions compared with a concrete or steel-framed building – around 30% less in this case. If the internal frame had been made of cross-laminated timber as originally intended, instead of concrete, as built, it could have saved around 75%.

The project marks the latest step of Taha’s and engineer Steve Webb’s radical campaign to bring structural stone back into use, after more than a century of it being relegated to cladding. It follows their striking Clerkenwell Close office and residential project across town, built from similarly rugged chunks of limestone, stacked with primal relish, which was shortlisted for the Stirling prize in 2021. The duo have become evangelical about the wonders of stone, creating experimental stone beams, laminated vaults and floor slabs, using pieces of rock that quarries often treat as waste.

Webb’s firm, Webb Yates, has even developed a slender pylon prototype, exhibited at the Royal Academy, using stone’s stiffness and buckling stability to reduce the amount of steel required. It’s only a matter of time, they hope, before the industry embraces the dawn of the new stone age.

Petra Heights is their biggest proof of concept yet. It rises above the station platform like an elemental cliff, with chunks of stone bulging out at points in bouldery lumps. The three towers, which taper as they climb, are connected to a central lift and stairs, and joined by a precipitous bridge at the upper levels. Wrapped with steel mesh, the stairway is open to the elements and spills on to a lush communal roof garden, all adding to the feeling of hiking up a rocky mountain path.

The foliage will soon grow its way up the facade, as at Clerkenwell, lending it the air of an ancient ruin. In a world first, even the lift shaft is made of stone. The slabs, three metres high and 10cm thick, were shipped from Norway and assembled on site, reaching the shaft’s full height in a single day. You half expect the lift itself to be a hollowed-out boulder winched up on a rope, but even Taha’s clients have their limits.

Originally designed in 2015, the project had a bumpy ride. As is not uncommon for developments in London, the site went through three different owners before the towers were built, each time seeing the original ambition somewhat diluted as successive developers cashed in on the increased land values. The proposed mass timber frame was deemed too expensive, although Taha says the switch to concrete ended up costing much more. That change also had knock-on effects, with stone elements getting chunkier to hold up the additional weight, and braced in places by steel diagonals.

The pandemic added further setbacks. The lower floors of Sicilian basalt were already up when Covid interrupted supply, leading the remaining floors to be built with igneous grey larvikite from Norway. Both were stained with a reddish wash to match. The colour variation gives an appropriately antique feel, heightened at the base by fragments of Celtic patterns carved into the pillars, as if these venerable columns might date back much further. This archaic quality is emphasised by the names of the architects, engineers, masons and contractors being carved in a runic typeface and picked out in gold. Perhaps more architects should sign their buildings, so passersby know where to direct their praise – or ire. “The common reaction from developers is that structural stone is too shocking,” says Taha. “They think the British population aren’t ready for it, and that people prefer brick. But if you look at the lists of the most popular towns and villages in the UK, it’s often Bath, Edinburgh, the Cotswolds. Guess what? They’re all made of stone.” Webb is fiercely critical of the scourge of carbon-hungry bricks as the default. “Bricks are the heaviest form of decoration you can imagine,” he says. “They require a huge amount of energy to fire – often using coal – and they’re weak as shit. They put a lot of weight on the building’s frame, so the frame and the foundations have to get bigger, and they’re really inconvenient because they expand and contract, so you have to put movement joints everywhere. And they’re not holding anything up – it’s just really heavy and expensive wallpaper.” In the last 10,000 years of building history, he argues, walls have held the floors up. But now we’ve got it back to front. “In the last 50 years or so, we’ve moved to floors holding the walls up,” he says, “which is utterly stupid.” He gestures out of the window of his office to a host of new high-rise blocks, where precast brick cladding panels are being craned on to concrete frames, each hefty piece of wall connected with steel brackets to the floor below. A stone-framed facade, however, can play the role of superstructure and cladding in one. It has a fraction of the embodied carbon, doesn’t move as much, and it’s cheaper. The slabs of Norwegian larvikite, for example, were rejects, of the kind usually used for motorway embankments. British quarries are slowly catching up. Taha and Webb see the most potential in smaller-sized offcuts, which could be used in the same way as bricks and laid by regular bricklayers, without the need for stonemasonry expertise. They have put their ideas to the test in a remarkable “stone demonstrator house”, a temporary structure in Earl’s Court that showcases pre-tensioned stone beams and columns, stone floor slabs and a self-supporting stone brick facade.

Commissioned by the Design Museum’s Future Observatory research hub, it represents up to a 90% carbon saving compared to conventional construction. And for anyone wondering if there is enough stone to go around, Webb has a sobering fact. If all eight billion people on the planet decided to rebuild their homes in stone, the total volume required would be about the same as Ben Nevis. Taha is busy on his next lithophilic project, a mixed-use development on the canal in Hackney using stone bricks and blocks, with dowel-laminated timber walls and floors, making it “carbon negative”. Incorporating photovoltaic brise-soleil shading panels and a canal water source heat pump, he says the building will generate 135% of its energy needs. It will sell power back to the grid in the warmer months, offering a bill-free life across the year.

Webb, meanwhile, is working on a load-bearing stone option for a 200-metre tower near Liverpool Street, which he says would do away with the usual colossal concrete core and columns. Heavy, dark granite elements at the base could transition to lighter, thinner limestone pieces towards the top, expressing the structural loads on the facade, and using each kind of stone for what it does best.

“It’s a massive opportunity for architects to change it up – a reason to make a new style,” says Webb. “The first iron bridge in Telford was designed with timber-like connections, because that’s all we knew. Similarly, the first concrete buildings copied stone techniques. At the moment, we’re basically just reinterpreting concrete buildings, but using stone. We’ve shown that you can make stone trusses, stone grid-shells, really high-tech stone structures.” His eyes widen. “Imagine a future of stone electricity pylons everywhere!”

This small Alaska town is swamped by cruise ship visitors every summer. But what happens when they all go home?

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 13:00:52 GMT

Skagway’s 1,100 permanent residents are caught between a boom time – when the ships bring more than a million tourists – and a lull in winter

October comes to the small Alaska coastal town of Skagway like a sigh. The shops that were bustling throughout the crazed tourist season are reducing their opening hours or beginning to close. The hordes of employees sleeping in overcrowded bunkhouses are leaving or have left.

The crowds of cruise passengers who have filled the streets since April, wearing lanyards emblazoned with the names of their ships, have dwindled to a trickle. Soon, they will all be gone. Snow is visible on the nearby mountains.

What is left after the season has ended and the last ship has disappeared from sight is a year-round community of about 1,100 people – on paper, at least – and the concern that, as the demands of the cruise ship industry grow, life in this small town is becoming more and more difficult.

“The year-round economy, the year-round population is one of my bigger concerns as someone who lives here,” says Skagway’s mayor, Orion Hanson. “What does Skagway do without a coffee shop to congregate in or without a restaurant open all the time? We don’t have a diner any more.”

Two local restaurants stay open, albeit with limited hours outside the cruise ship season. But the Sweet Tooth cafe, once a longstanding year-round diner, is gone. It is now a storefront for Diamonds International, a tax-free jewellery store that partners with cruise lines for onboard retail and shops in ports that open seasonally.

At the height of the Klondike gold rush, Skagway was the largest town in Alaska, with a population of about 10,000 people. In 1900, it became Alaska’s first official city. But by 1910, as the gold rush subsided, the population had dwindled to about 600 people.

It took a decade for that dramatic swing. Now, as one of the most popular cruise ship destinations in the world, it can happen in a single day, when thousands can flood on to Skagway’s streets from cruise ships, only to leave again when the sun sets. The most recent figures available show that more than 1.35 million tourists arrived in Skagway by cruise ship in 2025, alongside more than half a million crew – and the numbers are growing each year.

That means housing, services and infrastructure designed for a town of about 1,000 people having to accommodate an influx of thousands of workers who arrive in late winter and stay until early autumn.

“Part of the complication of Skagway is that you have such a boom in the summer and such a lull in the winter,” says Hanson. “In terms of revenue that’s not directly related to cruise ships there is not a lot.

“As we saw during the pandemic, we’re at risk,” he says. “If all your eggs are in one basket, it leaves you very vulnerable.”

Like many tourist towns, Skagway has a housing shortage. Unlike other towns, however, it is squeezed into a narrow valley set at the northern end of Alaska’s Inside Passage, a 500-mile maritime route that hugs the coast along Alaska and British Columbia. It is known for its rugged mountains, forests, glaciers and abundant wildlife; there are no realistic commuting options and no room to expand – the only road leads to Canada.

The Skagway Development Corporation commissioned a report in 2023 that found there were 644 housing units in town. In the years since, more have been added, but not enough for the town to accommodate the cruise ship industry and the businesses that support it, its permanent residents, seasonal employees and the workers and families who keep Skagway’s essential services running.

As a result, everything from warehouses to single-family homes, from tents to recreational vehicles or motorhomes, are accommodating the increasing numbers of seasonal workers each year.

“There’s a lot of congregate living and couch surfing,” says Al Wall, director of the town’s Dahl Memorial Clinic. “There are quite a few people that sleep in hammocks in the woods. And frankly, some would prefer to sleep in a hammock in a tree than stay in a crowded place with a bunch of people.”

In years past, many seasonal workers slept in camp sites. But a change in the town’s law forbidding season-long camping pushed them into traditional homes that previously housed the town’s established population.

Janilyn Heger, a longtime Skagwegian, owns the town’s distillery, Skagway Spirits. She and her husband Gary, who owns a construction company, once managed the town-owned camp sites.

“The city made the decision for whatever reason to abandon that type of housing, and that created a domino effect that has been a disaster for the community,” she says.

“Employers started buying buildings and displacing year-round housing and so now we’re at an absolute standstill. There’s none to be had.”

Skagway’s housing shortage has become so severe that many of the town’s limited hotels have been converted into accommodation for seasonal employees.

Longtime resident Mike Healy bought Sergeant Preston’s hotel from friends when he was unable to find land to build enough employee housing to meet his businesses’ needs.

“I didn’t want to purchase Sergeant Preston’s … I approached the city and said, hey, Municipality of Skagway, I am going to purchase the only year-round hotel in this community if you don’t free up some land for housing.”

Healy, not receiving an answer, duly converted the hotel into seasonal housing, part of a portfolio that provides off-season accommodation to visiting workers and contractors.

Jonathan Hillis, a town assembly member who owns the local Mountain Shop outdoor gear store, says that pattern is playing out across town.

“We have very few places now for independent travellers to stay, which is fostering this kind of cycle of more and more cruise ship tourists and fewer independent travellers.”

The scale of cruise tourism is a frequent topic of debate in towns throughout the Inside Passage. As the 2026 season winds down, these towns are consulting the docking schedules for 2027 and 2028, making note of the projected increase in tourism, and asking how much they can realistically handle.

One hundred miles south of Skagway in Alaska’s capital, Juneau, there have been repeated attempts to limit cruise ship tourism. After a ballot measure for “ship-free Saturdays” failed in 2024, the city introduced a voluntary limit on the number of ships that could dock daily.

Farther south in the Inside Passage, Ketchikan has reported more ships as a result of cruises adhering to Juneau’s limitations, while Sitka, also on the cruise ship destination trail, is reviewing its agreements with the industry after an anticipated increase in visitor numbers in 2027.

A survey conducted by Oregon State University reveals a nuanced position when it comes to the cruise sector in Skagway. Just over 40% of people who responded thought that the benefits of tourism outweighed the costs, compared with 25% who put it the other way round. Another 33% viewed the relationship as roughly balanced.

Whatever the sentiment, for a small town that is economically dependent on one industry for its livelihood, options are limited.

“There’s only so much we can do, even if we wanted to,” Hanson says. “We need to be incredibly careful about not rocking the boat.”

Ten air tankers were relocated to bases in Germany, Spain and Scotland, while Osprey transport aircraft were sent to nearby RAF Lakenheath. It is the second time the US has undertaken a hasty redeployment in the UK with some of its bombers pulled from RAF Fairford in October.

The latest incident was said to be in response to a threat from Iran, according to the Wall Street Journal, although British sources emphasised there was no immediate or direct danger to the base or the area nearby.

The prime minister’s official spokesperson said: “As you know, the US is one of our top security partners. We’re in constant communication with them, sharing intelligence and accessing threats together. Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”

Asked whether the government maintained that British bases were safe, he said: “Yes.”

Washington withdrew B-1 bombers from the Fairford base just over a month ago – a week after ⁠a suspected Iran-linked ​security incident in September. Two men have been charged with espionage offences on behalf of Iran after the episode.

The precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains ⁠under discussion among US officials, and the Pentagon has chosen to take a risk averse approach when it receives threats to planes on the ground after the first phase of the Iran war in the spring.

Five KC-135 Stratotankers, the same refuelling aircraft moved out of Mildenhall, were hit on the ground by an Iranian missile in Saudi Arabia in March, and the US is concerned about how well planes are protected on the ground.

UK security officials however believe that Iran does not have the capability to launch an explosive attack on a base in the UK, although Tehran may threaten to do so in an attempt to disrupt American military calculations.

Donald Trump, the US president, is considering whether to renew the bombing of Iran, although overnight he said further attacks were “highly unlikely” in the aftermath of last week’s midterm elections, when his Republican party was heavily defeated. Trump allies, including the vice-president, JD Vance, blamed the war for the poor results.

Luke Pollard, a British junior defence minister, told a military conference in Oslo “it was a decision for the US where they place their military assets” and that the UK was “investing more” in counter-drone capabilities and base protection.

Local residents are being advised to remain vigilant in case of any untoward developments in the vicinity of Mildenhall or other bases used by the US air force in the UK, though it was not said they faced any heightened risk.

However, the US had reportedly upgraded the security threat level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath on Monday, according to a US ‌official familiar with the ‌matter.

Cop31 may involve lots of talking about talking – but there are wins to be had

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:46:13 GMT

In this week’s newsletter: what to expect of the next two weeks at the critical UN climate talks. Plus, this week’s most important reads

Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The world has again convened for Cop, the annual ritual to confront humanity’s greatest-ever threat. Aside from its own lore and acronyms, this conference is starting to feel a little like Groundhog Day.

Representatives from almost all countries, bar the recalcitrant version of the US under Donald Trump, are here in Antalya, Turkey, to face a familiar if worsening challenge. (Even the Taliban are attending.)

The UN, which oversees these talks, has acknowledged the obvious fact that the previously agreed 1.5C global temperature-rise limit is set to be breached in just a few years, with the Earth amassing heat at an accelerating pace.

Wealthy countries, though, are still failing to meet commitments to assist poorer, vulnerable nations to cope with climate impacts. We are still cutting emissions far too slowly. We are still bickering over who should shoulder the most responsibility for this.

So what’s to be gained from Cop31? We’ll go into what to expect over the next two weeks, after this week’s most important reads – and a reminder that, through Cop31, Down to Earth will be coming to you twice a week from Guardian reporters here in Antalya.

Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?

‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate

Alien menace or victim of xenophobia? The battle over Britain’s parakeets

Since 1995, Cops have been vital in bringing the world together on the vexed question of the climate crisis, using the unwieldy cudgel of consensus decision-making and peer pressure to help forge the Paris agreement to limit the damage.

In many respects, this has been a success – at one point, the planet was staring down the barrel of a cataclysmic 4C temperature rise this century. That increase is now more in the range of 2.5C, aided by booming growth in clean energy. Such a warping of our climate is still disastrous (just think of the hellish summer many endured merely with the current level of global heating), but Cop has helped steer us away from even worse.

Still, some of the 100,000 delegates gathering here on the Mediterranean coast have been asking what, exactly, can be done here? The terms of the challenge don’t need further debate or agreement, we just have to start following through on our collective promise. Cop31 is another “implementation” Cop – its success hinges on countries going home afterwards and actually implementing things, rather than making more promises in an air-conditioned conference hall.

Political realities in other areas intrude like never before, too: the world is largely focused on war, inflation and a fracturing geopolitical order instead of the climate crisis. “This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer,” Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said yesterday at the opening of the two-week summit.

Cop is a holdout of an ideal where countries could thrash out problems by negotiation, as nominal equals. Whether that ideal still holds is being tested like never before. As Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and head of Cop31 negotiations, plaintively urged countries: “Friends, let’s show the world that multilateralism works. Let’s show the world we are equal to the challenge.”

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

Yet there are wins to be had at this Cop. The organisers (unusually, this summit is being shared between Turkey and Australia) are confident that a goal to increase the share of electricity in energy use can be adopted.

There won’t be a stunning breakthrough in eliminating the use of fossil fuels – the root of the problem yet still barely uttered due to the veto-like powers of oil- and gas producing states – but the Cop show should still stay on the road. To keep talking about keeping talking doesn’t feel adequate in the circumstances, but given where the world is now, that in itself is something to grasp on to.

Let’s see where the next two weeks take us.

‘The many v the money’ should frame the next US Congress

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:30:51 GMT

If Democrats want to keep the blue wave going into 2028, they have to take on the billionaire class

Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Judd Legum shined a spotlight on the role of dark money in US elections. Today’s edition was written by Naomi Klein, Guardian US columnist and author of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor.

To see the battle lines of the post-midterm era in sharp relief, look to Texas.

Just two days after her earthquake victory as the governor-elect, Gina informed reporters that she had already asked the parks and wildlife department to freeze a proposal to sell 1,300 acres (525 hectares) in a state park to SpaceX until she is sworn into her new office. The department complied with her request.

The Boca Chica state park is next door to Starbase, Elon Musk’s rocket launch facility and company town. That makes the park’s beaches and protected lands – a refuge for shore birds and sea turtles – the ideal location for SpaceX to expand.

“These are our beaches we’re talking about. I mean, selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “It’s unacceptable. Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas.”

This was not about shutting down “Elon Musk and his companies”, she went on, “but it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas. And that’s what changes now that I will be governor.”

When Hinojosa’s clips circulated on X, she was roundly mocked by Musk’s many fans: imagine valuing some “empty beaches” more than the need for ocean-front launchpads to the stars! Imagine caring more about some lowly birds than Musk’s hulking, phallic, silver rockets! She must be a [insert vomitorium of misogynistic, racist and ableist slurs here]. Musk, his boys and bots predicted, will just pick up his expensive toys and move them to still-Republican Louisiana or Florida, leaving economic carnage in his wake.

So far, Hinojosa seems unmoved. In Texas, she and Senator-elect James Talarico shaped their campaigns as battles of the many v the money, a vertical struggle pitting the vast majority of Texans, struggling to get by, against the increasingly concentrated wealth at the top – perfectly embodied by the man flooding their democracy with cash. As Talarico reminded an audience of supporters in Austin last month: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.”

The richest man in the world didn’t get his senator, or his governor, as the early clash over Boca Chica state park makes clear. What he did get – or rather, help produce – is an America polarized around a new political axis. On one side are ultrarich tech oligarchs, whose wealth is tethered to dreams of merging with machines and becoming multiplanetary, no matter the cost to our multispecies planet. On the other side are regular people, with human needs for things such as clean air, fresh water and healthcare – maybe even a day off at a public park – and who increasingly find themselves competing over these basics with sprawling datacentres and rocket launchers.

The oligarchs in this battle have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth, thus the threats that Musk will soon ditch Texas if its newly elected representatives dare to keep their promises to voters (just as he dumped California and Canada before that). If all else fails, maybe he will join his friend Peter Thiel in Argentina, which Javier Milei is rapidly turning into techno-libertarian laboratory (Interestingly, Tesla just launched an Argentine division.)

double quotation markThe oligarchs in this battle seem to have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth.

In sharp contrast, the masses of people in this battle, regardless of their political leanings, tend to be attached to where they live – to its cities, towns, public lands and to the only planet that we know of suited to human life. This is as true in Texas as it is in Tirana, Albania, where, under the banner of the “flamingo revolution” citizens have been in revolt for months against a different set of oligarchs who laid claim to a different beloved wildlife refuge for their private benefit.

In our book End Times Fascism, Astra Taylor and I characterize these as fights between “the leavers v the stayers” – and we make the case that they increasingly define our age. You can see these fault lines running through a great many of the hot-button issues that animated and energized this election cycle. There were the many ballot measures to tax the super-rich to pay for basic services, and entirely predictable tantrums from billionaires who threatened to pick and leave rather than pay up. There was the muscular, national backlash against artificial intelligence and datacenters, which focused on the ways this latest (final?) capitalist stage is devouring art, literature, incomes, lands, energy and wellbeing. (As the Guardian reported, “Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total.”)

The commitment to place, and to one another, was equally evident in the rage at the US war-of-choice in Iran, and at Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with many winning candidates including Abdul El-Sayed consistently stressing that the money being spent to kill children far away should be used to care for children at home, and that all children are equally deserving of life and opportunities.

Sign up to How We Win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

Similar dynamics were there, too, in the revolt against ICE: As Minnesota’s Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said in her victory speech, the movement that lifted her to power all began when Minnesotans decided to stand up to “masked goons shooting our neighbors”. And the faultlines were clearest of all in the white-hot anger at the legalized corruption at the heart of the US political system, now widely understood as the wellspring producing all the other depravities.

Writing in this space one month ago, Rebecca Solnit astutely characterized the midterms as “a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve”. Well, the results are in and they could scarcely be more decisive. The complicating factor, however, is that it is not only the GOP that is aligned with the tech overlords and their anti-human, anti-Earth agenda. Plenty of powerful Democrats have chosen to underwrite their political campaigns and their personal wealth portfolios by entangling themselves with the very individuals and corporations their voters just roundly and unequivocally rejected.

Shamefully, the campaign to defeat a California ballot measure that would have imposed a much-needed, one-time 5% tax on billionaires – one of few places where tech oligarchs clocked a victory last week – was only successful because powerful Democrats including outgoing governor (and presidential hopeful) Gavin Newsom sided with the billionaires (as did the incoming governor). Meanwhile, several Senate Democrats have joined with Republicans to push through a sweeping bill in the current lame-duck Congress that would dismantle a host of environmental protections and be a bonanza for fossil fuel companies and the datacentres that burn them.

This kind of betrayal is the surest path for Democrats to turn their historic midterm victories into entirely predictable defeats before the highly consequential 2028 presidential election.

In Texas, Hinojosa is showing a better way. By picking an early fight pitting public beaches against Musk’s private rockets, she is telling voters which side she is on – the side of life, not machines; the side of staying, not leaving. That is how the Democrats just won, and it is their path to continue winning.
