Slight fall in carbon emissions from fossil fuels as Iran war drives renewables push

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 11:55:06 GMT

However, authors of a comprehensive assessment to be presented at Cop31 warn talk of a global turnaround premature

Cop31 live – latest updates

Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.

The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.

Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The report was published in Nature Climate Change. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.

Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.

Glen Peters, research professor at the Cicero Centre for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak, unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions.”

About 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 will be emitted this year, according to the Global Carbon Budget, an annual assessment by scientists from scores of universities and science institutions around the world, published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

Energy demand continues to increase around the world, as more people gain access to electricity and are pulled out of poverty, but two-thirds of the increase is being met from rising generation from the sun and wind and the uptake of electric vehicles.

On the downside, emissions from deforestation and the conversion of land to agriculture have also ticked upward this year, leading to total carbon emissions rising slightly for the year, from 42.8bn tonnes last year to 43.3bn forecast for 2026.

The scientists warned that the world’s remaining “carbon budget” – the amount of carbon that can be poured into the atmosphere before global heating is likely to permanently exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels – was about 150bn tonnes, or less than four years at current rates.

Already, temperatures have exceeded the 1.5C threshold for more than two years, and El Niño conditions are heating the sea and air further. Global emissions must peak imminently and fall rapidly in subsequent years if the world is to have a chance of limiting the “overshoot” of temperatures above 1.5C.

after newsletter promotion

China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, is likely to reduce its carbon output by close to 1% this year, mostly because of a 5% reduction in oil use, following the Iran war. Peters said: “China has had flat emissions for the last few years after a fairly steep increase in the last decade. There’s been a lot of discussion about whether China has peaked or not. Whether this is just a one-off and China rebounds next year, we’ll have to wait and see, it’s too early to say.”

India’s emissions have grown strongly, mostly from an increase in coal use, while the country’s oil use has declined slightly. Emissions from the US are likely to fall by about 1.3% this year, as less coal is used, despite Trump’s attempts to boost it.

Bill Hare, chief executive of Climate Analytics, who was not involved in the research, cautioned against taking too much from the report. “The picture from the Global Carbon Budget is a flatline, not a decline – a projected fall of just 0.4% in 2026, a figure that is unfortunately statistically indistinguishable from zero,” he said. “We are heading towards a sustained breach of 1.5C by around 2030. With imminent overshoot, we are entitled to expect governments everywhere to move decisively to cut fossil fuel CO2 emissions.”

There seemed little sign of such a decisive move at Cop31, where more than 90 heads of state and government, and high-level representatives from more than 190 countries are gathering for a fortnight of talks on the climate crisis.

Hare said: “We see governments in countries such as Canada, the US and New Zealand rolling back climate policies as fast as they can, and countries such as Australia – co-president of Cop31 – continuing to press forward with massive coal and gas developments that are holding fossil fuel CO2 emissions at record levels. There is little sign yet that the Turkish and Australian leadership [of Cop31] intends to build on [the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels made three years ago] with stronger action.”

One leg in the air like you just don’t care? Eight classic power poses – and what they really mean

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 11:30:50 GMT

The pose of the moment is eye-catching and a little alarming. But it’s not the first to cause a stir. Here is a history of such stances, from the Angelina Jolie leg flash to Andrew Scott’s insouciant hand-in-pocket

You think you know your culture back to front, all the snooker moves that drove us to this point, and then something happens and you realise you haven’t been paying attention. I’m thinking of the modern celebrity power pose: one leg shooting high in the air, preferably while wearing a ballgown. It has to be a woman. If a man did it, he would be mocking a woman, making his power message: “I’m brave enough, and comfortable enough in my own skin, to mock ladies.” Which is powerful, to be fair.

When women do it – Victoria Beckham started it, Myleene Klass has dabbled, Amanda Holden does it all the time (even standing up) – other women liken them to a cat licking, sorry, grooming its butt. Once, memorably, Taylor Swift posted her cat doing this very thing on Insta. But what is this pose meant to be saying? “I may be a pop star or a TV celebrity, but with my flexibility and muscle tone, I am ready at any time to give my services to ballet”? “I don’t want to flash my pants, but I do want to show that I have a tan all the way up to that area, so while I fix this conundrum, may I treat you to one of my legs”? This can only be understood as the natural end point in the complete history of the power pose.

It wasn’t until a 2012 Ted talk by Amy Cuddy, a social psychologist, that the concept of the power pose went viral. Cuddy was not interested in the effect such a pose could have on others, but on whether it would make the poser feel more confident. While this remains a matter of scientific debate, the evidence seems to agree with her finding that it can boost confidence. Cuddy’s take was that anything open and expansive evokes power. The classic athlete’s V for victory, both arms outstretched as if to hug the sun, is open, but so is the slightly languid boss-of-the-room seated power pose, leaning back in your chair, legs crossed, feet on the desk and hands clasped behind your head. Cuddy also talked about the Wonder Woman, which caught on with celebrities because it needed neither context (such as a recent sporting win) nor equipment. You simply stood on the red carpet, hands on hips and legs apart. Triceps analysts praise its flattering upper-arm effects, but it’s more a timeless expression of confidence and agency.

Also in 2012, at the Oscars, Angelina Jolie posed with half her body as Wonder Woman and the other half with one leg jutting out from a Versace gown, as if it were making an escape. Who knows, this may have been a contractual agreement with the fashion house: “You can wear our dress as long as you make it look racy and not like a nun.” The important thing was a complication around coquettishness and power. Wonder Woman is not flirtatious: she is going to save whatever she’s there to save, and if you fall for her in the process, that is on you. The leg flash is more ambiguous. It is still very dominant, but it is undeniably erotic. Other celebs mimicked it, but more memorable were the memes, in which a long shapely leg was Photoshopped on to, among others, Miss Piggy, Meryl Streep and Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man. I think it was the assertion of power through sexiness that made people copy it, hold it up to the light, laugh at it and puzzle over it.

Jennifer Connelly loves shoving her hands in her pockets. If she were the only one doing it, it could mean anything – she might feel the cold. Only when you see Emma Watson, Olivia Palermo, Kristen Stewart and Marion Cotillard doing it can you place it on the power spectrum, and its vibe is rebellion. There is a trace of brat – taking your hands out of your pockets being the second law of the ladylike, after taking your elbows off the table – and a likable nonchalance. It’s not classically powerful, being a little more closed, but it’s very low cortisol. You don’t run away with your hands in your pockets.

Before Victoria Beckham popularised the radical high leg shoot, her look was the lean: hips forward, shoulders back. It’s quite a catwalk standard and makes more sense as a gait than a still photo. Walking along with a backwards lean, you look a bit gangster, whereas standing still, you look a bit out of whack. It transmits power, I guess, with the message: “I take no rules from anyone, not gravity, not the complex interrelation of muscle groups.”

Just before the TV adaptation of Normal People landed, in 2020, Paul Mescal was freaking out about his inexperience on the red carpet, and Andrew Scott gave him some advice: walk up to your mark, overshoot it, spin round, lean back, stick your hand in your pocket and – wham – you have maybe the most perfect guy-pose there is, the pocket-lean. Mescal and Scott can be relied on to do this on every red carpet, and it gives power-with-a-touch-of-humility, which is more important for a guy than for a woman. Yes, because of the patriarchy.

When Lupita Nyong’o poses on a red carpet, there is no discernible artifice. She stands up straight, her hands resting at her sides. You don’t need to flex all your muscles in a primal display of force and dominance. It is sometimes enough simply to hold your shoulders down and your neck long, your elegant collar-bone exposed, with the timeless message: “Come and have a go if you think you’re hard enough.” To be able to chill in a not-chilled environment is quite a statement.

This, you will immediately notice, is not a red carpet pose, since it is usually only attempted while sitting or lying down. Its visual language is heavily borrowed from the front of a Jane Fonda Original Workout video, circa 1982, and I think we have to assume involves some self-parody, since it takes all the elements of powerful body language – physical openness, muscular display, self-celebration – and chases them to their farthest edge, a stance no one has ever arrived at by accident. You would never watch TV with one leg perpendicular to the rest of your body.

Are the leg shooters mocking their own vanity, or the contradictory demands that a celebrity be superhuman yet relatable, strong yet fragile, and fantastical yet self-aware? You can tell when a power pose is effective because (to return to Cuddy), an interlocutor won’t mirror it, they’ll complement it. You loom, they shrink. Although how anyone would complement the shooting leg is impossible to say.

France’s response to protests is making Islamophobia worse. But ministers won’t even utter the word

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 11:22:05 GMT

French people like me live in fear because far-right hate speech goes unchecked. The consequences can be deadly

Anger at the dilapidated state of schools may have been the starting point for the unrest that has rocked France for over a month, but the protest movement has grown into something much bigger. It has widened to take in a far broader segment of society whose grievances, including institutional racism and Islamophobia, are now connecting.

I have no doubt that one of direct causes of this snowball effect is the repressive nature of the response to the initial protests, which were treated entirely as a matter of law and order – criminalised, not listened to.

Think back to the night of 17 October – the movement’s first major mobilisation – when the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, focused his response primarily on the looting in several cities. He called on the public to “choose a side”: either “the Republic – and therefore the security forces”, or “the rioters”. The following day, President Emmanuel Macron reaffirmed “the nation’s support” for the security forces, declaring that there was “no place for violence”.

What Macron did not say was what kind of violence we should reject. There was no mention of the shocking levels of brutality and force used by French police against protesters. Or the violence that has plunged nearly 10 million people into poverty.

And so, since 17 October, the protests have been met with increasingly harsh levels of repression, and the mobilisation of ever-larger deployments of security forces, including special police units and the military.

This needlessly securitised response to legitimate civic action reflects an “authoritarian drift”, as the head of one of the biggest trade unions said. But it also presents a serious, potentially lethal, threat to young people and racialised minorities.

Teenagers are now dealing with life-changing injuries because they took to the streets or blockaded their schools. Since 17 October, an estimated 5,000 people have been arrested in connection with protests, 85% of them minors, and many subjected to disproportionately harsh treatment in detention.

Seventeen children, for instance, spent the night of 20 October at the Bobigny police holding facility without bedding or mattresses. Lawyers who visited the site described conditions as inhumane and degrading. A photograph released by the lawyers brought me to tears. It showed teenagers huddled together, wrapped only in emergency foil blankets, curled up on the floor in fear.

The escalating “security-first” approach – of which young people are the victims – is setting up a dangerous future. We risk the emergence of a generation of young people who are maimed, scarred and traumatised by the forces who are supposed to ensure their safety. Clear democratic boundaries have to be restored urgently.

With further protests on the way, I feel a wave of overlapping emotions – and I know many others feel the same way. Anger, yes, and a determination to keep going because we still hope that our demands will ultimately be met. But there is also a profound sadness, exhaustion and fear. For me, as for many other French Muslims, this fear is visceral because we are so routinely vilified in a toxic public discourse by the far right.

This discourse can have deadly consequences. In the midst of the tension created by a militarised crackdown on protests, a racist and Islamophobic gun rampage in the town of Trappes, near Paris, on 23 October claimed the life of a young black man called Pengo Bossio Wangi. Five others, including a 12-year-old girl, were wounded. The suspect told police he had targeted individuals he perceived as “Muslim, African, or north African”. He also said he chose Trappes because he viewed it as a “hub for Islamists”.

That was a chilling echo of a remark made in 2022 by Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally (Rassemblement National), who described Trappes as “an Islamist republic in miniature”. Anti-terror investigators discovered stickers at the gunman’s home, some of which bore slogans such as “Long live France,” “RN” (National Rally), and “Proud to be French”. The suspect was not affiliated with the party and Bardella condemned the killings. Yet the media continues to platform far-right political figures – including those whose rhetoric regarding Muslim, Black and Arab communities is deeply troubling.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

To emerge from this crisis, France as a society must get over its collective amnesia around racist violence.

To consider the attack in Trappes as an isolated tragedy would be to erase a long history of violence directed at minority communities. We need only count our dead to understand the truth – which is that, for far too long, the lives of Black, Arab and Muslim French people have been placed in jeopardy by a failure to tackle systemic racism. We cannot simply accept as inevitable the sight of grieving families or tear-filled crowds – like those I saw in Trappes where Pengo was laid to rest on Saturday.

The authorities claim they are tackling the hatred shown to Muslims: Macron denounced the Trappes murder as racially motivated terror. But how credible is this when the French political class still challenges and disputes the term “Islamophobia”, and therefore fails to recognise it as a form of racism? Aurore Bergé, the minister in charge of combating discrimination, openly refuses to use what she calls an “invented” word.

The French media also needs to examine its biases urgently. Far-right political figures are granted repeated exposure, while the communities on the receiving end of hate speech often struggle to have their experiences heard.

The capacity of young people to take action – to claim their rights – in such bloody chaos should be recognised as truly admirable. But how do we hold on to hope for the future – for what lies ahead, and for the generations even younger than our own – when our own prospects seem so bleak?

Kamélia Ouaissa is a French journalist based in Paris

‘We said no, no, no, but they kept insisting’: the Paraguayan people battling a eucalyptus empire

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 11:00:49 GMT

It is Paraguay’s largest private investment but local people accuse a forestry giant of ignoring their contamination concerns over its vast plantation

When Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

But today, the minimum-wage work often dwindles and the well stops working during power cuts. More worrying are its eucalyptus plantations, which begin less than 200 metres from the community’s crops and homes.

Paracel is made up of the Paraguayan Zapag group, the Austrian pulp producer Heinzel and Swedish forestry company Girindus Investments. The project is expected to be the largest private investment in Paraguay’s history.

The company will reportedly invest about $5bn (£3.7bn) and create 7,000 jobs, mainly in the northern region of Concepción. Financed by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and Paraguay’s government, the company says it is protecting existing ecosystems while “reforesting” former ranchland with 162m eucalyptus trees to fight global heating.

It is also building an industrial plant to process these non-native trees – which already cover an area larger than New York City – into pulp for the global paper and packaging industry.

Paracel was championed by the then-president Santiago Peña, who headlined the construction launch of the company’s pulp mill in May.

Peña was removed from office and arrested this month over the collapse of Ueno Bank. He denies any wrongdoing. Though unrelated to Paracel, the case has cast uncertainty over the signature projects of his administration.

But an investigation by the Guardian with the local media outlets Consenso and the Paraguay Post, has documented accusations of water contamination, harmful pesticide use, worsening drought, land disputes and forced evictions in 12 communities.

Paracel is a “hidden monster that has quietly taken root”, says Benjamín Valiente, a human rights defender who works for the local Catholic diocese. “They’re murdering nature for profit.”

Official documents indicate that the plantations are being treated with sulfluramid, an insecticide that degrades into a “forever chemical” linked to cancer in humans. Sulfluramid is banned in the EU, one of Paracel’s two main export markets, along with China.

Paracel says it had “no record” of staff saying water near Tacuarita would be contaminated by its chemicals, as one of the company’s representatives had allegedly told the community. In a 39-page response to a request for comment, the company highlighted its “significant contributions to economic, social and environmental development in the area”.

Meanwhile, farmers in the town of Puentesiño, near Paracel’s plantations, accuse the company of occupying land earmarked for people living in poverty 50 years ago by presidential decree.

In March 2024, a local organisation occupied part of a disputed property and planted maize and cassava. At night, they say, the company used drones to spray the area with an unknown substance, leaving residents with headaches, vomiting and diarrhoea. After talks with Paracel, police evicted them in September 2025.

“We left crying like children,” says Bernardino Galeano, 67, the group’s leader, who now faces criminal charges.

Paracel says a government demarcation confirms its property title, and it conducted only ground-based spraying during the occupation.

The farmers also claim the plantations have dried up streams and wells. “It’s not just us humans that are suffering, but the animals too,” Galeano says. “What will they do without water?”

In the neighbouring region of Amambay, Paracel held consultations with the Indigenous Paĩ Tavyterã community of Cerro Akangué. “We said no, no and no,” says Ana Valiente, a local resident and an organiser with the Kuña Guaraní Aty (Association of Guaraní Women of Paraguay). “But they kept insisting.”

According to participants, Paracel indicated the project would go ahead regardless; the meetings were only to determine if they wanted solar panels, wells and jobs.

A report by the Bank Information Center and five other civil society organisations in 2022 said Paracel had not translated key documents into Spanish or Guaraní, had misled communities into consenting and failed to record those who objected.

Paracel “categorically” denies the claims, saying it had held 52 meetings in Guaraní accompanied by INDI, the government institute for Indigenous peoples. The year after the people of Cerro Akangué declined to participate, the company received an environmental licence to plant eucalyptus downstream of local watercourses.

Silvino Mendoza, another Paĩ Tavyterã local leader, asks of the process: “What sense does it make to consult us once the government has already given them permission?”

In interviews, residents say construction workers at Paracel’s plant – which the company says is being built to “the highest global sustainability standards” – suffered mass food poisoning from the meals they were provided, were made to work overtime, and were fired if they protested. “It’s gig work,” says Pedro Calonga, a 54-year-old local man, “not long-term employment.”

Paracel says it has not dismissed anyone over complaints, that forced overtime is prohibited by its internal code of ethics, and that it replaced the company blamed for the food poisoning. It employs 1,013 registered workers.

Documents obtained by this investigation show an official inquiry found that 252 hectares (623 acres) of forest cover – equivalent to about 350 football pitches – were lost at Rancho Z between 2004 and 2021, which Paracel bought in 2020. Paracel denies illegal deforestation, saying the loss predates its purchase. Satellite images show eucalyptus plantations on the former ranch a year before Paracel acquired it and the company says those plantations did not belong to it.

Margarita Amaral, 64, a retired teacher who once urged neighbours to support Paracel, now coordinates protests against it. “Those eucalyptus plantations will last five, six years. And what will be left? Sand, sun and earth.”

According to public statements, Paracel will harvest and replant its plantations every seven years. The company says it plans to operate in northern Paraguay “for the long term”.

The factory is in Paso Horqueta, one of Paraguay’s smallest and newest districts. “We started with nothing,” says the mayor, Cynthia Cabañas.

The district has no environmental officer and the taps are not working in the town hall; residents drink orange, silty water from a river downstream of the plantations.

Sign up to Global Dispatch

Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team

after newsletter promotion

Paracel pays no local taxes because the plant sits in a free trade zone.

Guillermo Achucarro, of the Paraguayan thinktank Base-Is, says Paracel has come to “replace the state in the poorest areas”, providing vaccination clinics, Red Cross medics and ID cards, and creating “a kind of enclave economy”.

“It’s like everything revolves around Paracel’s needs,” Achucarro says.

Paracel says it contributed $3.6m to the national treasury in 2025, having invested $1.4bn as of December 2025.

Drone images show a roughly 300-hectare area cleared of vegetation for the future pulp mill, whose treated wastewater will be discharged via an underwater pipe more than a mile away in the Paraguay River.

Yet experts say even state-of-the-art pulp mills can release contaminants when monitoring is weak or safeguards fail. In 2023, a plant owned by the Finnish company UPM in Uruguay leaked about 1m litres of caustic soda, killing fish and receiving a $188,000 fine. In March 2025, a tonne of sulphuric acid was released at an older UPM mill, resulting in a $40,000 penalty.

“The forestry industry has generated serious environmental, economic and social problems over the past 40 years,” says Daniel Peña Vergara, of the University of the Republic in Montevideo. “The promised jobs never materialised.”

The regional capital, also called Concepción, is 12 miles (20km) downriver of the factory and most of Paracel’s plantations; water is pumped from the river, treated and distributed to 30,000 households. “We drink that water,” says Crispín Díaz, 57, president of a fishers’ association. “With the poisons they’re using for the eucalyptus plantations, even young people and kids will get cancer,” he says. “Even the fish will suffer.”

According to a recent annual report, between 2023 and 2025, Paracel used 703 tonnes and 118,000 litres of herbicides, insecticides, fungicides, surfactants and spray oils, plus nearly 43,000 tonnes of fertiliser. Glyphosate, a weedkiller that Paracel uses in its plantations, was classified as “probably carcinogenic to humans” by the World Health Organization in 2015.

Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), which sulfluramid becomes when it degrades, was recently classified by the US Environmental Protection Agency as likely to be carcinogenic, with no safe level in drinking water. Chemicals used by agribusiness have been linked to paralysis and genetic damage among Paraguayan children. The UN has criticised Paraguay for failing to protect its citizens over several related deaths.

Paracel acknowledges the chemicals’ “known dangers” but says workers are trained to use them “responsibly”.

Meanwhile, Concepción’s governor, Liz Meza, describes how authorities have worked “hand in hand” with Paracel to pave roads and build a new hospital and a cancer clinic. “Every project has its pros and cons. Our job is to get ahead of the downsides,” she says.

Paracel, she argues, is a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” for a region trying to move beyond decades of deprivation and conflict between armed groups and the state.

Paracel says it monitors water quality and has not detected its agrochemicals in ground or surface water, sprays no closer than 100 metres from streams, communities and native forests, and complies with Forest Stewardship Council standards. It says drought in the area was mainly due to low rainfall, with its modelling showing plantations only reducing water levels by up to 2.3%.

“After six years working on the ground,” it says, “we have witnessed concrete transformations in the lives of hundreds of people.”

Multiple European pulp producers are looking at Paraguay, where labour is cheaper, trees grow faster and environmental laws are weaker. One UN expert has criticised the “flagrant double standards” of the US and Europe for exporting “highly dangerous” agrochemicals prohibited in their own countries to emerging economies such as Paraguay.

“The idea is to turn Paraguay into this whole pulping landscape,” says Jamie Gagliano, a Rutgers University doctoral candidate who is studying the sector. “But that’s only if this industry doesn’t collapse.”

In 2023, Verra, the world’s biggest carbon-credit certifier, rejected Paracel’s certification amid doubts about “additionality” – meaning the emission reductions would not have occurred without the carbon-credit revenue. The company had claimed it needed carbon revenue despite securing a $200m IDB loan.

Paracel’s own 2020 environmental review projected the project would be a net greenhouse gas emitter, with gross annual emissions of more than 400,000 tonnes of CO2-equivalent, similar to 93,000 petrol vehicles. The company says those figures are outdated.

In September, the company announced that Verra had approved its first batch of carbon credits, covering nearly 24,000 hectares of its plantations.

In the Paĩ Tavyterã village of Ita Guasu, amid one of Paraguay’s last fragments of Atlantic forest, a community leader, Luis Arce, 70, says individuals claiming to work for INDI put pressure on them to allow Paracel to plant their trees nearby. The community stood firm.

The forest, he says, is now disappearing. “Without it, the planet itself is growing weak.” Shown photos of Paracel’s “planted forests”, Arce and his family laugh at the empty space between the thin, identical trunks. “This is a forest,” the Indigenous elder says, gesturing to the surrounding hills.

Judging this year’s Booker prize taught me our humanity cannot be captured by algorithms and data

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 10:21:15 GMT

As the demand for information and transparency about our lives increases, these brilliant books dealt with shadows, mystery, privacy and intimacy

The first box of submissions for the 2026 Booker prize arrived by courier a few days before Christmas. As I made my way through 19 books over the next six weeks (they start you off at a leisurely pace) I spotted a theme: God is back. In novels set from antiquity to our contemporary world, from romances to comedies to thrillers, characters reached for transcendence and absolution and found themselves mired in all manner of sin, or at least spiritual confusion. Priests were popping up everywhere; people sought comfort in the ancient texts; near-biblical bouts of extreme weather would prove either cleansing or calamitous.

The boxes continued to arrive month after month, making me feel as though I was part of a very generous but exacting book club. There was the excitement of – as was the chair of this year’s judging panel Mary Beard’s method of choice – reaching your hand into the box, playing lucky dip to choose your next adventure. There was the joy of spotting recurring themes. Publishers decide which of their books to submit for consideration, and I’ve heard that it can lead to agonising second-guessing about what the judges may like (the preponderance of priests may have been due to the poet Patricia Lockwood, who wrote the wonderful memoir Priestdaddy, being on the panel). I heard reports of one publisher declaring: “Mary Beard hates sex scenes.” “I don’t hate them,” she said when I told her this, “but they can’t be bad.” She was true to her word. In our first meeting, I made the case for a novel I enjoyed. She later emailed us a description of a penis in it that was admittedly clumsy.

“Water is the chief of all metaphors,” a character says in Missouri Williams’s longlisted novel The Vivisectors, referencing John Donne. There were many drownings, and coasts proved to be fraught, charged spaces between the material and spirit worlds. Spring saw the arrival of novels about death, ghosts and karmic retribution. Time moved strangely in many books, appearing fuzzy and elastic. Surrealism was back. Bodies were failing and minds were unravelling. Three of the novels on our longlist featured characters with dementia, and their sense of being out of time and out of place in the universe seemed to reflect the emergent human condition. Glass houses were sparkling, foolish symbols of human ambition.

Why all these signs, and what could they possibly be pointing to? One answer could be found in how the future in these books often seemed like an implausible prospect. Gwendoline Riley’s longlisted The Palm House opens to a London awash in dust from fires in Europe and refers to “our Mad Max future”. The young protagonists in Djamel White’s All Them Dogs and Williams’s The Vivisectors only hope to survive a hostile present. The old world was falling away but, as Emma Cline observed in Switzy, “the new world not slurring over empty space”.

We had emerged out of the pandemic and into a time of war, an ongoing climate emergency and creeping transhumanism; novelists, too, were moving towards new forms and new ways of representing the world. Magic had arrived to fill the gap that reality left. Kenan Orhan’s The Renovation transports a Turkish prison to a bathroom in Italy to illuminate the agony of exile; a spell in Makenna Goodman’s Helen of Nowhere rounds out a parable about culture wars and male power. The characters in Chloe Aridjis’s The Shadow of the Object find themselves transfixed by the analogue magic lantern, a kind of projector with a light source, and the fantastical figures it casts.

Judging the Booker prize is a surreal combination of the public and private. For most of the time, you are at home alone with your books, then one day you’ll find yourself at a photoshoot next to Jarvis Cocker and Raymond Antrobus posing beautifully. This year, my own hermetic life of reading was mixed in with the recognition that out there, in the literary world, things were fractious. The debate about whether we have reached a post-literacy age rolls on. Accusations of AI misuse have started to swirl around literary prizes (only a handful of our novels discussed AI; I suspect we saw the dawn). Given how little money there is in it, there has long been a degree of masochism involved in being a writer. Now, the advent of large language models has made publishing any work feel like oiling the engine of our own obsolescence, providing fodder for the AI-generated summary, tithing the kingdom of gold belonging to three guys in the US.

The meeting to decide the winner took place last weekend. When I think of all six shortlisted novels, I think of how they undermine the idea that humanity is transparent and knowable, a thing to be data-mined and sucked into the machine. Here, instead, are stories about shadows and mystery, privacy and intimacy.

The gay men of Marlon James’s The Disappearers live by necessity in the hidden corners of Kingston, finding moments of release in the club; the king of Rebecca Perry’s May We Feed the King is a slippery figure, subject to many conflicting rumours within the court. Father and son remain unknown to each other in Douglas Stuart’s John of John; Luke Kennard’s Black Bag is, among many things, an ode to the perverse pleasures of literally denying the world your image (its premise: man encases himself in a black bag). “How blind we humans are,” the narrator observes in Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say. “We travel through life unsighted, grasping only the smallest details of one another’s selves, including our own. Thinking all the while that we can see.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The winner this year, M John Harrison’s The End of Everything, is filled with mystery and ambiguity. Aliens have arrived in Britain, ushering in a confusing and protracted apocalypse. The sea is full of strange objects; ghosts flit around the skies, and here it is the English who queue up at the coast to board ships in search of better futures. “I hoped for a future but it just isn’t here,” one character says to another. The book drops the reader into a Britain of thwarted hopes and dangerous nostalgia, of unintelligible technological progress and a decayed social contract, and in doing so, captures something about how it feels to be alive now. My favourite lines in it concern the old world. “In those days, many moments had been like that,” Harrison writes of the decadent “before times”, which sounds suspiciously like the New Labour 1990s: “Tainted by leisure chemicals, aspiration, the downwash of celebrity culture […] life had been like a huge silent beautiful blossom opening to the economic light.”

These are not soothing lines – it is not a soothing book – but it has bottled up something in the air and pinned it down in text. The before times have come and gone, and we seem to be moving towards something new, but do not yet know what. In the meantime, people will continue to write novels that will console and enchant, challenge and provoke. My year of reading has shown what a gift that can be.

Rebecca Liu is a Guardian commissioning editor

Jarvis Cocker on judging the Booker prize: ‘It’s just like being in a band’

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:00:34 GMT

The singer on how being in Pulp prepared him for judging a literary prize, reading 163 books while on tour, and feeling like the odd one out on the panel

M John Harrison becomes the first science fiction author to win the Booker prize

Judging the Booker prize is like being in a band. A band will often bring together a very disparate set of people, their only thing in common the fact they’re in the same group. And a good band takes account of the interests and strengths of its members – that’s how you get a unique sound. Being part of this year’s Booker prize judging panel – chaired by Mary Beard, and featuring the writers Patricia Lockwood, Raymond Antrobus and Rebecca Liu – felt much the same. We were all very different, but we had a common cause: to pick a good winner.

Both bands and Booker prize panels are, at least ostensibly, democracies (though in Pulp, I’m the singer, so I make more noise than everybody else). But they shouldn’t be bland democracies. Mary didn’t expect us to toe a party line, and our panel managed to avoid what can sometimes happen when you’re on a jury and you end up agreeing on the least offensive option.

Walking into the final judging meeting last Saturday, I had three books in mind that I would have been happy to see win, but I had no idea who we’d land on. We seesawed around quite a lot, and it took a while, but we eventually managed to settle on a winner. And no scones were thrown at each other in the process.

We agreed that The End of Everything by M John Harrison is not a particularly easy book to read. But that’s not because it’s badly written – it’s actually very well written. The author is telling us that the thing that has gone wrong with the world is something that no one can really understand. For too many readers, Harrison has flown under the radar – this book is a culmination of his craft.

I judged the Booker prize while touring – the 163 eligible novels helped fill long, usually very boring flights. I couldn’t lug around a massive bag of books, so I had to read them on my iPad. I wouldn’t recommend it as a reading experience, but in this case it did help me be fairly objective – I couldn’t be put off by a rubbish cover. I also wasn’t aware of the author’s name when I was reading a book, meaning any conscious or unconscious prejudices that I may have had towards them disappeared. I sometimes had to do a judging meeting while on tour – when in Sydney, the time difference meant one of the sessions ran from 1am to 3am (luckily it wasn’t the night we played).

I ended up reading The End of Everything three times. During the re-reading process, some of the books deepened – you saw bits that you missed on the first read – and others shallowed out – you felt like you’d got everything the first time round.

Going into the process, I was worried it would put me off reading. I also felt, rightly or wrongly, like I was the least qualified judge – the odd one out on a panel of established writers and industry professionals. So in some ways I’m surprised I enjoyed it so much. I’m definitely never going to read 163 books in a year again, but I’ve certainly become a faster reader – I now finish a book in three or four days (though I don’t know if that’ll last, or if I’ll slow down to my usual tortoiselike pace again). And I’ve discovered contemporary writers I love, who I’ll continue to follow.

I’d never been in a book club before this; reading had always been a solitary pursuit. But in the way that reading a book is sometimes a welcome relief from your own consciousness, listening to what the other judges, with different modes of life, had to say about the books was fascinating. Anyone who’s invited to be a Booker prize judge is in for a treat.

Will the Trump-supporting UK right share in his ignominy? No, it’s too dishonest for that

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:00:33 GMT

Sustained not by public opinion but by billionaire media owners, British rightwing commentators will embrace a Maga successor, not moderation

Hallelujahs and hosannas have been echoing around the democratic world over the last few weeks. The White House madman is a loser. Rejoice at Serbia, Hungary, Brazil and hold our breath for Israel.

Take heart from our best historians’ encouragements. Margaret MacMillan wrote in the Observer: “And now we can hope these elections will bring an end to cruelty, naked greed, contempt for decency, and the relentless vulgarity that tries to pass for boldness and authenticity. What a difference an election can make.”

Simon Schama in the Financial Times extolled “the majesty of the people expressed in free utterance, the sovereignty of laws enacted by elected legislatures and the institutionalised impermanence of leaders”, calling it the historian’s duty to mark “moments when the tide of history really does make a turn”.

I hope they are right. But I doubt Britain, Europe or other democracies will ever again altogether trust the “majesty” of US voters who could elect Donald Trump not once but twice. How blithely they overlooked the attempted coup after the 2020 election, pardoning his rioters, showering himself and family with gold and crypto, setting his immigrant-hunting ICE thugs to arrest people, promoting scoundrels, destroying the climate, weakening the judiciary, sabotaging international institutions, while betraying Ukraine to favour “humanitarian” tyrant Putin. Those same voters will always be there.

Are you astounded that Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since 1932, two years after electing Trump? These converts’ change of heart may run no deeper than Russell Brand’s Christianity. Vital fertiliser and fossil fuels blocked in the strait of Hormuz probably touched Kansas farmers more deeply than any epiphany about the values of the founding fathers or Trump’s moral and mental defects. That Clinton-era electoral maxim, “it’s the economy, stupid”, remains an eternal verity.

What do these US elections do for UK politics? Andy Burnham already knows to the tips of his toes that what matters is the cost of living and how things feel. “That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves. But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, and the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia,” he said at the Commonwealth summit.

I don’t know if it’s wise to admit to your voters that you are not in control, but at the mercy of the orange man in his veto hat. But saying the unsayable has done Burnham good, whether breaking the silence on Brexit harm or ending the pension triple lock. He has offered easements – £45 here, £100 there – knowing that horrendous energy bill rises and more ill-judged interest rate hikes by Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, could soon come. Burnham is right to be frank when renewed Iran warfare may send oil prices skyward. Last week’s AI market plunge will have reminded him painfully of the 2008 bank crash that he watched from his cabinet seat as Gordon Brown was swept from power. “Whatever they do, a crash takes every leader with it,” reminds Prof Rob Ford.

As US political winds sway British politics, Labour’s cheery morale beams from ear to ear. Burnham rides high, with recent figures better on growth, productivity, investment, and even wages up – though only fractionally above inflation. He is, reckons Ford, “at the peak”, by which he means as things inevitably get worse, tougher decisions will have to be made in the spending review: “Incumbency always drags leaders down.” His imminent 10-year plan may sharpen Labour’s purpose – or, as cynics say, bury problems into the never-never two elections ahead.

after newsletter promotion

Labour’s great asset is Burnham’s political intelligence. But how super-blessed they are in their opposition. Faragism fades and Kemi Badenoch ignores the changes in the air. Does she not read the polls? Tory voters, as ever, want lower taxes and curbs on immigration – but not her pledges to abolish any Brexit reset or new working rights, to leave the ECHR, reintroduce grammar schools or abandon climate net zero. No surprise that only 20% of Britons think her party is ready for government.

Against the winds of change, Badenoch is no readier to rethink direction than the flotilla of rightwing commentators, Trump apologists or fellow travellers who may criticise the US president, yet always prefer him to any Democrat opponent.

Let us not forget that the Spectator’s Roger Kimball backed Trump’s rebellion against the 2020 ballot. “Trump is right not to concede”, ran the headline. Douglas Murray backed Trump in Iran, after welcoming his re-election in the Sun: “Trump isn’t like most politicians. When he says he’s going to do a thing, he actually does it.” Andrew Roberts found historical justification for Trump’s glitzy Gaza riviera plan. Boris Johnson told the Sun: “When you look back at Trump’s last term in office, there is little doubt that the world felt safer and calmer and more stable.” Only the Daily Mail columnist Andrew Neil offered a mea culpa for his Trump support: “What fools we were not to take him at his own estimation but to think he could amount to something better.”

Sustained not by public opinion but by billionaire media owners, these commentators will switch to some Maga successor, not towards moderation.

Even if a fine Democrat president repairs friendships with old allies, everything has changed. Liberal democracies now know to stick together, defending ourselves. Admire that inventive, creative and bright-brained dynamo of a nation across the Atlantic. But, now that we’ve seen the underbelly of the beast, never quite trust it again.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Gen Z doesn‘t relish going to war – so what! You should worry more about the reckless generations that do

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 07:00:32 GMT

The right has found a new way to denigrate young people, but it is fatuous to assume that Britons of any age would not protect what is dear to them

Young people won’t go to war for Britain. So claimed numerous headlines last week, responding to findings in the British Social Attitudes survey. Except that the phrasing of the question was whether respondents placed importance on “the willingness to serve [in the military] in a time of need”, perhaps forgivably low for people thinking about things of more immediate importance to them such as getting on the housing ladder, getting a pay rise or finding employment at all.

Less than a quarter of under-35s regarded this as of high importance, and so here we are subjected to the same moralising as any vaguely leftwing politician who hesitates on the stock television interview question: would you push the big shiny red nuclear button? “An unbelievable attitude on display!” laments LBC’s Tom Swarbrick in response to a 23-year-old caller, Josh, who can’t imagine a circumstance where he would ever feel able to kill another person.

That belief that you could not take another person’s life is apparently the wrong instinct and an indication of everything that’s wrong with young people in the UK. The very worst charge: a lack of love for one’s country. Milk-livered zoomer communist pansyism, or whatever. The more generous interpretation has been that young people’s lack of commitment to Britain is unsurprising given the broken social contract: that our politicians are excessively deferential to the pensioner class, leaving young people with the bill, and young people don’t feel that they’ve been given a stake in society. According to Sophia Gaston, author of the report, a sense of generational fairness has had an impact on young people’s “willingness to put themselves on the line and defend [the] nation”.

But who wants war? Who views scenes of chaos and bloodshed and cheerfully imagines placing themselves within them? That simple question has been conspicuously absent from much of the discussion around the survey. What has shaped young people’s perceptions of war, and of Britain’s participation in it, more than the litany of strategic blunders and postcolonial overreach that have defined the conflicts of the 21st century? Besides, what kind of war should they be willing to serve in? Just any? Or one that will be determined illegal by many politicians and scholars, such as Iraq? Or one as catastrophic as the failed intervention in Libya?

And hang on, isn’t war supposed to be a terrible thing that we hope will never have to happen again? On the 100th anniversary of the outbreak of the first world war, my secondary school held a special assembly. The seats in the middle of the hall were arranged in a strange shape, and midway through the ceremony the boys sitting there were told to stand up. “That is how many students [from our school] died in the great war,” said my history teacher.

Young people are well aware of growing instability and that the old assumptions about peace in the west may not hold for much longer. Not with Vladimir Putin launching Europe’s largest and most destructive armed conflict since the second world war with the invasion of Ukraine – and with very real and credible threats against the UK from Russia, specifically Moscow-driven cyber and information attacks. In September, Nato allies upended a plot by Russian subs training to disable undersea cables , the basic infrastructure of the global internet.

So the question for young people is: what would we do in the case of a Russian invasion? Dover has been breached, there are tanks and troops closing in on Westminster, “good morning” is to be replaced by “доброе утро”. This is not a threat to be managed only by a conventional army, but one that requires resilience and belligerence from all of us. My answer to that is: look at what young people have done, in modern times and in history. Look at Ukraine – like anywhere, young people did not want war. When the moment came, they joined territorial defence units in their thousands, helped evacuate citizens and organised humanitarian responses.

Look at the young socialists and members of youth movements who joined the French resistance against Nazi occupation during the second world war, forming intelligence networks and carrying out acts of sabotage. Look at those who formed the Zazou counter-cultural movement, a subculture rebelling against the Vichy regime that was collaborating with the Nazis. These were young people who might not have joined a conventional army, but who nonetheless saw the need to defend their future.

See that quality, too, in Britain’s young people today. Many will point to their sacrifices during the Covid-19 pandemic, but I think more of youth-led movements and protests: resistance to immigration raids in defence of our neighbours, climate strikes, days of action protesting at the rising cost of education, even hunger strikes in solidarity with Palestine. These are not the chattering classes’ idea of bravery or rising to moments of peril, yet it is that spirit of asserting independence and control over one’s future that would need to be harnessed if ever a war were to reach these shores. Yet, like that young LBC caller, they are demonised for not being enthusiastic about going to war for a country that has not gone to war for them.

For all our discussion of patriotism, it is little said that people do not experience a nation through abstract ideas of borders and security, but rather through our communities, friends and families. When those are under threat, away from hypotheticals and chin-stroking debates about nuclear weapons, patriotism is a very different proposition: not about dying under a flag, but standing up for the people around you.

Shower orgasms, golf carts, spread-eagled on the stairs – it’s the 10 best Rivals sex scenes so far

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 07:00:32 GMT

From naked tennis to Richter-scale juddering near wildfowl, Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster features a whopping 33 romps. Ahead of season two’s return this week, gird your loins as we celebrate the busiest buttocks in Rutshire

Rejoice! Rejoice! Five months after it staggered off with its leotard around its ankles, Rivals has returned with six more bundles of ineffably filthy joy. Let perms be unconfined. What is Rivals about? Some say the bonkbuster is a fond take on the shoulder-padded excesses of the late 1980s. Others that this adaptation of the late Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire Chronicles is a flambéed critique of the era’s social and political mores, as the haves and have-somes fossick for glory among the cufflinks and consortiums of upper-class rural England.

And it is. But only slightly. Because what Rivals is really about is bums. Here a bum, there a bum, everywhere a bum bum. From the boisterous buttocks of the lower orders to the globular “cans” that besmirch the House of Lords, each of the series’ featured arses serves as a bouncing beacon of glee throughout Rivals’ many, many sex scenes. How many sex scenes? An astonishing 33 thus far, with the six new episodes promising more of the same, with clanging bells on.

But which of these sizzling set pieces have proved the most memorable? Let’s squat behind this unusually large saxophone and take a gander.

What better introduction to the MP for Chalford and Bisley than a closeup of his bum cheeks as they oscillate at 50,000ft to the “strains” of Robert Palmer’s Addicted to Love? “Gnnyarr,” says Rupert Campbell-Black (Alex Hassell), thrusting in the onboard loo as appreciative thrustee Beattie Johnson (Annabel Scholey) kneads his unleavened trouser-loaves. “Ooooh,” says everyone else, nodding contemplatively at what will become Rivals’ defining image: a Conservative minister’s buttocks quivering over the Cotswolds.

“Stop talking about Margaret Thatcher,” pleads Charles Fairburn (Gary Lamont), his erection wilting as aspiring MP Gerald Middleton (Hubert Burton) expresses his glee at the results of the general election. A political debate ensues (“You’re throwing away – puff – all your principles to work for a party that’s – oof – taking away gay men’s rights!” “I’m going to change things FROM THE INSIDE!” etc). And verily, tumescence is regained, the happy event flanked by those twin signifiers of 80s decadence: a budgie and a dead cheese plant.

Perhaps the most “it’s 1987” romp in the Rivals love-canon, its desk-slamming theatrics accompanied by high heels, flammable workwear and a perm the size of Sizewell B. While “business bastard” Tony Baddingham (David Tennant) snarls in his Man at C&A vest, poutingly ambitious actor Maud O’Hara (Victoria Smurfit) proceeds to pound his torso as if it were an executive stress toy. Frankly, the only thing that could make the scene more 1987 is if Thatcher burst in and privatised his hole-punch.

To Málaga, where a TV awards ceremony finds Rupert in full “Una Paloma Blanca” mode: jodhpurs puddling around his ankles in a swanky hotel suite as he brings on-off squeeze/business rival Cameron Cook (Nafessa Williams) to an “Olé!”-heavy climax. Teeth gnash and norks swing but the focus is, as ever, on Rupert’s tireless buttocks – which jackhammer with such intensity they’re little more than a gluteal blur, like paté smeared across the windscreen of a Honda Accord.

“You’re bloody brilliant,” says tiny-eyed electronics whiz Freddie Jones (Danny Dyer) to shy novelist Lizzie Vereker (Katherine Parkinson), the former’s sateen swim trunks trembling like flaps of ham pegged to a washing line. And yea, after many months of yearning, a splosh-centred union doth ensue, with sweet Freddie cradling Lizzie as if he’s about to baptise her. Which he is. Into the Church of Love. A nation wept.

“First of May, first of May, outdoor fucking starts today,” pouts Rupert, oozing towards Cameron like an oil spill in a cricket jumper. The bounder is right, by Jove, and here is the proof – a boggling “bonk montage” in which seemingly the entire population of Rutshire engages in acts of exterior ribaldry. Chief amid them: thrashing on a haystack; slamming against a golf cart; and Richter-scale juddering near wildfowl. It’s a scene of startling enthusiasm, even if the real-world consequences of such earthworks would surely be disastrous (eg structural damage to the A417).

“How delightfully ambitious of you, little brother,” smirks Tony, stumbling in on smarmy half-sibling Bas (Luke Pasqualino) as the latter engages in a “festive five-way” with a Jenga-tower of indistinguishable “lovelies”. A closer look at the enterprise reveals a Lovecraftian tableau of fleshy derangement, with a seemingly unclaimed lower leg rising vertically from the horror like a mast on HMS Sciatica.

Another “They’re at it again, Marjorie” montage of marmalade-dropping set pieces, you say? Accompanied by the theme to Ski Sunday? Why yes, as it happens. Now shush, because this one sees Rivals’ least satiable shaggers: a) bouncing on some manner of “bonking trestle” as Cameron thwacks Rupert’s glistening thighs with a riding crop; b) undulating in front of a mirror while watched by a pair of tutting labradors; and c) bellowing into one another’s faces while spread-eagled on the stairs.

Here, we are given a rare, courtside view of Rupert Campbell-Black’s clackers when Taggie O’Hara (Bella Maclean) stumbles upon his nude tennis match with the scheming Sarah Stratton (Emily Atack). “Gnnpfffft,” splutters poor Taggie, eyes on stalks as Rupert’s “ballboys” and “umpire” pendulate in the Rutshire breeze.

How best to describe the expression that grips TV presenter Declan O’Hara (Aidan Turner)’s densely moustached face as he endures an unexpected mid-shower orgasm courtesy of: a) faithless wife Maud’s “wandering hands”; and b) his arse? “Exalted horror”, perhaps? “Rapturous dread”? Or “ferret slowly realising he’s left a Findus Crispy Pancake in the oven?” Let’s go with the last one while agreeing the scene is a high-water mark in the Rivals sex-Jacuzzi, its frothy exuberance as hilarious as it is “blue”.

Russell Brand has been jailed. Now we have the power to identify more sex attackers like him

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 06:00:32 GMT

Workers in music, film, TV and theatre may not feel they can speak up about abuse, but the authority I lead is able to help them

Helena Kennedy KC is a Labour peer and the chair of the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority

Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in jail yesterday, after being convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. The details that emerged from his case have been shocking and at times deeply disturbing. We have witnessed the bravery of the women who came forward to seek justice – and the brazen and brutal sense of entitlement exhibited by a pampered star at the height of his fame.

The Brand trial brought into sharp relief many of the victim-blaming attitudes I have spent my professional life as a criminal barrister trying to challenge. Old tropes emerged about victims not screaming out during rape and not reporting immediately. This is why lawyers who conduct sex cases should be required to hold a certificate that they have undergone recent additional training. The justice system has to provide women with a fair opportunity to obtain justice, without subjecting them to discriminatory assumptions and further trauma.

However, I am encouraged that Brand’s convictions may indicate progress towards a more sophisticated understanding of consent, rather than simply writing off women who agreed to intimacy but are subjected to acts to which they gave no consent.

The case also tells us about the entertainment industry in which he operated. As the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said at the weekend: “I can’t say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is.” The abuse of power by senior people who exploit the vulnerability of others is certainly not confined to the creative industries, but the power dynamics in these industries are particularly acute. There are high-profile executives and “talent” whose fame and reputation can bring a hubris and sense of impunity.

The creative industries also rely on a huge freelance workforce, all on short-term contracts. Hiring practices are overwhelmingly informal – it’s all about who you know and what they think. For those at the bottom, reputation is everything. That’s why so many freelancers are scared to speak out when facing abuse or harassment; they are terrified they will be marked as “difficult” and jobs will simply dry up.

In my role as chair of the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA), I’m pleased to see the industry taking these issues seriously. We have worked with leaders in film, TV, music and theatre to develop and agree the CIISA Standards. These set minimum requirements for safe and inclusive working environments that apply to everyone; which in creative settings include informal spaces such as rehearsal rooms, tour buses and awards shows. The standards specify that everyone should know when, how and where to report concerns, anonymously if preferred, and how those concerns should be handled.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The BBC and ITV require production companies to adhere to these standards through their commissioning agreements, and Bafta has included them as part of the eligibility criteria for its film and TV awards. This kind of proactive preventive action and consistency of approach is vital. However, the vast majority of creative businesses are small. They don’t have HR teams, their budgets are shrinking while their workload is getting bigger, and they don’t always have the capacity to manage challenging situations as effectively as required. People can still fall through the cracks.

That’s why in June of this year parliament made CIISA an official whistleblowing body for those working in film, TV, music and theatre. Workers can now report confidentially to CIISA and be entitled to legal protections, even where they may have signed non-disclosure agreements – a pernicious practice that is far too prevalent for victims of harm in the creative sector. This means that for the first time we can now identify patterns of harmful or inappropriate behaviour across multiple projects, employers or even creative sectors. This will help us understand where problems persist, identify and report on emerging risks, and make evidence-based recommendations for change. In cases where there are urgent safeguarding concerns, CIISA can help people access the appropriate support and refer matters to the relevant authorities – which in the most serious cases will be the police.

This alone is by no means a solution itself to the problem of powerful men abusing their positions to exploit and abuse junior workers, but it is a start. We need to see more creative industry organisations adopt and implement these standards. Everyone deserves to work in dignity, and to know that unacceptable and abusive behaviour will be held to account.

Helena Kennedy KC is a Labour peer and the chair of the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority
