Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 06:00:30 GMT

Who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it

The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure.

1

One is the loneliest number, but it also allows you to stand out – especially in football, where you play by different rules and wear different attire. Nobody stood out quite like Yashin, the almost mythical USSR and Dinamo Moscow goalkeeper of the 1950s and 1960s. He often wore a flat cap in goal, and his trademark kit led to the nicknames “Black Spider” or “Black Panther” (strictly speaking, it should have been the less catchy Very Very Dark Blue Spider). Yashin remains the only goalkeeper to have won the Ballon d’Or; with a respectful nod to Dino Zoff, Peter Schmeichel and others, he was a simple choice.

2

It would be a crime against dynamism and flair if we didn’t give one of the traditional full-back numbers to a Brazilian. Some of their great right-backs didn’t actually wear No 2 – Djalma Santos and Carlos Alberto, World Cup-winners of 1958 and 1970, sported No 4 – but that still leaves us with the richest pickings. It’s hard to look beyond Cafu, a bullet train on the right for Brazil, Roma, Milan and others. He won two World Cups and is the only man to play in three consecutive finals. Chuck in more than 700 club games, and that’s a mind-boggling amount of runs up that right flank.

3

Few could dispute this choice. Maldini is No 3. Milan retired his number – it can only be used again if one of his sons plays for the club – and it’s almost a surprise Fifa didn’t do the same. As a left-back or left-sided centre-back, Maldini came as close as anyone to perfecting defending; on the ultra-rare occasions he was given a chasing, by Chris Waddle or Karel Poborsky, it was a JFK moment. It’s an oddity that he didn’t wear No 3 at Italia 90 or USA 94. But for most of his career, to see Maldini with any other number would have been like seeing James Bond in a shell suit.

4

For longevity and sheer class – on and off the field – Zanetti pips Pep Guardiola, Sergio Ramos and the aforementioned Brazilian right-backs to this number. A Swiss Army knife of a footballer, Zanetti was one of the first players to show that the positions of right-back and centre-midfield spoke the same language. He won 16 trophies in 19 years at Inter, 15 of them as a quietly inspirational captain. José Mourinho said “it was an honour to coach him”, while Maldini called him “my most respected enemy”. As was the case with Maldini, Zanetti’s number was retired by a Milanese giant.

5

With apologies to Zinedine Zidane, Fabio Cannavaro and Obdulio Varela, the terrifying and granite-willed captain of Uruguay’s 1950 World Cup winners, this was never in doubt. Beckenbauer, libero and captain of the all-conquering West Germany and Bayern Munich sides of the 1970s, was born to stroll around a football field, No 5 on his back, an imaginary Andrex-soft sax jazz soundtrack playing in the background. His biographer, Uli Hesse, wrote that the number “became synonymous with his unique interpretation of the libero role”. Nobody did it better; nobody ever will, which is essentially why, quite rightly, Bayern retired their No 5 shirt in December 2024.

6

Iconography trumps tactics on this one. In modern football, a No 6 is a deep-lying midfielder, but in the 20th century it was indelibly associated with a specific genre of centre-back: captains, leaders, legends. The list is headed by Bobby Moore, Tony Adams and the don; Baresi, a manager on the field for Arrigo Sacchi and Fabio Capello during Milan’s golden age, his shirt retired by the club in 1997. Baresi died this year; if you have any doubts that he is the definitive No 6, just look at the pictures from his funeral in August of this year.

7

This probably should have been given to Garrincha, who wore No 7 when he single-footedly won the 1962 World Cup for Brazil, but you can’t argue with a trademark. Never mind the trifling matter of almost 1,000 career goals, CR7 is a brand that includes fragrances, underwear, footwear, lifestyle hotels, a fitness app … even bottled water. It all started in 2003, when Sir Alex Ferguson encouraged the teenager from Portugal to embrace one of the most iconic shirts in football – Manchester United No 7s include George Best, Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and David Beckham. On a global scale, Ronaldo, now retired from international duty, is the most famous of the lot.

8

Desailly embraced the No 8 shirt when he was repurposed as a central midfielder at Milan then wore it when he played centre-half for the France team that won France 98 and Euro 2000. Desailly won the lot as a No 8, with the enduring memory of him in that number coming from the 1994 Champions League final, as the then 25-year-old rampaged through Barcelona to score the final goal. Xavi, for Spain, Andrés Iniesta, for Barcelona, and Socrates were strong shouts, all more traditional No 8s, but Desailly got the nod.

9

A choice that was painfully obvious, romantic and a bit dispiriting. Let’s start with the good stuff: Ronaldo 1.0 was the greatest young player we’ve ever seen, blessed like nobody before or since with the holy trinity of power, speed and skill. The dispiriting bit is that his Nike Mercurial R9 boots, unveiled in the buildup to France 98, catalysed an age of naked commercialism that football has never escaped. (Paradoxically, Ronaldo was wearing No 10 for Inter at the time, though that would soon change.) Let’s just remember the good stuff – R9, the first PlayStation footballer, and the platonic ideal of a distinctly Brazilian brilliance.

10

“No matter what happens and no matter who is in charge, the No 10 shirt will always be mine.” We’re not going to argue with Maradona, even if Lionel Messi, Pelé or Ferenc Puskas were the most compelling alternatives. To Maradona, the No 10 was a way of life, part of a uniquely Argentinian identity – that of the pibe, the creative genius from a poor background blessed with celestial skill and the vicious defiance of an alley cat. He even had the No 10 tattooed on his back. Close your eyes and you can probably see the font.

11

“I remember the first time I saw him,” said Sir Alex Ferguson. “He was 13 and just floated over the ground like a cocker spaniel chasing a piece of silver paper in the wind.” Giggs wore a lot of different numbers at the start of his career – 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 – but from the moment the Premier League introduced squad numbers in 1993, he was Manchester United’s No 11, even when he changed position in his dotage. There were other 24-carat contenders, including the Brazilian collective of Garrincha, Rivellino, Eder, Romario, Rivaldo and Ronaldinho, but none can match Giggs’s longevity or medal collection.

12

After an injury-ruined season with Milan, Van Basten started Euro 88 on the bench, both literally and numerically. He came in for the second game against England, scored a hat-trick and never looked back. A Hitchcockian late winner against the hosts, West Germany, was followed by an entirely preposterous volley in the final against USSR. From then on he was the Netherlands’ No 9. But the legend of No 12 endured, particularly when Thierry Henry was playing for France: he chose No 12 because of Van Basten. Were it not for the Dutchman, another Frenchman, the great Alain Giresse, would have been our choice.

13

The German sense of humour has always been underrated: they, more than any other country, have embraced the No 13 shirt. It’s been worn at major tournaments by Rudi Völler, Karl-Heinz Riedle, Michael Ballack, Thomas Müller – and Gerd Müller. He picked it for the 1970 and 1974 World Cups, and a triumphant Euro 72, as a nod to his childhood hero, Max Morlock, who scored in the 1954 World Cup final win over Hungary. Muller played 13 World Cup games and almost finished with 13 goals. The alternative ending was better: his 14th, in the 1974 final against the Netherlands, won the World Cup.

14

Cruyff’s first encounter with No 14 came by chance. Ajax’s Gerrie Muhren couldn’t find his usual No 7 shirt, so Cruyff gave him the No 9 and pulled the first spare shirt out of the bag. Ajax won, Cruyff kept wearing No 14 and embraced every connection: for example, he’d married his wife, Danny, on 2 December 1968 and pointed out that 2+12 and 6+8 both equal 14. The Cruyff Foundation later set up Schoolyard14, the key principle of which is the 14 Rules of Johan Cruyff. If he were a young footballer in 2026, Cruyff would be the first to have a symbol instead of a number.

15

This was the toughest of the teens, with nobody demanding selection. We plumped for a man who, as far as we can tell, spent only five games in the No 15 shirt. Falcão, an imperious box-to-box playmaker, missed all Brazil’s World Cup qualifiers for Spain 82 – Roma didn’t have to release him, so they didn’t – and as a result was not among Nos 1-11. But he played all five games at the tournament in the No 15 shirt and won the Silver Ball, which makes him officially the best player in the greatest attacking team many of us have ever seen.

16

Sham! Yes, it’s somewhat awkward having a certain era of Manchester City players on this list given “events” a few weeks ago, but, equally, it’s impossible to ignore them entirely given their achievements on the pitch, and that’s very much the case when it comes to Rodri, a man who completed football by the age of 30. He’s won the World Cup, the Euros, the Ballon d’Or, the Golden Ball, the Treble … the lot. When he moved to Barcelona in the summer, Rodri asked Fermin López if he could take the No 16 shirt that has served him so well. We assume it was a short conversation.

17

It’s all because of Wilfried Bony, you know. Bony was wearing No 14, the number Kevin De Bruyne wore at Wolfsburg, when De Bruyne moved to Manchester City in 2015. He picked No 17 instead. It’s apt there’s a “7” in there somewhere, such was De Bruyne’s devastating impact in the inside-right channel during his decade at the Etihad. His creative genius made him an irresistible choice, despite the appeal of Emmanuel Petit, Frank Rijkaard, Vitinha and even a young Cristiano Ronaldo. For a fair chunk of his time in England, De Bruyne was the best player in the best league in the world.

18

If you’re going to launch the toys, you might as well do it in style. When Ronaldo took the No 9 shirt at Inter in the summer of 1998 – the Brazilian had joined the club 12 months earlier and initially wore No 10 – the incumbent had an idea. Ivan Zamorano had worn No 9 for Chile, Sevilla, Real Madrid and Inter and took enormous pride in the symbolism of the shirt. So he switched to No 18 and had a plus sign stitched into the shirt: 1+8. Long before Lionel Messi, this was a different kind of false nine.

19

The Golden Ball winner at Italia 90 wore No 19. But enough about Toto Schillaci. Gascoigne’s unfettered, painfully innocent brilliance drove Bobby Robson’s team to the semi-finals of a tournament they were expected to stink out, and ultimately changed the game in his country. In 2009, England and West Germany met in a charity-match repeat of the 1990 semi-final. England wore Nos 1-11 – except Gascoigne, who had No 19 on his back. Robson, who died five days later, attended the match in a wheelchair. On the way home, he had one pressing question for his son: “How did Gascoigne play?”

20

Paolo Rossi, Clarence Seedorf and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are among those who have worn No 20 with great distinction but no one is, and probably ever will be, as synonymous with it as Jota. It was referenced in the song Liverpool fans sung about him with great lustre when he was alive and with great poignancy after he died, with the club’s retirement of the number and building of a ‘Forever 20’ memorial outside Anfield further tying the late Portuguese striker to the digits. Gone far too soon, Jota will never be forgotten.

21

The Italian was always a mature vintage, a smooth midfielder who could spot a pass from any angle. He could have played many of his games with a glass of wine in his hand and when he had his own vineyard, 21 Brut Rose was produced by Pratum Coller in honour of the great man’s squad number. No 21 adorned Pirlo’s back at Inter, Milan, Juventus and New York City, as he collected six Serie A titles and a couple of Champions League winner’s medals, not to mention a World Cup with Italy in 2006.

22

The 2007-08 Ballon d’Or was an inevitability for the magical Brazilian, who spent the year running riot with his third-choice of two little ducks. The attacking midfielder wanted No 8 or No 10 when he arrived in Milan but Gennaro Gattuso and Rui Costa were already in possession of those respective when he joined from São Paulo and the youngster was not going to mess with two legends. His time at Real Madrid, after a €67m move, was far less successful and Kaká returned to Milan after four years, taking back No 22 in the process.

23

With Raúl wearing No 7, Beckham needed a plan upon joining Real Madrid in July 2003. He turned to Michael Jordan for inspiration, asking for his iconic digits as he became a galáctico. When Beckham moved to LA Galaxy four years later, he stuck with No 23. “The connection with Jordan and how important the No 23 was, I just felt it was the right thing to do,” Beckham said. Sol Campbell was another strong contender for No 23 given he wore it at Tottenham and Arsenal, as was Marc-Vivien Foé, whose No 23 shirt was retired by Manchester City after his shock death in June 2003.

24

“I really hope to stay in the heart of this city so that one day, Napoli also retire the No 24,” Insigne said. The Naples-born forward spent 16 years with his boyhood club, which is certainly a good way to ingratiate himself with the fans, some of whom wanted him to take Maradona’s iconic No 10. “Maradona’s 10? I’m very superstitious, plus I wear 24 because it’s my wife’s birthday and it’s brought me luck,” Insigne said.

25

It says something about a player’s association with a number that his blessing is required before it can be passed on to someone else. And so it was in August 2023 that Zola gave Moisés Caicedo the go ahead to be Chelsea’s No 25, with no else deemed worthy of taking that status from the Italian for two whole decades. A bit much? Not really given the brilliance of Zola’s performances across seven seasons at the club. There was the skill, the goals, and that sense of joy that made him popular far beyond the boundaries of west London. Quite simply, everybody loved to watch Franco play.

26

Many academy graduates are desperate to rid themselves of their first squad number once they have settled into the first team but the Chelsea centre-back stuck with what he was given for 18 years. One of the reasons Terry did so was because he saw supporters getting it printed on their own shirts and did not want them to buy another. What a nice captain, leader, legend, and indeed why fix something that isn’t broke? When a mural of Terry and Antonio Conte was painted on to Stamford Bridge, the “26” was far more prominent than his face, which really does say something.

27

It was at Sampdoria where the No 27 became imprinted on Quagliarella’s back, and in tribute to his former teammate Niccolo Galli, who died in a road accident aged 17. “I have no doubt that had he lived, he would have been captain of Arsenal and of Italy,” Arsène Wenger said of Galli, who he managed in north London before his passing in February 2001. Quagliarella continued to honour Galli throughout his career, taking in moves to Udinese, Napoli and Juventus, every time ensuring he got the number he wanted. At Juve he spent two seasons with No 18, but the forward’s cherished number was with him for two Serie A titles.

28

History shows that No 28 is often discarded by those seeking fame and fortune – Cristiano Ronaldo had it at Sporting as a kid, Steven Gerrard likewise at Liverpool – but Touré wore it for four seasons at Arsenal, a period that saw him become an Invincible. That perhaps explains why, after a three-season dalliance with No 5, he reverted to what he knew upon joining Manchester City in July 2009, going on to win another Premier League title with this most random of numbers on his back. Quite clearly it meant a lot to him, and justifiably so.

29

“I have had it now for many years,” Havertz said of the number he’s worn at Bayer Leverkusen, Chelsea and Arsenal. “When I became a professional, I took it because it has some history with my brother – we used to take it always when we played video games together. Since then I just took it, and for me it’s the perfect number. I love to wear it in a red shirt again.” It’s as good a reason as any, to be honest, and given Havertz’s success in No 29, why he gets the nod over some other contenders, including Monaco-era Kylian Mbappé.

30

Sometimes it only takes a goal to etch a player into a club’s history, and when that goal is genuinely seismic, the number he wore at the time also takes on a grand status. And so it is that Grønkjær is our No 30 given that’s what the Danish winger had on when he scored Chelsea’s winner against Liverpool on the final day of the 2002-03 season. Chelsea subsequently secured Champions League football over Gérard Houllier’s side, which convinced Roman Abramovich to buy the club that summer and change Chelsea’s fortunes, as well as the landscape of modern football, for ever.

31

Upon signing for Manchester United in July 2015, Schweinsteiger was given the No 23 shirt. He quickly changed to No 31 and, really, that was no surprise given that was the number he wore throughout his golden 13-year spell at Bayern Munich, coming through the ranks to win eight Bundesliga titles and the Champions League. The midfielder kept it during his two years at United and also wore it during his two years at Chicago Fire. Quite simply Schweinsteiger is No 31 (albeit he mainly wore No 7 for Germany) and no one else comes close to challenging him on that.

32

This feels like a number that should have generated a lot of candidates but ultimately there weren’t many, and certainly no one as notable as Tevez. From the shock, awe and controversy of his three years at West Ham, to the rampaging success of his two-year spell at Manchester United, to the wild, wonderful and also controversial nature of his four years at Manchester City, Tevez well and truly made No 32 his own, going on to also wear it at Shanghai Shenhua and upon his return to Boca Juniors. With apologies to Joël Matip, but it wasn’t even close in the end.

33

This was an immediate lock-in given Cech’s reasons for taking this number upon joining Arsenal from Chelsea in 2015. He was 33 at the time, had played 333 games in the Premier League and – wait for it – 33 is number of vertebrae in the human spine. “Hope to be a part of the spine of the team,” Cech posted on social media on 11 July 2015. Seriously, what a guy. Speaking of Arsenal, Riccardo Calafiori was also in contention given he wore No 33 at Basel and Bologna before nabbing it upon his arrival at the Emirates two years ago.

34

The choice for this number came down to Nigel de Jong or Xhaka. The former wore it throughout his five seasons at Manchester City, four at Milan, one at LA Galaxy and one at Galatasaray. Strong but not strong enough given Xhaka wore it during his three seasons at Basel, four at Borussia Monchengladbach, five of his seven at Arsenal, two at Leverkusen and throughout his time so far at Sunderland. And here’s the clincher: the Switzerland captain adopted No 34 in the first place because that was the number of the bus he took to training when in the youth ranks at Basel. It just had to be him.

35

A couple of Argentinians were in the running for this number, namely Pablo Aimar, who wore No 35 at different times for Valencia and River Plate, and Diego Placente, who wore it throughout his five seasons at Bayer Leverkusen, a period in which he played an important role in them finishing runners-up in the Bundesliga and Champions League. But ultimately this was no contest given Akinfeev’s remarkable association with No 35, the Russian goalkeeper taking it on upon graduating from CSKA Moscow’s youth ranks to the first-team squad in 2003 and, 23 years later, still retaining it. That, folks, is dedication to your squad number.

36

Martín Zubimendi was a strong candidate for this number given the reason he adopted it upon joining Arsenal in July 2025 was because he also wore it when making his debut for Real Sociedad, his boyhood club, six years earlier. But, in the end, longevity overruled sentiment in favour of Darmian, who wore No 36 across a 10-year spell for Milan, Padova, Palermo, Torino, Manchester United, Parma and Inter. There doesn’t appear to be any specific reason why the Italian full-back was so wedded to such a random number, but he was, and for a long time.

37

Van de Ven has only worn No 37 for the past four seasons, ever since joining Tottenham from Wolfsburg in August 2023. He didn’t wear it while at the German club or at Volendam, where the Dutch centre-back began his career. But his reason for doing so is why he’s the clear choice. “A friend of mine passed away when we were young and it was always his favourite number,” Van de Ven revealed in a February 2024 interview. “So when I had the opportunity to choose No 37 when I signed for Tottenham … to be honest, it’s for him.”

38

Born in Australia and raised in Macau, Tombides joined West Ham’s academy in 2008 as a promising teenage striker. He had talent and dedication and made his first-team debut in a League Cup tie against Wigan in September 2012. That game came a year after Tombides had been diagnosed with testicular cancer. He died from the disease in April 2014, aged only 20. Shortly after, West Ham retired his No 38 shirt. It was only the second time the club had done such a thing, the first being with Bobby Moore’s No 6 shirt, a sign of just how well thought of young Tombides was in east London.

39

Guimarães chose No 39 upon making his debut for Athletico Paranaense in 2017 and has worn it ever since, at Lyon, Newcastle and now Arsenal, because it was the dispatch number of the taxi his father drove in Rio de Janeiro. Quite clearly it means a lot to the Brazil midfielder, as he made clear in an article published by The Players’ Tribune in February 2023. “For me 39 is special. No, it’s more than that. It’s magical. It gave me everything in life”. Sorry Marcus Rashford in his first season at Manchester United, but you’re not topping that.

40

Idrizaj joined Swansea from German club Eilenburg in August 2009 as a promising 21-year-old striker. He went on to make three first-team appearances that season with plenty more seemingly on the horizon. But on 15 May 2010, Idrizaj died of a suspected heart attack while at home in his native Austria. It was a sad shock that led to Swansea retiring the former Liverpool player’s No 40 shirt. That showed how much everyone at the club thought of him, which was seen again when Swansea’s players wore T-shirts bearing Idrizaj’s name after winning the 2011 Championship playoff final.

41

Rice’s reason for wearing No 41 throughout his time in West Ham’s first team and ever since joining Arsenal in July 2023 is pretty straightforward. “It was a number I was given in the [West Ham] academy by the kitman, Jamo. It’s stayed with me since,” he said. “Regardless of what happens in my career, I might stay with 41. ‘Rice 41’ has a nice ring to it”. That’s debatable, but what’s for sure is that Rice has become distinctly associated with the number as he’s gone about establishing himself as one of the best midfielders in the world.

42

Touré chose No 42 upon joining Manchester City in July 2010 because it was the reverse of the No 24 he had worn at Barcelona. A simple if somewhat odd motivation that very much did not backfire as the Ivorian went about making the number his own during an eight-year spell at City that saw him win three Premier League titles, two FA Cups, two League Cups and become one of the most impactful, impressive midfielders on the planet. Touré retained No 42 upon joining Olympiakos in September 2018 before going back to 24 at his final club – Qingdao Huanghai in China.

43

“It was my first number in professional football, it’s a lucky number I guess”. Klich’s reason for wearing No 43 is, like with many others, based on what was given to him at the start of his career, which in Klich’s case occurred at Cracovia in his native Poland. He subsequently wore it for two seasons at PEC Zwolle, one at FC Twente, six at Leeds, two at DC United, one at Atlanta United and now back at Cracovia. Klich never wore No 43 at Wolfsburg, Kaiserslautern or Utrecht, so it clearly doesn’t mean that much to him, but he’s done enough to make it on this list.

44

Has a man ever loved No 4 as much as Perisic? It feels unlikely given he has worn various versions of it – namely “4”, “14” and “44” – throughout his career. He’s not No 4 on this list because that is Javier Zanetti, which is also the reason why Perisic couldn’t have No 4 upon joining Inter in August 2015 – the number had been retired by the club in honour of the Argentina great the previous year. Perisic subsequently took No 44, which the Croatian also wore at Club Brugge and Borussia Dortmund. That’ll do as far as this list is concerned, especially given his only real rival is Massimo Oddo.

45

Why [always] him? Well, it could’ve been Roméo Lavia or one or two others, but ultimately it had to be the man who wore No 45 with great fuss and furore at Inter, Manchester City and Liverpool before also doing so at Milan, Brescia, Monza, Adana Demirspor, FC Sion and Genoa. No 45 has become the number for one of the careers of the modern era and the association is only strengthened by its sweet origin story. As Balotelli explained: “When I first played with Inter, the numbers for young players were No 36 to No 50. I took No 45 because four plus five is nine – and I scored. It brings me luck.”

46

The Italian goalkeeper represented 12 different clubs in a 19-year career and only wore No 46 at one of them. But he gets the nod because of the nice, circular nature of the association. Sirigu wanted No 6 before making his Serie A debut for Palermo in 2009 but was told he couldn’t because it wasn’t appropriate for a keeper by the manager, and someone who knows a thing or two about shot-stopping, Walter Zenga. So he chose No 46 because it was the one worn by the legendary Italian motorcyclist Valentino Rossi. Sirigu left Palermo in 2011 before returning 13 years later. The number he chose upon doing so? 46.

47

This was a shoo-in for a couple of reasons: Foden has worn the number throughout his time as a first-team player at Manchester City, which is verging on a decade and seen him win everything going, and because of the origin story. Foden’s grandfather Ronnie, a big City fan, passed away when he was only 47. “I was young when we lost him,” said Foden in a 2024 interview. “My dad said he loved playing football with me and that it would be amazing if I took the shirt number. I have loved it ever since.” Foden’s tribute to Ronnie extends to having “47” tattooed behind his right ear.

48

There’s no point sugarcoating it – this is a stretch. Jones only wore No 48 for two years at Liverpool, from 2018-2020, and there appears no interesting reason for him doing so. But the midfielder gets the nod because the competition is razor-thin bordering on nonexistent. It certainly helps Jones’s cause that he wore No 48 when scoring the winner in Liverpool’s FA Cup third-round victory over Everton at Anfield in January 2020. It was a superb, long-range curling finish that made Jones, at 18 years and 340 days, Liverpool’s youngest goalscorer in a Merseyside derby since Robbie Fowler in March 1994.

49

“Forty-nine, forty-nine, Lewis-Skelly” sing Arsenal supporters in praise of their academy graduate as well as in recognition of why he has kept hold of such a random number even after establishing himself in Mikel Arteta’s first-team squad. Lewis-Skelly was given the choice of changing to a more established number ahead of last season but stuck with No 49 because of its association with Arsenal’s Invincibles-era unbeaten run of games, and an Arsenal song ever since (‘Forty-nine, forty-nine undefeated’). Sound reasoning and enough to earn the 20-year-old a place on this list ahead of Ronaldinho, who wore No 49 at Atlético Mineiro and Querétaro.

50

Another shoo-in given the unsurprisingly sparse options for this number and the fact Markovic has worn it for the bulk of his long, nomadic career. He first adopted it when he broke through at Partizan Belgrade in 2011 and continued to do so at Benfica and Liverpool, as well as at Fenerbahce, Hull and Anderlecht – who he joined on loan during his time at Anfield – before taking it again upon his permanent return to Partizan in 2019. The Serbian winger has since gone on to wear it at Gaziantep FK, Trabzonspor, FC Baniyas and Apollon Limassol. Markovic is No 8 at current club, FK Cukaricki, but clearly, at heart, he’s Mr No 50.

Who have we missed from our this ultimate 1-50 list? Tell us the male player (or players) we should have included and why. Feel free to let us know why they mean so much to your club or country. Let us know in the form below.

How a Jordan mosque is recycling ritual water to create a green oasis

The Guardian Tue, 10 Nov 2026 05:00:29 GMT

In a country of severe water scarcity, the Abu Obeida mosque in Deir Alla captures ablution wastewater before it reaches the sewers to use for irrigation

The Abu Obeida mosque in Deir Alla, Balqa, to the west of Amman, stands in one of the hottest and most arid stretches of the Jordan valley. Yet an oasis of trees and flowerbeds surrounds it, improbably green against a landscape of bare ochre hills, watered by drip irrigation lines that run along the ground between the roots.

The water does not come from the municipal network, but from the taps where worshippers wash their hands, faces and feet before prayer.

Five times a day, Muslims across Jordan perform wudu – the ritual washing of hands, face and feet required before prayer. In a kingdom that receives just 61 cubic metres of renewable fresh water per person a year – less than one-eighth of the UN’s absolute water scarcity threshold of 500 cubic metres – every drop carries weight.

“People here understand water scarcity because they live it every day,” says Ahmed al-Rawsan, founder of the Jordanian Aqua Conservation Association (JACA), which manages the system at the mosque. “What we wanted to show is that the mosque, which already teaches conservation as a religious value, can practise it too.”

Jordan, with a population of 11.3 million, nearly 11 million of whom are practising Muslims, imports most of its food. Municipal water is rationed, delivered by pipe for as little as 12 hours a week in some areas, with households dependent on rooftop tanks to bridge the gaps. Which makes water used for ritual washing significant, says JACS.

According to a 2025 peer-reviewed study, 3.6m mosques worldwide use an estimated 22.5m cubic metres of water for ablution annually. In Jordan, there are more than 7,600 mosques, according to the Ministry of Awqaf.

JACA has been working on the issue since 2008. Pipes installed beneath the ablution area at the Abu Obeida mosque carry the used water to a treatment unit. From there, cleaned and filtered, it flows to the garden outside, to bushes and trees that would otherwise require watering from Jordan’s strained municipal supply.

“Mosques do not use soap during wudu, so there are no chemicals to complicate treatment,” al-Rawsan explains. “The water can be treated through natural sedimentation alone – passed through five layers of gravel and sand – before being redirected to irrigation.”

A white sign on Abu Obeida mosque’s stone wall declares the goals are to conserve water and improve the mosque’s environment. The Ministry of Awqaf’s logo is on the sign, a key project partner.

Sign up to Global Dispatch

Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team

after newsletter promotion

What began as a straightforward idea of capturing ablution water before it reaches the sewers took JACS 18 years to reach 18 mosques and schools. Expansion, al-Rawsan says, hit financial, technical and bureaucratic walls.

“In every mosque, the same question arose: who would take responsibility for the system once it was installed? The imam or the caretaker? Both are employed by the ministry but their roles are different. Without a clear assignment of responsibility, systems went without the maintenance they needed,” he says.

JACS collaborated with the ministry to incorporate water conservation into Friday sermons, and organised awareness seminars for preachers.

“Our training and awareness programmes have reached 1,200 muezzins, 750 female preachers, 110 imams and 28 technicians across the kingdom,” says Mohammad al-Tawalbeh, a ministry spokesperson. “Between 2017 and 2024, the ministry has implemented rainwater harvesting projects in more than 50 mosques. More than 35 mosques are already using ablution water for irrigation and cleaning.”

Mu’tasim Sa’idan, a former minister of irrigation, says Jordan is already among the world’s leaders in water reuse. “Approximately 150m cubic metres of wastewater are fully reused annually, with about 90% directed to irrigation,” he says.

But he is sceptical about ablution water’s potential. “The quantities are not what we imagine,” Sa’idan says.

Awareness has limits too. Abdullah Khaled, a worshipper at mosques in Amman, has often heard imams speak of Jordan’s severe water shortage and Muslims’ responsibility to ration water usage. The message, he says, does not always carry.

“A person may listen on Friday to a sermon about conserving water,” says Khaled, “then go home and leave his tank overflowing or the tap running.”

The Lights Go Out at Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s Bravest Newspaper

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

For more than 30 years, the paper covered an increasingly repressive Russia. “The process of silencing us started many years ago,” one of its journalists said.

By Valerie Hopkins

Photographs by Nanna Heitmann

Reporting from Moscow

Outside a five-story office building on Potapovsky Lane in Moscow, a group of journalists took down a metal plaque and installed a plastic one in its place: Novaya Gazeta Lived Here. White carnations, the flower that Russians associate with mourning, were placed on top of it.

Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s most daring independent newspaper for decades, closed its doors on Monday, the latest blow to Russians who value freedom of expression and human rights.

Its forced closure is emblematic of the Kremlin’s erasure of opinions, ideas and people that do not conform to its views. That process has been underway for years, but it has dramatically accelerated since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Novaya Gazeta’s journalists were packing up their offices when I visited on Monday. Its co-founder Dmitri A. Muratov, who shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for defending press freedom, was giving away personal items to colleagues and well-wishers.

He handed his emerald banker’s lamp to one of the paper’s last recruits, a video journalist. He kept for himself a fire evacuation floor plan, on which he asked staff members to sign their names where their offices had been.

The office once occupied by Anna Politkovskaya, an investigative journalist and Kremlin critic who was gunned down on President Vladimir V. Putin’s birthday in 2006, had already been cleared out. Her computer, eyeglasses and notebooks, left in place for 20 years after her murder, are now in storage.

While the occasion was somber, the journalists were not despondent. In many ways, it was a miracle that the newspaper had survived for as long as it had.

After its start in 1993, less than two years after the fall of the Soviet Union, Novaya Gazeta chronicled Russia’s chaotic 1990s, its consumerist 2000s, its increasingly repressive 2010s and Mr. Putin’s near-total consolidation of power in the 2020s.

It carried on even as six of its journalists were killed and others violently attacked. It kept publishing after its website was blocked, its media license revoked, its printing press seized and one of its journalists detained.

But it could not, at least in its current form, outlast Russia’s war in Ukraine. The double death blows came last month, when its landlord refused to renew the lease and the banks that had processed reader donations, the paper’s sole form of income, said they would stop doing so. None of the journalists consider this a coincidence.

“No one is in shock here,” one of the paper’s journalists, Tatiana Britskaya, said as she walked the halls amid the boxes and plastic wrap. “The process of silencing us started many years ago.”

The journalists had tried to adapt to Russia’s wartime reality. They did not report about what was happening on the front lines, because censorship laws passed in March 2022 had made it a crime to use anything but government sources for such reports.

Internally, they debated whether it made sense to keep operating under those conditions, and the newsroom had been divided about it, said Ms. Britskaya, 43. But she said their readers overwhelmingly wanted them to continue, even if they had to abide by the new laws.

“They said, ‘Continue, because many of us are post-Soviet people, and our entire lives were spent reading between the lines. What matters to us is that you stay with us,’” Ms. Britskaya said.

The paper published front pages with the word “war” blurred out. But its journalists wrote unflinchingly about lives that were taken or forever damaged by the conflict. With philanthropy and activism at the core of its mission, Novaya Gazeta also encouraged readers to help those in need of assistance and organized fund-raisers of its own. The paper made its antiwar position eminently clear, withstanding the pressure until it became insurmountable.

At noon on Monday, the journalists gathered for their final editorial meeting, as dozens of reporters — mostly foreigners — filmed the scene. The editor in chief, Sergei Sokolov, listed the articles and columns that would run in the final issue.

There was an investigation into an orphan rescued from an abusive psychiatric hospital, who was subsequently drafted and killed in the war. An article about teenagers who had fallen prey to scammers. A report on representatives from the antiwar Yabloko party taking office in the Parliament of Nizhny Novgorod, the only region of Russia that allowed the party to field candidates.

After announcing that Novaya Gazeta’s website and social media channels would stop being updated with new content at midnight, Mr. Sokolov recalled the words of the exiled Orthodox priest Andrei Kordochkin, a columnist for the paper who was stripped of his Moscow congregation because of his antiwar position. Despondency, Father Kordochkin had said, is the seventh sin.

Slowly, the journalists took down portraits of their six slain colleagues that had watched over every editorial meeting: Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Stanislav Markelov, Anastasia Baburova, Natalia Estemirova and Ms. Politkovskaya.

“We are not saying goodbye,” Mr. Sokolov said. “We definitely will return, because Novaya Gazeta is not a newspaper, not a website, it is an idea, a way of life for those who work here. And it is impossible to kill and impossible to close. We will live. I am sure that society, caught in this terrible time, will finally stir.”

The journalists went outside for a final photo as “Eto Vsyo” (That Is All), a popular rock ballad, played on a sound system. The song, a hit in 1994 for the Russian rock band D. D. T., is about loss and mourning, but also about the triumph of love. Its lead singer, Yuri Shevchuk, recorded a new acoustic version in honor of Novaya Gazeta after it announced that it would close.

Mr. Shevchuk is Russia’s Bruce Springsteen. After declaring that he opposed the war, he was interrogated, charged with “discrediting the Russian armed forces” and effectively blacklisted from performing in Russia. Now he only tours abroad, like all of Russia’s antiwar singers. The Kremlin has instead promoted nationalist artists who sing about the country’s greatness.

Mr. Muratov used the media coverage of the paper’s closure to call for distinguishing the Russian authorities from the people of Russia.

“This is not a war of Russia with Ukraine — it is a war of the Kremlin with Ukraine,” he said. “The people in our country who stand for peace were not given the opportunity to read what they want — we see this today — or to vote for the antiwar party, Yabloko, that they would have liked to vote for.”

He called for freedom for Russia’s thousands of political prisoners, and for humanitarian evacuations for Ukrainians trapped by the war. “This madness, this slaughter must be stopped,” he said. In contemporary Russia, those are dangerous words.

Among those who came to bid farewell was Yan Rachinsky, the former head of Memorial, the Russian rights group that shared the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize. Memorial, which was created to preserve the memory of those persecuted by the Soviet regime, was officially labeled “extremist” in April, making it a criminal offense to be affiliated with the group.

A small museum that was operated by Memorial, with rotating exhibits about life in the Soviet gulag, is now closed. Since Memorial was labeled an extremist group, memorials to victims of the gulag in public squares across Russia have been dismantled.

The Russian authorities have also gone after nonconformist communities. “Promoting” L. G. B. T. Q. relationships or a “child-free” lifestyle has been illegal for years. The police in Moscow recently carried out raids in the neighborhood of Kitai Gorod, a popular gathering place for counterculture youth.

The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, called the closure of Novaya Gazeta a “normal process of turnover.”

“Of course, every year some media outlets close, and new ones take their place,” he said on Monday during a call with reporters.

But Novaya’s journalists, and many of its readers, know this was not a matter of economics.

“When voices like these disappear from public life, it starts to feel like there are fewer and fewer people who think differently, like you’re alone in what you believe,” said a 21-year-old reader, Danila, a recent university graduate with a degree in computer programming. He asked that his last name not be published, to avoid trouble with the authorities.

“The less you hear people expressing views different from the official narrative,” he said, “the harder it gets to speak up yourself.”

Valerie Hopkins covers the war in Ukraine and how the conflict is changing Russia, Ukraine, Europe and the United States. She is based in Moscow.

With Its Giant I. P. O., Anthropic Ties Itself Closer to Nvidia

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Nvidia planned to invest $10 billion in Anthropic alongside its initial public offering, the largest of the new financial commitments from several giants to the A. I. company.

By Cory Weinberg

Reporting from San Francisco

For years, the artificial intelligence powerhouses Anthropic and Nvidia kept a distance from each other in their tightly connected industry.

They grew into two of the most valuable companies in the world without needing to do much business together, and their influential chief executives publicly sniped at each other over how the U. S. government should regulate A. I. technology.

But the two companies’ fortunes are now tied together as one prepares for its Wall Street coming-out party while the other braces for a prolonged corporate drama that has shaken up the A. I. industry and has investors on edge.

Anthropic, a leading maker of A. I. software tools, began wooing investors Tuesday for an initial public offering that could value it at up to $1.4 trillion. And in a reminder that Nvidia has become the financial engine behind the A. I. boom, Anthropic said Nvidia would be among the roster of A. I. companies to invest alongside the deal.

The chipmaker plans to invest about $10 billion in Anthropic immediately after its I. P. O., according to the investor prospectus. That would represent roughly 10 percent of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise this month, including in the I. P. O.

“Nvidia and Anthropic’s future are more intertwined than ever before,” said Kevin S. Xu, chief investment officer of Interconnected Capital, which invests in publicly traded A. I. companies.

Nvidia’s investment would far exceed the planned new investments by other companies that sell important hardware and cloud services to Anthropic, including Microsoft and the Taiwanese chip manufacturer TSMC. Alphabet, one of Anthropic’s largest existing backers, already planned to invest $10 billion as part of a previous investment obligation. The companies would buy a class of stock that would not give them votes over Anthropic’s corporate matters.

The investment comes at a difficult moment for Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, a prominent A. I power broker whose company has become one of the most valuable in the world.

On Sunday, he admitted he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, who U. S. intelligence agencies determined was a spy. The company’s board of directors said it would launch an investigation.

(China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)

Some of the world’s largest fund managers are now hoping Anthropic’s I. P. O. is successful enough to help make up for a weekslong slump in A. I. stocks. Nvidia’s stock has dropped by more than one-fifth over the past week, wiping away more than $500 billion of value.

A strong public debut for Anthropic also would represent a consolation for Nvidia, which is relying on selling advanced A. I. chips to Anthropic and companies that supply Anthropic with computing power, including SpaceX. The I. P. O. would raise up to $100 billion for Anthropic to help pay the bill.

It became more clear that the two companies needed each other toward the end of last year. Anthropic’s business had started growing more rapidly, surpassing $1 billion in quarterly sales last September, largely because of more sales to software developers for its tools that could automate much of their work.

That sent Anthropic in search of more computing capacity. But the company struggled to get enough chips and data center capacity to meet its needs from its existing partners, according to its prospectus. That led to Nvidia and Microsoft, significant allies of Anthropic’s rival OpenAI. The two tech giants signed their first major deals with Anthropic last November.

Mr. Huang along with Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, and Microsoft’s chief executive, Satya Nadella, stood in separate rooms in a split-screen video announcing the deal.

“Nvidia has led the way in this field and, in many ways, helped make this entire A. I. boom possible,” Dr. Amodei said, adding that the deal was the beginning of the companies’ relationship. “That’s just where we’re starting.”

The new partnership was a stark departure for both companies. Anthropic was started in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, just as the technology started progressing quickly. They used Nvidia’s chips for their early A. I. research.

But Anthropic, led by Dr. Amodei, later raised billions of dollars from the tech giants Alphabet and Amazon, which moved more aggressively to invest than Nvidia, Mr. Huang said on the A. I.-focused Dwarkesh Podcast this year. “That was my miss,” he admitted.

The investment that did not happen had other consequences for Nvidia.

Anthropic’s early employees wrote software programs so its A. I. model, called Claude, would work well across different types of chips, including Nvidia’s. But Anthropic took a stronger interest in chips developed by Alphabet and Amazon, which were trying to build their own chip businesses to compete with Nvidia.

Other C. E. O. s talked about begging Mr. Huang for access to his chips. But Anthropic did not have to go hat in hand to Mr. Huang’s company.

The strategy helped Anthropic. Its business started bleeding less cash than OpenAI’s, which relied more heavily on chips and financing from Nvidia. In its I. P. O. prospectus this week, Anthropic pointed to its “multi-chip compute approach” as a crucial competitive advantage that helped boost its financial performance.

“What Anthropic has done very shrewdly is they’ve diversified their hardware suppliers,” said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, an investment research company. “In retrospect, it looks like an incredibly smart decision.”

Nvidia was still amassing huge profits, but Anthropic’s growing success was a rare miss for its market dominance. Mr. Huang vowed to not let another A. I. investment opportunity pass him by, and Nvidia spread its growing cash pile across the industry, from start-ups developing A. I. applications to data centers.

For a while, where Mr. Huang appeared to have a clear edge over Dr. Amodei was in political influence. Mr. Huang talked frequently with President Trump, while Dr. Amodei was frequently at odds with administration officials, particularly at the Pentagon.

Dr. Amodei, who has compared the development of A. I. to a high-stakes project akin to the development of the nuclear bomb, has always taken a hard-line stance against chip sales to China. He said at the World Economic Forum in January that allowing Nvidia to sell chips to Chinese firms would be like the United States’ allowing sales of nuclear weapons to North Korea “because that produces some profit for Boeing.”

Mr. Huang pushed back on the analogy. “Lunacy,” he said on the Dwarkesh podcast this year.

Sri Muppidi contributed reporting.

Alina Habba Mildon Loses $50 Million Contract That Enraged Trump

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The former Trump lawyer had signed the contract with a family company weeks before the president gave the family’s patriarch a pardon.

By Tyler Pager

Alina Habba Mildon, one of President Trump’s former lawyers, was fired last week by the family company that gave her a $50 million contract weeks before Mr. Trump granted a pardon to the family’s patriarch.

In a letter dated Nov. 4, the company, Concord Partners, terminated Mrs. Mildon citing a “failure to perform duties,” according to a person close to the family and documents obtained by The New York Times. The person said Mrs. Mildon’s priorities appeared to shift away from Concord after she started dating Turhan Mildon, a 25-year-old Turkish investor, earlier this year.

The firing came days after the disclosure of the deal by The Times prompted an angry outburst from Mr. Trump, who called the deal “totally obnoxious and outrageous” and urged the Herrera family not to pay her.

Mrs. Mildon will keep $6.5 million that was already paid to her and her signing bonus of $8 million. But she had signed a four-year contract that would have paid her $10 million a year for four years along with a range of bonuses.

Concord Partners was set up in Florida late last year by Isabela Herrera, the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, a billionaire banker from a prominent Venezuelan family who was facing felony bribery charges in Puerto Rico before Mr. Trump pardoned him.

Representatives for the Herrera family declined to comment. Mrs. Mildon declined to comment, but a person close to her said she was planning to pursue legal action.

Mrs. Mildon, who was serving as a senior adviser to the attorney general at the time, began working for Concord on Jan. 1. She was brought on as general counsel, though the full scope of her responsibilities remains unclear. The person close to the Herrera family said she was hired to help with Mr. Herrera’s criminal case and with the company’s operations.

At the time, Mr. Herrera had already secured an unusually lenient plea deal that had reduced his charges to a misdemeanor campaign finance violation, and his legal team was trying to secure him a pardon. Ms. Herrera had donated $3.5 million to a super PAC tied to Mr. Trump.

Weeks after Mrs. Mildon started, Mr. Herrera was granted a full and unconditional pardon from Mr. Trump.

Mrs. Mildon has denied playing any role in the pardon and has declined to discuss her work for Concord.

“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D. O. J. — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” she said previously in a statement, referring to the Department of Justice.

Mrs. Mildon was a special government employee at the time, a status that allows people to work for the federal government for up to 130 days and maintain outside employment with conflict-of-interest restrictions.

After Mr. Trump was made aware of The Times’s disclosure of Mrs. Mildon’s contract last month, he erupted in anger. He told aides and allies that the Herrera family should stop paying her and suggested to some that Mrs. Mildon should donate to his future presidential library or another entity.

Mr. Trump also publicly criticized the deal and Mrs. Mildon.

“I thought it was terrible,” the president told reporters last month. “I told her, and I said, ‘I don’t want her paid.’ I thought we had somebody speak to the people that did it, and she used her relationship to do that. And it was far too much.”

In September, the Mildons were married in a lavish ceremony in New York with several senior Trump administration officials in attendance. Since then, Mr. Mildon has come under scrutiny over his various business dealings. The Times has found he has made misleading, exaggerated or disputed statements about his businesses, his influence with global leaders, his marriages and even his age.

Mr. Mildon is also at the center of a White House investigation after Mrs. Mildon accused Richard Grenell, another longtime Trump ally, of skimming money from a philanthropic donation made by her husband. Mr. Trump directed his aides to investigate her claims, and they concluded that a key element of the Mildons’ story did not add up.

White House officials said they found that the money in question, $17.6 million, came not from Mr. Mildon but instead from a government account in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Mr. Mildon has built ties to leading politicians and won business contracts.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Tech’s Biggest Companies Will See a Giant Payday From Anthropic’s I. P. O.

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Amazon and Google are the largest investors in the A. I. start-up, and their shares could gain hundreds of billions of dollars in value.

By Karen Weise

Reporting from Seattle

When Anthropic goes public this month in what is expected to be one of the biggest initial public offerings in history, it will mint billionaires and flood its hometown, San Francisco, with new wealth.

But some of the biggest beneficiaries will be tech industry giants that are already worth trillions of dollars. Amazon and Google invested in Anthropic and are its largest outside shareholders, together owning more than a quarter of its shares.

If Anthropic’s I. P. O. goes as it hopes, the company will be worth as much as $1.4 trillion. Amazon’s $18 billion investment could balloon to be worth more than $250 billion, and Google’s $33 billion into $140 billion.

The size and sheer speed of the gains are without parallel in the history of corporate venture investments. And they reflect a paradox of the artificial intelligence boom: While start-ups are at the forefront of A. I. development, the industry’s biggest companies have profited the most from demand for the technology.

Gil Luria, a tech analyst at the investment bank D. A. Davidson, estimated that more than $1 trillion in market capitalization — largely from providing the start-up cloud computing and offering its A. I. to their customers — for each of the companies was a direct result of their relationship with Anthropic.

A. I. is “an extraordinarily unusual opportunity to forever change the size” of Amazon, Andy Jassy, the company’s chief executive, told investors this year.

The big tech companies were in the position to benefit from Anthropic’s rise because they ran some of the most profitable businesses in the world. Like its close competitor OpenAI, Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago, needed huge cash infusions to pay for its A. I. development. Only a handful of companies were capable of providing that much money.

Even Nvidia, now one of the most valuable companies in the world, did not have that much money on hand a few years ago. The company simply wasn’t “in a position to make the multibillion-dollar investment into Anthropic so that they could use our compute,” Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, said on a podcast this year.

The bets on Anthropic were made when two factors collided. After Anthropic was founded in 2021, its early investors were primarily wealthy individuals, including Jaan Tallinn, a co-founder of Skype, and the cryptocurrency mogul Sam Bankman-Fried. After Mr. Bankman-Fried’s company collapsed in scandal and bankruptcy, Anthropic’s future was uncertain.

Just weeks later, OpenAI quietly released ChatGPT and ignited the A. I. race.

Amazon was an initial donor to OpenAI when it started as a nonprofit in 2015, but passed several years later when OpenAI was looking for a major partner to fuel its ambitions. Instead, Microsoft invested $1 billion in OpenAI in 2019.

The early success of ChatGPT, and its halo over Microsoft, set off a scramble for everyone else.

The big tech companies have seen a strategic benefit from working with Anthropic. They provided advanced chips and computing power to the start-up, and have access to Anthropic’s systems to sell to customers.

Google made its first Anthropic investment in 2023, and Anthropic committed to using Google’s in-house chips. In September 2023, Amazon, which was dogged by the perception that it was an A. I. laggard, put in its first $1.25 billion. At the same time, Anthropic named Amazon its primary provider of cloud computing services.

The relationship was “very symbiotic,” Adam Selipsky, who led Amazon’s cloud services division, said in an interview that fall. “Folks at Anthropic are very smart — some of the best technical minds in the world.”

Anthropic gave Amazon a cutting-edge customer that could push the tech company to radically improve its in-house A. I. chips, which aim to compete with Nvidia’s. And Amazon committed to provide Anthropic vast amounts of computing capacity.

Mr. Selipsky called the equity investment in Anthropic “a natural outcropping of that strong, strong business relationship.”

For Mr. Jassy, the investment was a low-risk bet because Amazon could promote its cloud relationship with Anthropic, said Matt McIlwain, a managing partner at Madrona Venture Group in Seattle.

“The upside,” Mr. McIlwain said, “came in the form of being a significant equity holder.”

Marc Benioff, the chief executive of Salesforce, said on a recent podcast that his company had also invested in Anthropic as a Plan B. He said Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, had told him that OpenAI’s relationship with Microsoft prevented Salesforce, a competitor, from investing.

“We felt like, ‘Whoa, we can’t go here — we’re going to have to go everywhere else,’ and so we ended up with Anthropic,” Mr. Benioff said. “I think we’ll make not just billions but maybe tens of billions of dollars on it,” he added.

Amazon and Google added to their investment over the years, and expanded their computing deals. Amazon is building one of the largest data centers on the globe specifically for Anthropic’s needs.

After the public offering, few expect the big tech companies to sell off most their stakes quickly. Google, Microsoft and a few others are planning to buy more shares in the private placement alongside Anthropic’s I. P. O. “Their stake is strategic,” Mr. Luria, the tech analyst, said, and the relationship gives them access to computing volumes and chip deals.

Whether the big tech companies are ultimately winners depends on whether A. I. demand ultimately justifies the enormous investments.

“There is a circularity in investing here, partly driven by not wanting to be left out,” said Aswath Damodaran, who teachers corporate finance and valuation at the Stern School of Business at New York University.

He likened the A. I. frenzy to building the biggest factory ever, but not knowing exactly what the factory will make, whether people will buy what it produces or how much they will pay for it.

“It is a loaded bet,” he said, “but I don’t think anybody wants to be left out of the bet.”

Karen Weise writes about technology for The Times and is based in Seattle. Her coverage focuses on Amazon and Microsoft, two of the most powerful companies in America.

On the Defense: Takeaways From Hegseth’s Remarks on Articles of Impeachment

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Hegseth Faces Impeachment

Advertisement

Supported by

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth broke a monthslong drought of press briefings to defend his record in office.

By John Ismay

Reporting from Washington

In a half-hour of remarks from the Pentagon press room, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday repeatedly attacked the motives of Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky, for introducing eight articles of impeachment against him.

He did not address Mr. Massie’s main argument: that he had taken U. S. military forces to war illegally by ignoring the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which limits the president’s ability to initiate or escalate military actions abroad without consent from Congress.

A preliminary vote on the articles of impeachment is expected Tuesday evening.

Mr. Hegseth had not addressed reporters at the Pentagon since May. Here are five takeaways from his on-camera appearance.

Mr. Hegseth said that an attack on him constitutes an attack on the military personnel who carried out his orders.

Mr. Massie’s actions, he said, put “a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time.”

“This is not patriotism,” he added. “This is sabotage.”

“Put the secretary on trial today, and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow,” Mr. Hegseth said.

Mr. Hegseth predicted that supporters of impeachment would fail, just as they twice failed to convict President Trump after impeaching him.

“They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week,” Mr. Hegseth said.

Mr. Hegseth repeatedly insisted that he had simply been following orders from the president in the military actions he has overseen.

“Every one” of the military operations and attacks he launched, the defense secretary said, “was a lawful operation ordered by the commander in chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress and executed by American warriors who did their jobs.”

“These are not high crimes,” he said. “This is the job.”

Ultimately, however, Congress will decide whether the secretary’s actions violated the Constitution and federal laws.

Mr. Massie’s articles sketch out a broad range of accusations along those lines, mostly focusing on times Mr. Hegseth has carried out offensive military action without the express permission of Congress.

The congressman cited Mr. Hegseth’s air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen that killed at least 208 civilians, airstrikes on dozens of boats in the Eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea that have killed 244 civilians, and the war with Iran as being legally problematic.

“In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of war or secretary of defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations,” Mr. Hegseth said at the beginning of his remarks.

However, one of Mr. Hegseth’s predecessors, William Belknap, was impeached in 1876, even though he resigned before the scheduled vote.

Mr. Hegseth cited examples of military actions that did not result in impeachment proceedings, including President Ronald Reagan’s decision to send troops to Lebanon. But Mr. Reagan received congressional authorization in 1983 to do so.

Mr. Hegseth also cited President Barack Obama’s and President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s strikes on Iraq and Syria, which were both carried out under the authorization for use of military force against Al Qaeda passed by Congress after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Mr. Trump repealed that authorization in December, months before launching the Iran war alongside Israel on Feb. 28.

Mr. Hegseth repeated his refrain that what he is doing is “peace through strength” — a slogan used by Senator Barry Goldwater, Republican of Arizona, during his 1964 run for the presidency and popularized by Mr. Reagan in the 1980s.

“Peace through strength,” Mr. Hegseth said on Tuesday morning. “Not as a slogan, but as a way of war.”

However, even as a candidate for office, Mr. Reagan said: “We have heard the phrase ‘peace through strength’ so often, its meaning has become blurred through overuse.”

John Ismay is a reporter covering the Pentagon for The Times. He served as an explosive ordnance disposal officer in the U. S. Navy.

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Supported by

The 41-year-old man, who was not named, was in custody pending possible charges after a joint investigation with the F. B. I. and U. S. military intelligence.

By Michael D. Shear

Reporting from London

Britain’s counterterrorism police said on Tuesday that they had arrested a member of the U. S. Army on suspicion of spying on behalf of Russia after a joint investigation with the F. B. I. and U. S. military intelligence.

The 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, England, about 100 miles west of London, and was in custody pending possible charges, officials said.

Officials did not name the man but said in a statement that he had been detained on suspicion of violating Section 1 and Section 3 of Britain’s National Security Act 2023. Those sections relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The police did not offer any other details, including about what the man was suspected of having done. In the police statement, the F. B. I.’s director, Kash Patel, is quoted as saying, “This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”

Mr. Patel added, “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this F. B. I. has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

The Metropolitan Police also said in a statement, “The country to which the allegations relate is Russia.”

The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of the U. S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in the police’s statement, “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”

The counterterrorism police in Britain have investigated several high-profile terrorism cases related to the United States in the past months, including two cases of arrests near air bases in England where the American military operates.

In September, five men were arrested and then later released on bail near R. A. F. Fairford in southern England. Two Latvian men were arrested in October on suspicion of a national security offense after breaching the perimeter of R. A. F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire, England.

In the statement on Tuesday, the police said the arrest of the U. S. Army member on suspicion of espionage was “not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.”

Valerie Hopkins contributed reporting.

Michael D. Shear is the chief U. K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

House Republicans Pick Jim Jordan, a Close Trump Ally, as Their Next Leader

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In choosing Mr. Jordan over Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, House Republicans signaled a desire for fresh leadership after their biggest election losses in decades.

By Michael Gold

Reporting from the Capitol

Divided House Republicans elected Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio to be their leader on Tuesday, elevating a pugilistic firebrand who has been a close ally of President Trump as they reel from a crushing defeat in the midterm elections.

Mr. Jordan, the current chairman of the Judiciary Committee, will replace Speaker Mike Johnson next year, when Republicans are relegated to the minority and effectively shut out of power. He will inherit a fractious and diminished conference that was already plagued by bitter infighting before it lost control of the House.

Mr. Jordan, 62, who was elected in a closed-door party meeting, will play a critical role in his party’s efforts to chart a path back to the majority. He will also lead Republicans’ efforts to shield Mr. Trump and his administration from an anticipated barrage of congressional investigations and oversight efforts from House Democrats.

In choosing Mr. Jordan, House Republicans signaled a desire for fresh leadership after their biggest election losses in decades. Mr. Jordan defeated Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, who is currently the No. 2 Republican and who has been in leadership since 2014.

But the conference was divided. The vote was 106 to 73, according to a person who attended and shared confidential details of the meeting on the condition of anonymity.

Drawing on his history as a fiery television commentator and his experience leading both the Judiciary and Oversight Committees, Mr. Jordan pitched himself as the candidate best prepared to fend off the coming Democratic majority.

Representative Warren Davidson of Ohio, a close friend of Mr. Jordan, said that case was central to his appeal to fellow lawmakers.

“Jim has spent his career exposing abuses of power by Democrats, bringing their political misconduct to light and challenging their efforts to use government authority against political opponents,” he said.

But Mr. Jordan faced some skepticism from members worried that his long history of incendiary talk could turn off moderate voters who repudiated hard-line MAGA politics in last week’s elections.

Before the vote, Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas said he believed Mr. Scalise, who is not as far to the right, would be better positioned to help Republicans reclaim the majority.

“To win back the House in the next election in 2028, we’ve got to speak to those swing districts and those swing voters that went to the Democratic side,” he said.

Both men had repeatedly eyed the top job over the years only to come up short, including when they competed for the speakership in 2023 after Republicans essentially deposed Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

But the political battle cost them both. Though Mr. Scalise had the support of a majority of House Republicans, he ultimately withdrew after right-wing members continued to support Mr. Jordan, who had been endorsed by Mr. Trump. Embittered supporters of Mr. Scalise then refused to select Mr. Jordan, clearing the way for Mr. Johnson’s sudden ascent.

Neither Mr. Trump nor Mr. Johnson, who abruptly took himself out of the running after Republicans’ stunning losses last week, publicly weighed in on who should hold the top G. O. P. slot in the House.

In the years since the speakership slipped away from him, Mr. Jordan worked to shore up the political vulnerabilities that have kept him out of Republican leadership.

A co-founder of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus, he became known for his combative stance not only toward Democrats but to his party’s leadership. Speaker John Boehner, whom Mr. Jordan helped pressure out of his job, once called Mr. Jordan a “legislative terrorist.”

But that same pugnaciousness helped him build support with his party’s conservative base, particularly as Republicans veered to the right under Mr. Trump. Since coming to Congress in 2007, Mr. Jordan has become a mainstay of Fox News. A former wrestler, he was an aggressive defender of Mr. Trump during the president’s first impeachment trial.

Still, Mr. Jordan’s factional attitude cost him support from mainstream Republicans who were turned off by his hard-line politics and his reputation as a firebrand. Nearly two dozen Republicans refused to vote for him as speaker in 2023, some of them vulnerable lawmakers in battleground districts and congressional institutionalists concerned about Mr. Jordan’s past demands for extreme spending cuts.

Many were also dismayed by a sexual abuse scandal at Ohio State University that threatened Mr. Jordan’s political career after it came to light in 2018. Mr. Jordan, who served as an assistant coach on the Ohio State wrestling team, was accused of turning a blind eye to abuse, an allegation he has denied.

Mr. Jordan has shifted his approach over the past year, particularly as polls suggested that Republicans would lose control of the House and create an opening for new leadership. While other right-wing Republicans have repeatedly stymied Mr. Johnson, Mr. Jordan has been a reliable ally to leadership.

He also became a strong fund-raiser for Republican candidates, lending financial support to candidates across the conservative spectrum.

During this year’s midterm campaigns, Mr. Jordan made a pointed effort to help vulnerable mainstream Republicans, including some who staunchly opposed his becoming speaker. On the trail, he stressed to right-leaning voters the importance of staying unified against what looked like an inevitable Democratic majority.

“What I’ve been doing is going all over the country reminding voters that if you elect Democrats, they’re going to pursue this radical agenda, and it is frightening,” Mr. Jordan said at an event in Myrtle Beach, S. C., the week before the election.

Catie Edmondson contributed reporting.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.
