This School Moves to a Different Beat

The New York Times November 10, 2026

In the South Bronx, the first program of its kind offers the same classes as any high school. Only these classes are dope.

In the South Bronx, the first program of its kind offers the same classes as any high school. Only these classes are dope.

Scenes from the inaugural weeks of the Bronx School of Hip Hop. Credit...

Supported by

By John Leland

Visuals by Anna Connors

It was just after 8 in the morning, and the D. J. in front of the school was spinning vintage hip-hop at celebratory volume.

Teenagers milled sleepily on the Bronx sidewalk, their internal clocks still on summer hours. It was a new school, and they were not sure what to expect.

Like: There’s a D. J.?

Inside, they entered through a 16-foot mural of a boombox, by the Bronx graffiti legends Tats Cru.

“Y’all made history this morning,” Jason Reyes, the principal, greeted them, beaming. His voice filled the auditorium. Now, he said, “All you got to do is step into your greatness.”

So began Day 1 at the Bronx School of Hip Hop, an experiment in public education that officials say is the first of its kind in the world.

It is not a performing arts school. Instead, the school uses hip-hop culture to teach the standard curriculum in a borough that has a long record of educational failure.

Fifty years ago, teenagers in the South Bronx created a culture that changed the way millions of people all over the world talk, walk, socialize, dress and dance. Now Mr. Reyes was asking a new generation to bring their own Bronx energy inside the classroom, not leave it behind when they enter.

For the inaugural class of ninth graders — the school will add another grade each year — it was a heady way to start high school.

“You are the 65 trailblazing students who are going to be the creators, the producers, the innovators, the artists, the entrepreneurs, the future teachers,” Meisha Porter, one of the school’s founders, told the assembly. “There are people thinking about you around the world that you don’t even know, and that is a powerful thing.”

The school’s genesis dates back to 2012, to a hashtag, #HipHopEd, posted by a Columbia University professor named Christopher Emdin. Dr. Emdin, who favors bow ties and speaks in equal parts Ivy League and hip-hop, had seen bright students in city schools tune out because the material did not seem relevant to their lives. Yet these same students would toil like monks writing rhymes or mastering dance moves.

This struck Dr. Emdin as a failure of the schools, but also an opportunity. Instead of demanding that students conform to a school’s norms, Dr. Emdin asked, what if schools adapted to the culture that the students brought with them?

He began to imagine a school where hip-hop — not just rap music, but the broad swath of post-civil rights Black and Latino culture — was central to the teaching.

“I’ve always been like, Yo, these schools suck,” Dr. Emdin said. “Let’s start a new school.”

In the South Bronx, Mr. Reyes was on his own journey toward hip-hop pedagogy.

Raised in the Soundview neighborhood, Mr. Reyes, 48, grew up in foster care or with an aunt who did not speak English. He wrote his first rhymes in sixth grade, using the rap name Opie because of his abundant freckles.

School did not interest him. “I just had to do what the teachers said, and I remember how awful that was,” he said. But rhyming made him want to improve his verbal skills, and beat-making stirred his interest in math.

He studied communications in college and in 2004 became a substitute teacher at a South Bronx middle school, using his hip-hop brio to connect with students.

When students struggled with fractions, he showed them how to take apart a 16-bar rap verse, breaking down the mathematical patterns in the rhyme schemes. At the same time, he had them analyze the texts and write their own verses. He kept his classroom door closed because he was diverging from the prescribed lesson plan.

“But the results spoke for themselves,” he said. Students’ test scores and attendance rose. He became a full-time teacher and finally the principal.

“My school started to hit numbers that we never hit before,” he said. “And that was all due to just celebrating who the child was and where they came from.”

Inside the education department, there was a push for “culturally responsive education” — essentially a D. E. I. program for the curriculum — and for small, “themed” high schools. The Bronx especially seemed ripe for a new approach: less than half of the borough’s students enter high school proficient in math or English.

A working group — academics, administrators, rappers, community organizations — began to coalesce. Part of hip-hop’s attraction was that it opened career paths in music, film, fashion, advertising, law and other fields.

Dr. Emdin and another professor, Edmund Adjapong, wrote a proposal for a school in the Bronx “that cultivates the genius in every child through culturally affirming, intellectually rigorous learning rooted in hip-hop.”

Then Covid shut everything down.

Six years later, in a building shared with two other schools, opening day at the Bronx School of Hip Hop brought not just Mayor Zohran Mamdani, but also the rappers Fat Joe and Grandmaster Melle Mel.

“Not everybody wants us to win,” Dr. Emdin said. “We know that, and they’re waiting for us to not win, so they can say, ‘Told you so.’ I know that, but we’re built for it.”

Mr. Reyes said he hired this year’s seven teachers less for their hip-hop prowess than for “how much they are going to value what kids are bringing to the table.”

By lunch on the first day, Rahmell White, a lanky 15-year-old with a downy wisp on his upper lip, already seemed at home. Like the other students, he did not have a clear idea of what hip-hop pedagogy was, but he knew that he liked the music.

“I want to start a record company,” he said. “I want to make music, and I want to do all of that.” Already he imagined recording a hip-hop compilation album with his new classmates. “I’m a student who can like school, but doesn’t like it a lot,” Rahmell said. “But this school, I feel like I can definitely like it a lot.”

Three weeks into the school year, Yasmin Silvera was showing her math class, called Geometry/DJing, a video of Johnny Dang, a jeweler who creates diamond-encrusted dental grills favored by rappers.

Using only a compass and straight edge, Ms. Silvera asked the students, could they construct a square like those in the grills Johnny Dang designed?

It was a real-world application of an abstract principle, one tailored to the students’ interests.

“There’s a lot of mathematical precision in this,” she told them. “And our job today is to recreate some of his precision.”

Students struggled with the exercise. Many had little or no prior instruction in geometry. Zyaire Baxter, who hopes to go to New York University to study acting or anime after high school, grew frustrated. “Ms. Silvera, I don’t know how to do it,” he said.

“Let’s go back in our notes,” she said. “Because I know you take copious notes. So let’s try it again.”

This time Zyaire figured it out. Ms. Silvera looked at his square. “Can you go show this to Kenneth and Gabriel?” she asked.

Down the hall, Michael Alba Lamb was getting a class of English 1/Emceeing students to write three sentences about Robert Moses and the Cross Bronx Expressway. The students had read short excerpts from Robert Caro’s “The Power Broker” and Jeff Chang’s “Can’t Stop Won’t Stop: A History of the Hip-Hop Generation,” which describe the highway as a destructive force that uprooted previously stable communities.

“Asking you to write analysis,” Mr. Lamb told the class. “Use evidence to support your claim.”

Mr. Lamb, 49, had discovered hip-hop in the late 1980s by watching “Yo! MTV Raps” as a teenager in Scarsdale, an affluent and predominantly white New York suburb. The music introduced him to questions of racial justice and ultimately led him to teach in the South Bronx.

The theme of his class was America versus the Bronx, exploring the conditions that gave rise to hip-hop in one of the city’s poorest neighborhoods.

Mr. Lamb read a statement from a student in the class: “The goal of Robert Moses’s urban plan was for roads to connect from Manhattan to the suburbs for rich white people, causing Black and brown low-income communities to be displaced.” How did the students — all Black or Latino — evaluate this statement? Mr. Lamb asked. What evidence could they bring to bear?

It was rudimentary, but it connected with the class. The highway was visible from the school, and most of the students lived amid the conditions created in its wake.

Allys Garcia and Edith Perez took different sides of the question. Edith saw displacement, but Allys questioned the explanation: If white people voluntarily fled to the suburbs, she asked, how did that displace Black and Latino Bronx residents?

Students were still writing as a beat played over the intercom to signal that second period was over.

Students were starting to adapt to the school’s rhythms. As with the teachers, each had a different idea about what made the school feel hip-hop.

Keira Binns, an aspiring choreographer and dancer who goes by Kie, lit up at the question.

What was hip-hop about her new school?

“Everything, honestly,” she said. “Everything. Everything. Hip-hop just screams everywhere.”

Ezequiel Garces went a step further. Ezequiel likes to D. J. but ultimately wants to be a firefighter. His favorite class so far was biology, learning about the human respiratory system.

“I feel like this is something different than school,” he said. “It’s not just relying on students to do all the work. It’s teachers actually helping you one-on-one and using hip-hop to teach you something.”

But the school really hits its hip-hop stride on “Freestyle Fridays,” when students can rap during lunch hour, using a boombox from Mr. Reyes’s office. On a Friday in late October, four students lined up for a chance on the mic. Another recorded video.

Jalen White, who stood a head taller than most of his classmates, was first in line. At the beginning of the semester he had been very quiet, but now that side of him was forgotten.

Jalen’s rhyme was about how he was slowly raising his profile on TikTok. “I was quiet in the room, now they listen when I speak,” he rhymed. “I put my hustle and I put my pain in the beat.”

Everybody whooped. Then Mr. Reyes spit a few verses.

It is too soon to say how effective the school will be, and for which students. The six-year graduation rate for Bronx high schools is just above 80 percent, which means one out of five students doesn’t graduate. (Citywide, the average is 87.5 percent.)

The school accepted any student who applied. Nearly a third receive special ed services, and several are new to English. Many arrived with spotty preparation from middle school.

“They didn’t really care in middle school,” Jalen said. Students walked out of class, with no real consequences, he said. “But here, everything you do has a consequence and it hurts your learning.”

So far, the students appeared genuinely happy to be in school, free of the resistance common among ninth graders. And they were strikingly supportive of one another, whooping whenever anyone had a good line in class. Two months into the school year, attendance was over 95 percent, well above the citywide average.

“It feels very different,” said Shakyra Johnson, who seemed to glide through her early classes. “I feel I’m able to understand how even things like hip-hop can be related to school because I didn’t know you could relate the two things in one. And I like the environment.”

The school has as yet avoided the longstanding criticisms of culturally responsive teaching: that it dumbs down the instruction or panders to what students already know.

Kamar Samuels, the schools chancellor, dismissed such criticisms. “One thing we know is that when you are connected to school,” he said — “when you’re elevating your culture, with rigorous instruction, especially for marginalized people — this is when most kids will succeed.”

In limited studies, schools that added culturally responsive curricula have seen improvements in attendance and standardized test scores, and teachers have reported that students are more motivated and engaged, better at critical thinking.

Mr. Samuels cited Zaretta Hammond, author of “Culturally Responsive Teaching and the Brain,” that all teaching is culturally responsive. “It’s a matter of whose culture it’s responding to,” he said.

In coming years, the school will stress entrepreneurship and offer technical classes, including certification programs in Pro Tools, Adobe Illustrator and Final Cut Pro. For this year, Mr. Reyes wanted students to understand “that lived experiences, dialects, Bronx identity” — realms in which they are masters — “are sources of profound wisdom and intellectual power.”

By graduation, he said, students should be able to present themselves confidently — to “command the mic,” as he put it — and to apply their Bronx voice to their world, as their peers did a half century ago.

“Public speaking becomes leadership,” he said. “This is not just, I gotta learn about ‘Romeo and Juliet.’ Ninth graders are fully aware of where they live, their conditions and what needs to be addressed, and we want our young people to go out in the world and create and effect change.”

For a public school in the Bronx, this is not a small order. And for the Bronx School of Hip Hop, it is still aspirational. The school’s plan calls for it to evolve as students shape and eventually help teach some of their classes. As Mr. Reyes told them on Day 1, “You are going to make this school what it is.”

But in its sheer swagger, the school is nothing if not hip-hop. “What we are building,” Mr. Reyes said, “is a new model for what public education can become.”

John Leland is a reporter covering life in New York City for The Times.

The Woman in the Middle of Nvidia’s Spy Scandal

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Alice Huang, who U. S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset, emerged from the high-flying world of Shanghai finance to work with tech titans and obtain essential A. I. chips.

By Paul MozurAna SwansonTripp Mickle and Michael Forsythe

Paul Mozur reported from Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia. Ana Swanson reported from Washington. Tripp Mickle reported from San Francisco and Michael Forsythe from New York.

In December 2023, a Chinese executive who goes by Alice Huang met with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, and a small group of colleagues at an Italian restaurant in Singapore.

In a photo of the previously unreported meeting, which was confirmed by The New York Times, Ms. Huang smiled as she posed next to Mr. Huang, who was in his trademark black leather jacket. He held a glass of red wine.

For Ms. Huang, there was reason to celebrate. Backed by wealthy investors in Shanghai, she had just restructured a company that would soon buy billions of dollars in Nvidia artificial intelligence chips. The U. S. government had barred Chinese companies from buying the advanced chips, but Ms. Huang had sidestepped this prohibition by creating a firm, Megaspeed, through a Singaporean shell company.

Her close relationship with Nvidia’s leader also appeared to smooth the way. Four days after the ownership change Megaspeed was named an Nvidia cloud partner, giving it access to the coveted components.

Their relationship is now at the center of a global geopolitical competition between China and the U. S. government to dominate A. I. It has also shaken and captivated the tech industry on both sides of the Pacific, surfacing often invisible details of the fierce technological race, like spy craft and the human vulnerabilities of A. I. kingmakers like Mr. Huang.

The meeting in Singapore was a sign of how Ms. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Huang goes back further than previously known. It also speaks to the close social and business ties that grew during years of tech collaboration between China and the United States, and how they have persisted despite the icy geopolitical divide of the past decade.

The Times was the first to report Mr. Huang’s dealings with Megaspeed and Ms. Huang last year. Last month, The Times reported that U. S. officials had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had developed a close relationship with the Nvidia leader, and that President Trump had taken no action when briefed on the situation last year. Last week, The Times reported that Ms. Huang had been recruited to spy by China’s Ministry of State Security. On Sunday, Mr. Huang, 63, acknowledged that he had an affair with her, and Nvidia said it was conducting an internal investigation.

Many details of the relationship between Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang, including when they met and when she may have been recruited by Chinese intelligence, are not known. But Ms. Huang’s work with Megaspeed put her in the middle of a sprawling effort to accumulate A. I. chips across Southeast Asia and provide access to the technology to China’s companies.

Photos from Ms. Huang’s social media, which were verified by The Times, show that she and Mr. Huang met across the globe over the past three years, including in Shanghai; at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters; at a golf resort south of San Jose, Calif., and in Taiwan.

After the 2023 meeting in Singapore, Ms. Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le, used her experience and connections in the world of Shanghai finance to work her way into tech circles. She turned Megaspeed into a destination for Nvidia technology, working with a longtime business partner who was often introduced as her husband.

The success attracted the attention of authorities. By 2024, the United States had dispatched a Commerce Department official to check on Ms. Huang’s company. She was monitored by Taiwan’s government during her visits to the island, including when she appeared publicly with Mr. Huang. For part of 2025, she was not allowed to leave Singapore because of an investigation.

Behind Megaspeed was a network of wealthy tech investors in China with links to domestic data centers, the government and the defense industry. Between 2024 and 2026, the firm bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s advanced A. I. technology, bringing Ms. Huang further into Mr. Huang’s orbit.

Details about Ms. Huang, much of which have not been previously reported, are based on a Times analysis of 15 years of corporate documents, as well as interviews with more than half a dozen people and government officials familiar with her and her business.

Ms. Huang did not respond to a request for comment. Nvidia and Megaspeed declined to comment. China has denied the espionage claims.

For many years, Ms. Huang’s life was rooted in the high-flying world of Shanghai finance. She mingled easily with tech executives from China and the United States alike, according to people who have met her.

In China, Ms. Huang is closely linked to a business partner named Kang Wei. Mr. Kang, a 51-year-old fund manager, has been introduced as Ms. Huang’s husband to Chinese investors and Megaspeed employees, according to people familiar with the matter. The Times could not verify whether the two are married.

Mr. Kang rose to prominence at a young age, earning a reputation as a savvy stock market strategist in the 2000s. Chinese financial media treated him as a sort of boy wonder. By the 2010s, he had moved into private equity, including investing in online gaming firms.

China’s securities regulator has fined Mr. Kang at least twice for failing to disclose his stakes in listed companies. He has also struggled with fellow investors for corporate control, according to regulatory filings. Mr. Kang has bragged about Ms. Huang’s connections to Nvidia’s Mr. Huang and used those ties to raise money for their businesses, according to one of the people.

Mr. Kang did not respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Huang’s career mirrored Mr. Kang’s focus on finance. According to her online résumé, she spent four years as a television reporter before working at HSBC’s private bank and CITIC Securities, a Chinese state-backed investment bank.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Occasionally, she appeared with Mr. Kang. In an August 2023 photo, the two visited a state-backed, auto-tech company in the eastern city of Nanjing.

The earliest corporate records bearing Ms. Huang’s name trace back to a small “sports and leisure club” company registered in 2010 inside Beihu No. 9, a private golf club in Beijing that drew officials and featured themed saunas, steam rooms and a buffet of foie gras, hairy crabs and Häagen-Dazs.

Over the next few years, Ms. Huang branched out, investing in a Chinese medical equipment maker that would list its shares in Hong Kong. She acquired her stake through an offshore company, corporate records show.

By 2020, Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang were known in some of Shanghai’s investment circles. They operated an interconnected web of companies to carry out corporate takeovers and invest in companies. That spring, their network landed a major project, helping build and operate an A. I. computing center in Shanghai for the internet giant Tencent.

That set the stage for Ms. Huang’s next effort: a push abroad to acquire critical chips.

In late 2022, the U. S. government began instituting restrictions on the sale of advanced A. I. chips to China. The United States feared that the components could potentially give Beijing an economic and military edge.

To have any hope of getting the chips, a company had to be domiciled outside China and have no obvious ownership ties leading to the country.

In 2023, Ms. Huang used a British Virgin Islands company to buy a Singaporean subsidiary of an online gaming company that was linked to her Shanghai network, called 7Road. It was renamed Megaspeed. It would become her first major venture into chips.

Later that year, Megaspeed was transferred to a Singaporean shell company, Singapore records show. After the transfer, Ms. Huang remained in control of Megaspeed’s day-to-day operations, according to people familiar with the company.

By June 2024, Ms. Huang was close enough to Mr. Huang that she bragged about her access to Mr. Huang at a tech event in Taipei. Just after midnight, she was mingling with a crowd of tech executives when she offered to ask Mr. Huang to join them, recalled Parker Schmitt, who attended.

“She said, ‘I bet you guys I can get Jensen here,’ and then Jensen immediately showed up,” said Mr. Schmitt, who is chief executive of NetThunder, a data software provider. Shortly after, Mr. Huang arrived and drank a whiskey shot with the group.

Mr. Huang was with two other Nvidia executives and had planned to attend the party, said a person close to the company.

Mr. Schmitt, who stayed in touch with Ms. Huang, said her social media was littered with photos of her and Mr. Huang, including pictures of them at a golf course and at restaurants drinking wine. She wanted to be seen as a talented sales executive, Mr. Schmitt said, and “photos with Jensen are a point of pride” in the tech industry.

That same month, Ms. Huang’s fledgling business had a series of breakthroughs. Megaspeed began receiving large shipments of Nvidia’s most advanced A. I. chips, eventually securing more than $4 billion of the precious hardware.

The company also landed a major new customer: the Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba. Months after its sale to the Singaporean shell company, Megaspeed had created a Malaysian subsidiary, which then pledged its servers and intellectual property to a subsidiary of Alibaba called Apex. Alibaba became Megaspeed’s dominant customer, according to a person familiar with the business.

Before long, Ms. Huang’s large A. I. chip orders began to attract attention. In late 2024, the U. S. Commerce Department sent an official to inspect a Megaspeed data center and confirm that the Nvidia chips delivered were on site. Some Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, raising concerns that it was being shipped in or out and was not installed at the location.

That year, Taiwanese authorities began to monitor Ms. Huang’s trips to the island at the suggestion of the U. S. government, a person familiar with the matter said. She entered Taiwan on a Hong Kong passport and made trips beyond her public appearances with Mr. Huang.

In March 2025, Ms. Huang traveled to the United States and visited Mr. Huang at Nvidia’s offices with other executives, according to a Times analysis of photos from the meeting. Two months later, she was pictured dining with him and others in Taipei, where she posed for a photo and kissed him on the cheek.

Yet trouble was brewing in Singapore, where officials had also been looking into Megaspeed. The Singaporean government prohibited Ms. Huang from leaving the country and brought her in for questioning in 2025 as part of an investigation into false declaration of imports, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

There was insufficient evidence to suggest that Ms. Huang was complicit in the false declarations and investigations against her were concluded, the person said. Singaporean authorities have said they are still investigating Megaspeed.

Ms. Huang subsequently flew to Shanghai and a new boss began giving orders to Megaspeed employees, said a person familiar with the company.

Megaspeed has pressed on. It is nearing completion of the first phase of a data center in Malaysia, for which A. I. chips have been secured. In Ms. Huang’s absence, another executive tied to her network has visited the Malaysia office to help obtain permits and ensure work continues, a person familiar with the operation said.

Other help has come from China. Shanghai Shuoyao, another company in Ms. Huang’s network, has sent large groups of Chinese engineers to work on the project, the person said.

In Shanghai, local officials have held up Shuoyao as a model. A July report from the Songjiang district government showcased the company’s new A. I. server factory, where, it said, more than 100 technicians can repair servers down to the chip level and reconfigure them.

The woman at the center of this story — a presumed Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang — has captured the attention of Washington and the tech world in recent weeks. But my colleagues and I first came across Alice Huang over a year ago, when photos surfaced of her sitting next to Mr. Huang in a bar in Taiwan. New photos that have emerged in recent weeks show their relationship went back years, and coincided with the formation of her company, Megaspeed, which U. S. authorities have been investigating for chip smuggling.

Pei-Lin Wu and Chris Buckley contributed research from Taiwan. Aric Toler and Sanjana Varghese contributed reporting.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

Wachtell partner Joon H. Kim, a former acting U. S. attorney, is leading the inquiry into the chip maker’s chief executive.

By Lauren Hirsch and Kalley Huang

Nvidia has hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to help lead an investigation into Jensen Huang, its chief executive and co-founder, after he admitted to an extramarital relationship with a business executive who U. S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy, according to two people briefed on the decision.

Wachtell, which is known in corporate America as one of the foremost law firms for counseling executives on how to navigate complex challenges, will advise Nvidia’s board of directors on the inquiry into Mr. Huang.

The Wachtell partner Joon H. Kim, who focuses on high-stakes litigation and enforcement, is directing the investigation for the firm, the people said. He was previously acting U. S. attorney for the Southern District of New York in 2017 and early 2018.

In 2021, Mr. Kim was hired by New York Attorney General Letitia James to help investigate accusations of sexual harassment and other questionable behavior by former governor Andrew Cuomo, who eventually resigned.

Nvidia announced the investigation on Sunday, saying that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that “the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” It said Mr. Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.”

China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of having the relationship with the Nvidia chief executive and of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.

Mr. Huang has viewed Nvidia’s board primarily as a governance requirement, rather than as an important part of the company’s strategy or execution, The New York Times has reported.

Nvidia’s 10-member board of directors includes a collection of early investors, longtime partners and other business executives. Its members have served on the board for a combined 161 years, and many have a long history with Mr. Huang.

Two board members, Mark A. Stevens and Tench Coxe, have ties to the venture capital firms that first invested in Nvidia in 1993. Another two, Harvey C. Jones and A. Brooke Seawell, were executives at a chip designer that worked with Nvidia in the 1990s.

Despite Denial, Trump Was Told on Trip to China About Spying on Nvidia Leader

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Before Jensen Huang boarded Air Force One en route to Beijing, the president was reminded of intelligence showing that he was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

By Maggie HabermanJonathan SwanJulian E. BarnesAna Swanson and Tripp Mickle

President Trump was told aboard Air Force One in May en route to China that the United States had obtained sensitive intelligence showing that Nvidia’s chief executive was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, people with knowledge of the matter said.

The message was delivered by Marco Rubio, his secretary of state and national security adviser, shortly before the Nvidia leader, Jensen Huang, joined the presidential trip to Beijing at Mr. Trump’s invitation. It marked at least the second time in seven months that the president had been told of intelligence about Mr. Huang’s involvement with the woman.

The existence of the previously unreported update given to Mr. Trump contradicts the president’s assertion on Monday that he had not known at the time of the trip about Mr. Huang’s relationship with the woman, who U. S. officials had concluded was working for China’s Ministry of State Security.

“No, I didn’t hear about it then,” Mr. Trump said when asked at a news conference whether he knew about Mr. Huang’s ties to the woman when he headed to a summit meeting with Xi Jinping, China’s leader.

The disclosures about the relationship have rocked the company and driven down its stock price. They have focused new attention on the intensity of the competition between China and the United States for supremacy in artificial intelligence — a rivalry in which Nvidia’s advanced chips are integral to the current American advantage. And they have put a new spotlight on Mr. Huang’s influence with Mr. Trump and the administration on A. I. policy and issues affecting Nvidia.

Ever since American officials first warned him last year that a woman having an affair with Mr. Huang was believed to be working for Chinese intelligence, Mr. Trump has played down or dismissed the concerns. When first briefed on the issue late last fall, Mr. Trump chose to take no action, The New York Times reported last month.

When pressed on Monday about whether he had received a briefing on the issue last year, Mr. Trump, who has embraced Nvidia as key to U. S. technology competitiveness and a driver of the stock market’s rise over the past several years, said he would have to check.

“I’d certainly check with the intelligence people,” he said. “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

Mr. Trump is scheduled to visit China again next week. He initially indicated he might invite Mr. Huang again, but on Monday he said the Nvidia executive will not accompany him on the trip.

But the president continued to vigorously defend Mr. Huang, saying he had spoken to him and asked him if he knew that the woman, known as Alice Huang, was a spy. Mr. Huang said he did not, Mr. Trump said. The president said he did not plan to raise the matter with Mr. Xi when he meets the Chinese leader next week.

“I just know Jensen very well,” Mr. Trump said on Monday. “I just think he’s a very honorable man.”

Mr. Trump’s previous trip to China, in May, has come under new scrutiny since the disclosures about the Nvidia leader’s relationship with Ms. Huang, who had been an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that purchases advanced Nvidia chips. The United States began restricting sales of advanced chips directly to China in late 2022, but it still allows Chinese companies to rent that computing power at data centers in Southeast Asia, like the ones Megaspeed operates.

In the weeks before the trip, Mr. Rubio had overseen the drafting of a memo about Mr. Huang, which was circulated to a small number of top administration officials. It was not intended for Mr. Trump, according to one person with knowledge of the matter, and it was not shown to him aboard Air Force One.

Mr. Huang, among the most pivotal figures in A. I., was initially left off the invitation list of business and tech leaders traveling to China in May, a fact that generated headlines before Mr. Trump departed the United States. With little warning, Mr. Trump invited Mr. Huang to meet up with Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska. Mr. Rubio was among more than a dozen administration officials on Air Force One for the trip.

A U. S. government official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly, confirmed that when Mr. Rubio learned that Mr. Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he “briefed the president on the issue.”

Mr. Trump was not particularly moved by what he heard from his national security adviser, and continued with the plan to pick up Mr. Huang, the people with knowledge of the events said.

Mr. Huang, once aboard Air Force One, saw the president “very briefly” but “remained in the separate part of the plane for almost all of the trip,” the official said.

The State Department declined to comment. Asked to comment, the White House press office declined to do so on the record. Instead, the office emailed a statement on background that pointed to Mr. Trump’s remarks from Monday. The email disputed the reporting for this article, without elaborating.

After The Times reported last month that U. S. officials had determined that Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and that she was in a relationship with Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives and Mr. Huang both insisted that the relationship was a routine engagement with a customer. On Sunday, Mr. Huang admitted to a romantic relationship with Ms. Huang. Soon after, Nvidia announced that the company would conduct an independent investigation.

Mr. Huang has long favored a more expansive policy on chip sales, well before Mr. Trump returned to the White House in 2025. His defenders have often noted that he has publicly said the U. S. must lead China in the A. I. race. Mr. Trump has largely sided with Mr. Huang and other technology executives and investors, amid a growing divide about the global risks of A. I.

Earlier this year, at an investor conference, Mr. Huang reiterated that China should not be able to access Nvidia’s top-tier products, and that the United States should have “the first, the most and the best.” But, he added, “Simultaneously, all American companies should compete globally.”

It was unclear whether the Rubio memo from last spring played a role in Mr. Huang’s having been excluded from the initial invitation list for the subsequent China visit.

At the time, the president was considering opening sales to China of Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell chip. Mr. Huang, along with some other major tech leaders, has supported such a move, although many of Mr. Trump’s advisers opposed it. The administration has not approved the sale of Blackwell chips to China, although the U. S. government ultimately permitted the sale of less advanced H200 chips to approved purchasers.

Luke Broadwater contributed reporting.

A Beloved Nurse Was Arrested, Shackled and Hidden in ICE’s System

The New York Times November 10, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

A nursing professor in California is among thousands of immigrants excluded from a public detainee database under a new policy to expedite their deportation.

By Miriam Jordan

Miriam Jordan, a national correspondent, is documenting the effects of Trump’s deportation policies on immigrants and communities nationwide.

Ann Lawani, a highly regarded nurse and professor, was still in her pajamas when federal agents detained her at her home in Lodi, Calif., on Sept. 16.

She placed a call that day to family from a nearby holding facility. After that, however, her siblings and lawyer could not find her in a public database that shows where detainees are being held. They got no answers from Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Ms. Lawani had simply vanished.

“It was the worst time of my life, knowing she had been siphoned into an abyss and there was nothing I could do about it,” said her older brother, Sam Lawani, 45, a U. S. citizen. When he heard from her three days later, Ms. Lawani was at a detention center in Louisiana.

Her disappearance was no accident. Ms. Lawani, a 39-year-old from Nigeria, was arrested the day after the Department of Homeland Security conveyed that most detainees with final deportation orders — tens of thousands of immigrants — would no longer appear on the public database. A document announcing the change, which was obtained by The Times, provided a script for contractors to use with callers looking for immigrants, explaining that the information was not public.

Lawyers across the country said the new policy has exacerbated the chaos of the sprawling network of more than 300 ICE detention sites, causing them to lose track of clients. Detainees are often shuffled between facilities, and not knowing their whereabouts hampers the ability of lawyers to provide timely, effective representation, the lawyers said. The decision to hide detainees’ locations was first reported by The Associated Press.

“The government is trying to deport immigrants as quickly as possible, and disappearing people from the system helps accomplish that by making it very difficult for family members and attorneys to find people,” said Cassandra Charles, senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Law Center. The consequences, she said, can be “life-altering and devastating.”

About 30 percent of all detainees, more than 20,000 people, have disappeared from the database, according to a lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston last month by the National Immigration Law Center and several other groups, which assert that the change is unlawful.

The groups argue that many immigrants with deportation orders still have legal avenues to seek release and win the right to remain in the United States. If lawyers know where their clients are, they can file motions to rescind the order, reopen their immigration proceedings and halt removal to third countries.

The motions must be filed before ICE deports them. Removing immigrants from the system deprives them of due process, the groups assert in the lawsuit.

Detainees can call lawyers or loved ones if someone has deposited money into their individual account at a specific detention center to use for phone calls, food, toiletries and other items. If lawyers or relatives cannot find their client or loved one, the detainee might not be able to place calls.

In response to questions, D. H. S. said in a statement that detainees have “several ways” to communicate with family and lawyers and noted that “the appropriate process” for someone with final deportation orders is “removal, plain and simple.”

The changes to the detainee database come as the Trump administration has intensified its effort to deport more than 1 million immigrants annually. As of March 2026, there were about 1.5 million immigrants in the United States with final orders of removal who were not detained, according to the government. Many had been allowed to remain in the country and have worked, paid taxes and built lives.

Ms. Lawani entered the country in 2007 on a visitor visa and applied for asylum. In 2013, an immigration judge denied her asylum but granted her “withholding of removal” to Nigeria, based on the finding that she would “more likely than not” face persecution if returned. D. H. S. did not appeal the decision and issued her a work permit in 2014, which she had regularly renewed and is valid until 2029.

D. H. S. said in a statement that Ms. Lawani had been detained because she had been ordered removed in 2013. The agency did not comment on her “withholding of removal.”

Ms. Lawani was the youngest of five siblings to arrive in the United States. The four others are American citizens, but they could not sponsor her because withholding of removal cannot lead to a green card or citizenship.

At the University of San Diego, where she earned her master’s and doctorate degrees in nursing, Ms. Lawani was a standout pupil and president of the student nurses’ association. She worked through the Covid pandemic and developed expertise in palliative, hospice and elder care.

One of her instructors, Eileen Fry-Bowers, became dean of the School of Nursing at the University of San Francisco and recruited her to fill a position there in 2023.

“I have given her increasing responsibilities because she continually demonstrates tremendous skill, knowledge and commitment to our students and the nursing profession,” said Ms. Fry-Bowers.

Ms. Lawani ascended to program director, overseeing some 250 master’s degree candidates on three campuses. She taught several courses, advised students preparing for licensing exams and job placements and supervised faculty. On weekends, she worked in the cardiovascular stroke unit at John Muir Hospital in Concord.

On the morning of Sept. 16, Ms. Lawani heard noises outside the house she owns and shares with her 83-year-old father, who is fighting cancer. Through her security camera, she saw officers wearing vests emblazoned with “police.”

“I thought there had been a break-in or issue in the area,” she said in a phone interview from the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, La.

In pajamas, hair bonnet and flip flops, she raised the garage door to ask if everything was OK, she recalled.

Ms. Lawani was handcuffed. When she asked why she was under arrest, the agents did not respond, she said. When she requested a warrant, none was presented. They ignored her pleas to speak with her father, who remained alone asleep inside. They shoved her into an unmarked vehicle, and 20 minutes later she was at an ICE facility.

Ms. Lawani texted Ms. Fry-Bowers to inform her that she might be late for a meeting. Soon after, her phone was taken away. The dean would later learn that Ms. Lawani had been shackled at the ankles, waist and hands and moved through four facilities.

“This is a Ph. D. nurse doing amazing work with students and with patients,” she said. “It’s hard to reconcile.”

The university helped Ms. Lawani’s family find a lawyer.

Her family wanted to file a habeas petition to secure Ms. Lawani’s release and try to block her deportation. The judge had stipulated in 2013 that she must not be sent to Nigeria. However, ICE could try to deport her to a third country.

But where was Ms. Lawani? She was not in the database, and ICE did not share her whereabouts. Normally, a habeas petition must be filed in the district where the person is being held.

“That’s usually simple,” said her lawyer, Natalia Vieira Santanna. “In Ann’s case, it wasn’t, because nobody would tell us where she was.”

Ms. Vieira filed the petition in the Eastern District of California, her last known location, on Sept. 18. A few days later, D. H. S. asked the court to transfer her habeas petition to Louisiana, which would require Ms. Lawani to find new representation and restart her case. Ms. Vieira opposed the motion, arguing that the usual rules should not apply because her client’s location had been concealed.

In support of Ms. Lawani, she included letters from Ms. Fry-Bowers and the president of the University of San Francisco, who described her as an outstanding professional whose absence was disrupting the nursing program.

On Sept. 29, the judge rejected the government’s request to change venue, finding that “no diligent attorney could have known” Ms. Lawani was in Louisiana. He also barred the government from deporting Ms. Lawani while her habeas case was pending and ordered it to explain why he shouldn’t release her.

If the judge grants the habeas petition, Ms. Lawani may still face a legal battle to remain in the United States.

“It’s painful to hear her wear down a little more with each conversation,” said Ms. Vieira.

On the 51st day of her confinement, Ms. Lawani described her emotional state as “holding on.”

She was worried for her father, whose health had deteriorated, she said. He had been hospitalized.

“I have given most of my adult life to serving my patients and students,” she said. “I have been treated like a criminal, but I don’t even have a parking ticket.”

As of Monday, Ms. Lawani was still missing from the detainee locator.

Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting.

Miriam Jordan reports from a grass roots perspective on immigrants and their impact on the demographics, society and economy of the United States.

Voters Backed Democrats, but Broke Right on Many Ballot Measures

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Many Republican and moderate voters who chose Democratic candidates did not do the same on transgender and other social issues.

By Jack Healy and Maia Spoto

James Payne, an independent voter living outside Phoenix, wanted to punish Republicans for the high cost of gas and food, so he voted blue up and down his midterm ballot.

Then he got to a Republican-backed referendum to require transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms aligned with the sex listed on their birth certificates.

“I was turned off by that question,” said Mr. Payne, 58, an insurance agent. “But I voted yes. Boys should play boys’ sports. Girls should play girls’.”

The measure, known as Proposition 318 — or the Protect Girls Sports in Arizona Act, to its supporters — passed with nearly 60 percent support. It was one of several Republican-backed referendums that voters approved even as they drubbed scores of Republicans out of office in Arizona and across the country.

The votes, for a string of measures largely opposed by progressive activists, revealed a red undercurrent to the blue wave that gave Democrats thunderous wins across swing states and Democratic strongholds.

The measures include new laws to require voter identification, restrict transgender students from sports, and create mandatory minimum sentences for child trafficking and fentanyl crimes. Even California, a bastion of Democratic policy, killed a measure to tax billionaires.

The dissonant results show that voters do not always move the same way all at once — even in a wave election. While economic frustrations and anger at President Trump propelled Democratic wins across the nation, many voters were moderates and Republicans who did not stampede left when asked to take sides on hot-button social issues.

The Democratic Party is divided over whether the midterm results indicate voters are seeking more progressive or moderate leadership. Voters did approve several progressive-backed measures last week: Virginia and Nevada added abortion protections to their state constitutions, and Virginia passed a referendum restoring voting rights to felons. Montana banned corporations and groups with anonymous donors from spending on state campaigns.

Still, political analysts said the results offered a cautionary message for resurgent Democrats: Don’t interpret the landslide election as a blank check for a liberal wish list.

“This is much more of a wake-up call from voters on the right to the Republican Party than it was an endorsement of the Democratic agenda,” said Frank Luntz, a longtime Republican pollster.

Mr. Luntz recently held a focus group with 14 Trump voters who voted Democratic in the midterms and asked them what had motivated their switch. Twelve said they wanted to send an anti-Republican message. Just two said their votes were for Democrats.

Consider Colorado, a solidly Democratic state where Republicans suffered a near wipeout last week. Voters elected a new Democratic governor by one of the largest margins in state history. They also gave Democrats supermajorities in the state legislature and are poised to unseat three of Colorado’s four Republican U. S. House representatives.

But voters in the state also supported four ballot measures opposed by Democrats and liberal activists.

Two measures were related to transgender issues — one requiring school and college athletes to play on teams consistent with their “biological reproductive system” and another prohibiting gender-transition surgeries on minors. The measures were put on the ballot by Protect Kids Colorado, a group that says it is devoted to “biblical and biological truth.”

Recent opinion surveys have found that most Americans oppose gender-related medical treatments like puberty blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy for adolescents, and that a majority — including some 40 percent of Democrats — believe transgender athletes should compete on teams matching their sex assigned at birth.

Two other Colorado proposals focused on criminal justice: One makes it a felony to possess any amount of fentanyl and sets an eight-year mandatory prison sentence for distribution, while another imposes a mandatory life sentence for child trafficking. Liberal groups argued that the measures would imprison addicts who need treatment, tie the hands of judges and potentially discourage sex-trafficking victims from reporting crimes.

Joshua Buster, 48, who runs a sandstone quarry in Northern Colorado, voted straight Democratic and against the transgender restrictions, and he supported a graduated income tax proposal that narrowly passed. But seeing the toll of fentanyl use on homeless people across the populous Front Range region of Colorado prompted him to vote for the tougher penalties.

“I think the dealers of these drugs are just absolutely immoral human beings,” he said. “There needs to be severe accountability for the people who are propagating the problem.”

Measures barring students assigned male at birth from girls’ sports also passed in Republican-leaning Nebraska and heavily Democratic Washington State. Voters in Missouri, however, rejected a ban on gender-transition procedures for minors, a measure that was coupled with an abortion ban.

“You can have a lot of voters disgusted about the Republican Party and Donald Trump, but a fair number of them are conservative on social issues,” said Seth Masket, a political science professor at the University of Denver. “They voted that way, freed of the party label.”

In 2008, Barack Obama was elected America’s first Black president and Democrats won large majorities in Congress, but California voters also passed a ballot measure banning same-sex marriage. This year, California voters soundly rejected a wealth tax on billionaires, even as they voted for Democrats who railed against billionaires’ influence on politics.

Some voters said that they were simply not as far to the left as the Democrats they had voted for.

Russ Moore, 66, a retired civil engineer in Oakland, Calif., voted for Democratic candidates but against the billionaire tax, which he worried would be bad for business. He said that he considered himself fairly progressive, but that the tax “was just maybe a bit too much.”

“You’re picking a certain class of people and deciding that they need to pay an extra tax on top of, you know — we already pay a pretty high tax rate in California as it is,” he said.

In Scottsdale, Ariz., Jeff Clow, a former Republican who registered as an independent after President Trump’s first term, was thrilled to see Democrats win the governorship and — for the first time in 60 years — majorities in both state legislative chambers. Mr. Clow said he wanted an end to Mr. Trump’s era of angry, polarizing politics.

At the same time, Mr. Clow said he also had misgivings about transgender girls competing in girls’ sports. He said that he supported equal rights for L. G. B. T. Q. people, but that when it came to athletics and children, “there’s got to be some boundaries.”

“Let’s face it, there are physical differences between men and women,” he said.

On Tuesday, voters in seven states also passed measures to ban noncitizen voting or require voter identification — ideas long pushed by conservative groups worried about voter fraud. Among them were Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio, states where Democrats flipped governorships and Senate seats.

Bonnie Kay, a 76-year-old in Baldwin City, Kan., said she had always voted Republican. But this year, she said, she canvassed for the Democratic candidate for Senate, Adam Hamilton, because “our country was hungry for change.” Mr. Hamilton won, becoming the first Democrat to win a U. S. Senate election in Kansas in nearly a century.

And when Ms. Kay, a dual citizen of the United States and Canada, reached the ballot question requiring citizenship to vote, it was a no-brainer.

“There’s not a lot to think about,” said Ms. Kay, a retired financial adviser. “You have to be a U. S. citizen to vote.”

Meghan McMichael, 33, a lifelong Democrat in Canton, N. C., voted for her party. But she also supported the constitutional amendment requiring voters to present photo identification at the polls.

Democratic groups in North Carolina opposed the amendment, but it made sense to Ms. McMichael, who works for a state agency helping people with disabilities.

“We do that when we go to the liquor store to buy alcohol, and we do that when we get to the movies to see an R-rated movie,” she said. “I don’t really see anything necessarily wrong with verifying who you are, especially when it’s something so important as voting.”

Reporting was contributed by Jonathan J. Higuera, Leo Dominguez, Ilana Arougheti, Coral Murphy Marcos and Mark Barrett. Sheelagh McNeill and Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Jack Healy is based in Colorado and covers the west and southwest for The Times.

Maia Spoto is a reporter covering disability issues for The Times and part of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

America’s Measles Problem Has Reached Endemic Level

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

A panel of scientific experts will convene on Tuesday to evaluate the United States’ measles elimination status. But genetic data already shows the virus is once again endemic.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

Measles is once again endemic in the United States, 26 years after it was declared eliminated in the country, an analysis of genetic data from outbreaks of the disease has found.

Data from the outbreaks will be the focus of deliberations by an international panel of scientific experts convening on Tuesday to decide whether the United States should lose its official designation as a nation that has eliminated measles. An announcement of the decision is expected on Nov. 17.

The New York Times asked several scientists to analyze the publicly available genetic data before the meeting.

Achieving elimination status in 2000 was a hard-fought public health victory for the United States. But with skepticism about the safety of vaccines growing in recent years, outbreaks have become more frequent. Over the past two years, cases have soared, with nearly 5,200 reported so far this year. Last week alone, Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin each reported a death associated with measles, bringing this year’s total to eight, more than the combined deaths from 2000 through 2024.

To officially lose elimination status, a committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a branch of the World Health Organization, must determine that the country has had uninterrupted transmission of measles for more than 12 months.

Publicly available data shows that several chains of transmission have continued for more than a year in the United States, according to scientists who analyzed the data at the request of The New York Times.

Three chains that were continuing in July 2026 — two in Utah and one in Arizona — can all be traced to an outbreak in Texas more than a year earlier. One of those, which was still continuing in Utah in September, had been circulating for over a year in that state, occasionally spilling over into Oregon and Washington.

“This alone is strong evidence that there has been ongoing transmission for over a year,” said Bill Hanage, a co-director of the Center for Communicable Disease Dynamics at the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health.

Another transmission chain detected in Virginia at the start of the year was still spreading in Iowa, Indiana and Pennsylvania as of mid-October. (There is often a delay of several weeks before genetic data is available online.)

“There’s a general pattern of outbreaks seeding other outbreaks,” said J. T. McCrone, an evolutionary biologist at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center who helps oversee Nextstrain, the publicly available database that contains genetic information for measles and many other pathogens.

“Measles is very contagious; it spreads very easily,” Dr. McCrone said. “We have a lot of connected communities in the U. S., and so you can hop from population to population and maintain a transmission chain.”

Some critics consider the potential loss of elimination status a referendum on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for decades questioned the safety of vaccines in general and the measles vaccine in particular. He has falsely said that the measles vaccine can be fatal, that it contains fetal debris and that its effectiveness plummets over time. None of the eight Americans who died from measles this year had been vaccinated against the disease. (Four were infants who were too young for the shot.)

Mr. Kennedy has repeatedly noted that measles is on the rise in many countries beyond the United States. Due in large part to a rise in vaccine hesitancy and misinformation since the pandemic, seven countries, including Canada, Spain and Britain, have lost their elimination status in the past two years. Mexico is expected to lose it this month along with the United States.

But the explosion of cases in the United States has coincided precisely with his time in office. Last year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recorded nearly 2,300 cases and three deaths.

Most cases of measles in the years since elimination were linked to travel abroad, particularly in countries where the disease is still endemic. But those importations did not spread widely and died out quickly because more than 95 percent of children in the United States had been immunized against the disease. That percentage dropped to 92.4 percent in the school year beginning in 2025, leaving nearly 300,000 kindergartners at risk.

Rising vaccine hesitancy has led to sharp increases in parents seeking exemptions for their children from school vaccination requirements. The Covid pandemic exacerbated the problem, first by derailing routine immunizations and then by intensifying mistrust of vaccines. Mr. Kennedy’s statements from his pulpit as the country’s top health official also fueled misplaced fears that childhood vaccines might be more dangerous than the diseases they are intended to prevent.

Regaining elimination status will require more than ending the current transmission chains, experts said. Public health officials will need to increase immunization rates across the country and cut down on the number of pockets into which the virus can jump.

The measles virus evolves slowly, allowing the vaccine to be effective even without frequent updates. But its slow evolution also means that pinpointing how the virus is changing or moving requires deeper analyses.

Scientists have typically relied on snippets of the measles virus, which was enough to identify the sporadic cases in the country. But they now have the technology to decode the full genetic sequences of the samples, giving them clearer insight into how the virus is changing and moving, and enabling them to distinguish endemic circulation from travel-associated cases.

“If this outbreak had occurred in 2006, we wouldn’t have the technology to be able to do this,” said Robert Potter, a clinical microbiologist at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

“We never really had to study measles from a genomic perspective before because there was no measles to sequence,” he added. “It’s giving us a lot of new information, but it’s information that we didn’t necessarily need to have.”

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.

We want to hear from couples who married in the last five years about how they approached their wedding budget: where they splurged and saved and how they brought their vision to life.

By Sadiba Hasan

The average cost of a wedding in 2025 was $34,200, according to a survey by the wedding planning website The Knot that polled about 10,000 couples who married in the United States.

In some cities, that number can double, even triple. In New York City, for example, couples spend an average of about $88,000 on their weddings.

But those numbers don’t tell the full story. Two couples could spend the same amount on their weddings and have vastly different celebrations. One might have an intimate backyard celebration and splurge on Michelin-star meals, while the other might choose a multiday affair with hundreds of guests. Location, guest count, personal preferences and even the time of year can dramatically shape a couple’s wedding budget.

We want to know how much couples spend on their weddings, what drives their financial decisions and what matters most when planning a wedding.

We are looking to hear from couples, domestically and internationally, who married within the last five years, across a range of incomes, cultures and budgets. Whether you spent $5,000 on an elopement, $500,000 on an extravagant multiday bash, or somewhere in between, we want to hear your story. Our goal is to bring greater transparency to wedding costs and show how couples with similar budgets can create entirely different experiences.

We invite you to share as many financial details as you’re comfortable providing. Couples who are selected for the project must be willing to disclose their total wedding costs and how their budget was allocated.

We will read every response to this questionnaire and may contact you if we’re interested in learning more. We won’t publish any part of your submission without reaching out to you first to hear more about your story. And we won’t share your contact information outside The New York Times newsroom or use it for any other reason than to follow up with you.

Sadiba Hasan reports on love and culture for the Styles section of The Times.

Stephen Miller Is No Loser

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Thomas B. Edsall

Mr. Edsall contributes a weekly essay from Washington on politics, demographics and inequality.

What does a rattlesnake do when it’s trapped?

Appoint Stephen Miller chief of staff.

There is no question Donald Trump suffered a self-imposed body blow of enormous proportion last Tuesday. There is, in turn, no question that Trump will continue to refuse to take responsibility for an election outcome he wrote and directed.

At 10:37 p. m. on Election Day, the president declared on Truth Social: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Reality: Trump was not on the ballot, but he and his policies were on voters’ minds as they pulled the Democratic lever in states ranging from deep blue to dark red.

The norm for a president suffering devastating midterm losses is to take responsibility, humbly: Bill Clinton in 1994, “I accept my share of the responsibility in the result of the elections”; George W. Bush in 2006, a “thumping”; Barack Obama in 2010, a “shellacking.”

No such nonsense for Donald J. Trump.

Trump’s intransigence reflects his intense aversion to acknowledging that in the midterms the nation’s voters rejected, en masse, the most corrupt, anti-democratic president in the nation’s history, bringing an abrupt halt to our descent into authoritarianism.

In this context, Nov. 3, 2026, ranks high among those moments when American democracy survived a crucial challenge.

These include the nation’s first peaceful transfer of power after the 1800 presidential election, the re-election of Abraham Lincoln in 1864 in the midst of the Civil War, the resignation of Richard Nixon in 1974 and Trump’s rejection of the 2020 results, which culminated in the Jan. 6 insurrection at the Capitol.

But Election Day a week ago is, in some respects, even more consequential: The opposition to Trump and the MAGA movement found expression in every contest in which candidates had an R or a D beside their names, from state legislative seats to seats in the U. S. Senate.

Doug Sosnik, a former top aide to President Bill Clinton who is now a political consultant, posted data on his blog that gives a sense of the scope and depth of the Democratic victory:

Democrats flipped governorships in Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas and now control 30 governors’ mansions in states with 75 percent of the population (pending final results in Alaska and Kansas). The party now holds trifectas (governor and both branches of the legislature) in 22 states while Republicans have 18. Nationwide, Democrats gained at least 452 state legislative seats while flipping 12 legislative chambers.

As a reporter who has covered the South for decades, I find it hard to put into words my reaction to seeing Georgia elect a Democratic Black woman governor, Texas elect a white liberal senator and, as seems increasingly likely, Mississippi elect a Black man to the U. S. Senate.

Despite its historic nature, the elections’ outcome has not yet cleansed the political system of the rot clogging the system of rules and procedures crucial to a democratic government.

On one side of the aisle, Republican leaders equipped with integrity and purpose have yet to emerge.

On the other side, Democrats are watching the most impressive new generation of prospective Democratic presidential candidates materialize in recent memory: Jon Ossoff, Josh Shapiro, Rahm Emanuel, Andy Beshear, Mark Kelly and JB Pritzker.

Whoever emerges with the Democratic presidential nomination will, however, have to cope with the public’s currently dismal assessment of the party.

A Feb. 3-5 CBS News poll found, for example, that 64 percent of voters describe the Democratic Party as weak compared with 43 percent who say the same of the G. O. P.; 23 percent say Democrats are “strong” versus 46 percent for Republicans; 23 percent see Democrats as “effective” and 40 percent see Republicans as “effective.”

In other words, after an election signaling that this is a moment of opportunity for Democrats, it is not at all clear the public perception of the party will let them take it.

William Frey, a demographic specialist at Brookings, does not share my doubts. He wrote by email in response to my queries:

I think this is a long-awaited tipping point election where the South — especially rapidly growing, diverse Southern states, like Texas and Georgia, North Carolina and perhaps even Florida — is reflecting the political demographics which will continue to impact their future.

Younger, Hispanic, Asian and Black populations led the charge in the Democratic surge overall — both nationally and in Southern states. The Democrats now have an opportunity to capitalize on their demographic advantage with these traditionally Democratic-leaning voting blocs, which will be a large part of the region’s future growth.

Frey provided The Times with poll and census data showing huge shifts toward voting Democratic among young voters and minority voters and their growing share of the population in key, previously Republican states in the Sunbelt, driving Democratic victories in the region.

From 2024 to 2026, the margin of support for Democratic candidates grew among 18- to 29-year-olds by 33 points and among voters 30 to 44 by 25 points, far more than their elders.

At the same time, these younger voters make up a far larger share of the electorate in most Sunbelt states than elsewhere, according to demographic data compiled by the U. S. Census Bureau.

Take the distribution of population growth from 2020 to 2025 in Texas, for example: Under age 18, it was 8.12 percent; among 18- to 44-year-olds, 38.0 percent; 45- to 64-year-olds, 22.26 percent; and age 65 and older, 31.56 percent.

Compare that with California and New York, where the share of the population in every age group declined except for those 65 and older.

In addition to strong growth in the number of Democratic-leaning young voters in the Sunbelt, if, in Texas for example, Democrats can hold on to the governorship and the State House in 2030, they will dominate post-census redistricting, reversing the recent history of Democratic losses.

“My new blog,” Frey wrote,

shows that, nationally, the under age 30 population is now minority white, which is especially the case in Southern states.

The 2020 census was the first to report that more than half of the nation’s population under age 18 was made up of Americans who identified either wholly or in part with nonwhite racial or ethnic groups.

Now, the latest Census Bureau population estimates show diversity moving up the age spectrum, such that now more than half of the population under age 30 identifies with racial or ethnic minority groups.

Frey described on the blog how the blue wave of 2026 was driven in part by the slow but steady rise of pro-Democratic nonwhite minorities:

The 2020-to-2025 shifts in nonwhite racial and ethnic minority population shares have now led to a tipping point for the under-30 population, such that more than half identifies all or in part with a nonwhite racial or ethnic group.

This is the case for each individual age between zero and 29, as well as for the entire under-30 population, where the combined minority groups comprise 52.8 percent of the population — substantially higher than those groups’ 43.9 percent share of the total U. S. population.

One of the crucial questions in the South is whether nonwhite minority populations will grow large enough to produce more Democratic victories in governors’ races and state legislative contests, preventing Republicans from taking full advantage of redistricting before the 2032 election.

“The democratically elected governments in these Southern states,” Frey wrote, “now have the opportunity to reach out to new fast growing voting blocs and younger generations by addressing their issues, be they economic or cultural, in order to sharply change the politics of this fast-growing region.”

Some scholars of politics are more cautious than Frey in drawing broad conclusions from the midterms.

Gary Jacobson, a political scientist at the University of California-San Diego and an expert on Congress, wrote by email in response to my inquiries:

I’d never read one election as indicating “a real, long-lasting shift in partisanship.” The 2026 midterm was clearly a rejection of Trump, especially by younger and minority voters, but they had swung toward the Republicans only two years earlier and there is no reason to think they are permanently settled on the Democratic side.

Much will depend on what happens in the next two years. If Trump continues as before — and his appointment of Miller as chief of staff indicates that he plans to do so — it may solidify the recent alienation of voters who have shifted from his party. And what the Democrats are able to do to please these voters or at least to convince them that they are trying to address affordability and other matters, even if Trump stymies them, will also be a factor.

Jacobson acknowledged that “long-term demographic shifts — the population becoming more ethnically diverse as older white voters die off — favor the Democrats, but it is a slow and somewhat erratic process.”

Jacobson suggested, however, that the demographic trends described by Frey may pay off for Democrats during redistricting:

The results show that what appeared to be solidly red states can be won by the right Democrat and this will surely figure into both parties’ calculations for 2028. The movement of people from blue to red states and the reallocation of House seats that will follow in 2030 will not help Republicans much if the receiving states become less red in the process.

This seems to be happening in Texas and elsewhere in the South, although we can’t be sure how durable the change is for another couple of elections.

The Democrats are now better positioned going into a presidential election than they have been for decades, perhaps going as far back as 1974. But two wild cards — Donald Trump and his enforcer, Stephen Miller — will be major players over the next two years. Whatever else happens, they will be sources of chaos and disruption.

Trump is still wincing from his 2020 defeat and the current public repudiation of his presidency — an intolerable mark to leave on the history books.

Few could match Trump’s recklessness in the face of loss, except he may have met his match in Miller.

If Democrats are a “radical left group of lunatics” in Trump’s view, in Miller’s assessment the left is a threat to the survival of America as we know it.

Here’s Miller on the Democratic Party in an Aug. 25, 2025, interview by Sean Hannity on Fox News:

The Democrat Party does not fight for, care about or represent American citizens. It is an entity devoted exclusively to the defense of hardened criminals, gangbangers and illegal, alien killers and terrorists. The Democrat Party is not a political party. It is a domestic extremist organization.

Or take Miller’s remarks at the Sept. 21, 2025, Charlie Kirk Memorial Service:

To those trying to incite violence against us, those trying to foment hatred against us, what do you have? You have nothing. You are nothing. You are wickedness. You are jealousy. You are envy. You are hatred. You are nothing. You can build nothing. You can produce nothing. You can create nothing.

Trump, in other words, has unleashed a man who sees Democrats and liberals as “devoted exclusively” to the protection of criminals, gangs and terrorists, an ideologue who feels called upon “to save this civilization, to save the West, to save this republic.”

No one is safe when Stephen Miller — a man bent on destroying the opposition, a man who would treat half of the nation as mortal enemies — is the guiding hand behind the president’s agenda.

Matthew Tobin contributed research to this essay.

Thomas B. Edsall has been a contributor to the Times Opinion section since 2011. His essays on strategic and demographic trends in American politics appear every Tuesday. He previously covered politics for The Washington Post.
