‘I Know How Much You Love the American People,’ Trump Told Biden in 2021 Letter

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The letter, which former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. details in a new book, is remarkable for a warm tone starkly at odds with his predecessor’s public comments.

By Tyler Pager

In his first week in office, President Joseph R. Biden Jr. told reporters that his immediate predecessor, Donald J. Trump, had left him a “very generous letter” in the Oval Office. Since then, Mr. Biden has refused to discuss the contents.

But in his new book, “Promise Me, America,” Mr. Biden reprints the letter in full, according to an excerpt obtained by The New York Times. The Times also reviewed a photocopy of the original letter, which was dated Jan. 20, 2021, and left in an envelope addressed “To ‘46’” — a reference to Mr. Biden’s status as the 46th president.

The letter, written on White House stationery with Mr. Trump’s signature black Sharpie, is a remarkable document for how discordant it is with Mr. Trump’s public comments about Mr. Biden and the 2020 presidential election. Mr. Trump did not criticize Mr. Biden or challenge the results of the election. Instead, he wrote almost poetically about his experience working in the White House and how he believed that Mr. Biden “will be true to yourself and the American people.”

“Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats,” Mr. Trump wrote. “Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.”

In his book, which will be released next Tuesday, Mr. Biden, 83, writes that it was “as if there were two Donald Trumps.” He says Mr. Trump “deeply destabilized our democracy” and had “not offered the traditional meeting between presidents.”

“But here he was, offering his best wishes in warm language that sounded like it was coming from an old friend,” Mr. Biden writes.

During the 2020 campaign, Mr. Trump attacked Mr. Biden relentlessly. He called him “the worst candidate” in American history, warned that his election would unleash violence across U. S. cities, questioned his mental faculties and accused him of corruption. After Mr. Biden won the election, Mr. Trump challenged the results, culminating in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Afterward, he refused to attend Mr. Biden’s inauguration.

To this day, Mr. Trump still falsely claims the 2020 election was rigged and blames Mr. Biden for an array of problems, a note the White House struck again on Tuesday.

“Joe Biden should have heeded the president’s wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, said in a statement. “Biden is a disgrace, and America is better off with him no longer as president.”

In an excerpt from his book published on Monday in The Atlantic, Mr. Biden recounts the “traditional meeting” he held with Mr. Trump after his 2024 election win. He described a similar version of Mr. Trump that “surprised me by adopting a tone so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on.”

“You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends,” Mr. Trump told him, according to the book.

For Mr. Biden, the book comes at a complicated moment. Many Democrats are eager to move past him, still frustrated by his decision to run for a second term and how it paved the way for Mr. Trump to return to the White House.

After leaving office, Mr. Biden was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that spread to his bones. He said on Sunday that his cancer treatment would limit the number of public appearances he would make to promote the book.

“Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down,” Mr. Biden wrote on social media. “What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped.”

Hunter Biden, the former president’s son, said in an interview over the summer that his father’s condition was worsening and causing him pain.

The former president has made few public appearances since leaving the White House. He has been spotted on Amtrak trains between Delaware and Washington, attended events at the Biden Institute at the University of Delaware and given select speeches, including one on Social Security in Chicago and one for the South Dakota Democratic Party.

Here is the full text of Mr. Trump’s letter, as rendered in the photocopy viewed by The Times:

Dear Joe,

Coming to work every day in the Oval Office is a blessing beyond imagination. History resounds from every wall, every statue, every beautiful painting, and every corner of this magical place. Each staircase, hallway, and door leads to yet another door and memory, another inflection point in the glorious story of America.

I hope you take a moment every single day to take stock of where you are and the people who came before you, the titans who shaped the course of human events. You now have the opportunity to choose your place in history, and I know you will be true to yourself and the American people.

Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats. Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.

Not only are you joined by the past, but you carry the hopes and dreams of the entire nation on your shoulders. The gravity of that fact never leaves you, it is the anchor that grounds every decision you make.

Your strength, your deepest reservoir of energy, comes from the knowledge that millions upon millions of people are depending on you. Their ambitions and aspirations are the reason you are here, with so many counting on your success.

May God bless you and Jill, and may God bless America!

Sincerely,

Donald

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

A Top Target of Newly Empowered Democrats: Corey Lewandowski

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The former Trump administration adviser has been urged to preserve his records, as part of Democrats’ bid to rein in the Department of Homeland Security.

By Madeleine Ngo

Reporting from Washington

A Democratic senator set to have a key oversight role urged Corey Lewandowski to preserve records of his time as a top adviser at the Department of Homeland Security, signaling that Democrats plan to heavily scrutinize him once they take control of Congress.

Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, who is in line to chair the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a letter to Mr. Lewandowski, a Trump ally, this week that accusations of misconduct against him “remain serious.” She said she planned to exercise the committee’s power to investigate his time at the department.

“I intend to use the committee’s full authorities — including where necessary compulsory process — to expose corruption and waste,” Ms. Hassan wrote.

Mr. Lewandowski, a Republican operative who was the first manager for Donald J. Trump’s 2016 campaign, enjoyed an outsized role in Mr. Trump’s second term as an adviser to Kristi Noem while she was homeland security secretary. He built an expansive portfolio in which he had wide influence over personnel, contracts and department operations. His involvement in the contracting process drew particular attention from homeland security officials, who expressed worries that Mr. Lewandowski was trying to enrich himself.

Ms. Hassan said she was concerned about accusations that Mr. Lewandowski demanded personal financial compensation from government contractors in exchange for favorable contracts. NBC News reported in March that Mr. Lewandowski had requested payments from GEO Group, a contractor that runs private detention facilities, based on its business with the Department of Homeland Security.

The Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into Mr. Lewandowski over accusations that he profited from his role, The New York Times reported last month. Adam Trigg, a lawyer for Mr. Lewandowski, has denied assertions that the former adviser had done anything improper or illegal. He has also rejected accusations that Mr. Lewandowski demanded payment from any potential or current government contractors.

Representatives for Mr. Lewandowski did not respond to requests for comment about Democrats’ pledges to investigate him. During an interview with “The John Fredericks Show” last week, Mr. Lewandowski said that he was “happy to have any conversations with anybody” and that he had “nothing to hide.”

When a new Congress is sworn in, Democrats will be in the majority and have the power to hold hearings and issue subpoenas. The investigation into Mr. Lewandowski is just one piece of their bid to rein in the Homeland Security Department, which is responsible for executing Mr. Trump’s deportation drive. Democrats have already vowed to scrutinize the aggressive tactics of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the fatal shootings of at least three U. S. citizens, and efforts to deport people to countries where they have no ties.

Ms. Hassan said that she had previously requested Mr. Lewandowski’s records but his lawyers had rejected her requests and said he had no legal obligation to comply at the time. She called on Mr. Lewandowski to voluntarily work with her office and produce the records this month.

“When somebody in Corey Lewandowski’s position at Department of Homeland Security is holding up contracts or engaged in, as it is alleged, pay to play, this costs taxpayers money,” Ms. Hassan said in an interview.

Other Democrats have also said they wanted to probe Mr. Lewandowski’s time at the department, including Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, and Representative Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the top Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee.

“We’ll see where the evidence leads us,” Mr. Thompson said in an interview.

But they could find it challenging to obtain information directly from Mr. Lewandowski. Jonathan Meyer, the Homeland Security Department’s general counsel during the Biden administration, said Mr. Lewandowski could invoke the fifth amendment, which is the constitutional right not to incriminate himself.

Mr. Meyer, now a partner at Sheppard focused on congressional investigations, said Congress could still try to obtain information from people in Mr. Lewandowski’s orbit and companies that he engaged with while advising the Homeland Security Department.

Democrats are planning to go beyond investigating Mr. Lewandowski to try to check the department’s powers. Ms. Hassan said she planned to investigate the administration’s efforts to reduce training for ICE officers, and how its focus on deportations has diverted resources away from counterterrorism efforts and drug enforcement.

Ms. Hassan said she also wanted to examine the billions in funding that Republicans in Congress have approved for the department in recent years. A top issue will be a lucrative contract for deportation planes, which was approved by Ms. Noem and has come under intense scrutiny.

Mr. Thompson, who is in line to lead the House Homeland Security Committee again, said he planned to investigate acts of violence by immigration agents, including the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good. And he said he wanted to examine the administration’s so-called third-country deportation deals. Those agreements have involved expelling migrants to countries where they are not from because they cannot legally be deported to their home countries, often because they could face persecution.

“Someone is going to have to come and explain to this committee who developed that policy and why,” Mr. Thompson said.

Even with the power to issue subpoenas, Democrats could face obstacles obtaining information from the Homeland Security Department. Trump administration officials have already signaled that they will push back on their investigations.

James Percival, the Homeland Security Department’s general counsel, said in a social media post last week that Democrats were “more interested in political shenanigans than in governing,” and that department officials were “well prepared to deal with this nonsense.”

Madeleine Ngo covers immigration and economic policy for The Times.

Failure of Billionaire Tax Strikes Blow to Progressive Agenda

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

News analysis

A wealth tax on billionaires seemed like a political layup. The outcome of a California ballot initiative shows otherwise.

By Andrew Duehren

Andrew Duehren covers federal tax policy from Washington.

Of all the progressive arguments in favor of a wealth tax, the most clear-cut was supposed to be the popularity of such a policy. Even people who may not vote for Democrats would support such a tax, the thinking went, out of frustration with the opulence and power of the ultrarich.

And then voters in California rejected what would have been the nation’s first tax on wealth. Proposition 40 called for a one-time, 5 percent tax on the assets of California’s roughly 250 billionaires. It failed with roughly 53 percent of voters opposed as of the tally on Monday evening, when The Associated Press called the race.

The outcome is a stark setback for a progressive political project aimed at fundamentally changing taxation in the United States. Even in an election cycle when Democrats surged to huge victories across the country, a policy idea at the heart of the progressive agenda could not muster a bare majority in one of the country’s most liberal states.

“The conditions were probably the best they could have been to get this to pass, and even then it failed,” said Antoine Levy, an economist at the University of California, Berkeley. “That suggests there is a reluctance to pass wealth taxes.”

As the Democratic Party figures out how to wield its newfound power, that result may now weigh on decisions about how to raise taxes, even on the fabulously rich. In the party’s upcoming presidential primary, some candidates may now think twice about adding a wealth tax to their policy agenda. But the exact political consequences will depend on whether Democrats ultimately view the California loss as an idiosyncratic fluke or a reflection of a deeper opposition to taxing wealth.

There were, after all, several bespoke factors at play in California. The billionaire tax was mired in internecine conflict among the state’s elected officials, labor leaders and activist groups, diluting its support. Billionaires spent heavily against it, airing ads that claimed the tax could expand beyond the superrich. Several tech moguls even moved out of California to avoid the tax, fueling fears about its impact on the state’s tech sector. And even then, the proposition was not blown out: with 83 percent of the estimated vote counted, it trails 53 to 47.

Last week’s election also showed other signs that voters support raising taxes on the rich. A separate California ballot initiative, focused on sustaining higher taxes on high-income residents, passed easily. Elsewhere in the country, many Democratic candidates, like James Talarico in Texas, routinely attacked billionaires as they campaigned to commanding victories in historically-red states.

So some progressives still believe that taxing wealth could be a popular idea, despite the California outcome.

“I think we need to be careful about over indexing on this one result,” said David Mitchell, senior fellow at the Washington Center for Equitable Growth, a liberal think tank. “Voters rejected one specific wealth tax, but they support taxes on the wealthy generally.”

At the same time, the dynamics that helped bring down the California proposal may not be so distinctive. Any other proposed wealth tax, in another state or at the federal level, will be unlikely to unanimously unite Democrats behind it. One might expect that, like they did in California, the ultrarich would vigorously campaign against another proposed wealth tax. (Candidates like Mr. Talarico were able to prevail last week despite a gusher of spending against them, suggesting that the California tax was more vulnerable to the billionaire-financed advertising.)

Ultimately, any effort to pass a wealth tax will have to contend with the potent anti-tax sentiment in American politics. A wealth tax would constitute a drastic increase, even if it only applied to a tiny number of people. In their advertisements, the billionaire-funded opposition tried to stoke fears that such a tax would eventually apply to middle-class Californians. “Prop. 40 is not just a billionaire tax, it’s a tax on all of us,” one advertisement stated.

With its focus on billionaires, the California initiative was intended to neutralize this line of attack. Previous wealth tax proposals would have applied to multimillionaires, but the full 5 percent tax under the California proposition would have applied only to people worth at least $1.1 billion. The expectation was that billionaires were so wealthy and so unpopular, even compared to someone worth $500 million, that the public would not sympathize with their arguments against paying a novel new tax.

The fact that focusing the tax on billionaires did not make Proposition 40 politically unassailable could be a troubling sign for Democratic plans to raise taxes more broadly. Even before the party won control of Congress in last week's election, many Democratic policy experts had been grappling with the dire fiscal situation they are set to inherit. Just paring back President Trump’s tariffs and reversing health care cuts, two top priorities for the newly elected Democrats, could cost trillions of dollars.

Democrats will most likely need to raise substantial tax revenue to at least partly pay for those changes, as well as any other new programs they hope to enact in the future. That is one of the main reasons progressives have favored a wealth tax for so long: It could help raise the money needed to finance an ambitious liberal agenda.

Wealth taxes would be a new way to raise revenue, though, and they raise complicated questions for tax collectors and the public. While income taxes apply only to earnings on stocks, bonds and other assets once they are sold, a wealth tax would seek to tax those assets before they are sold. How to value some of those assets, and how to collect taxes on holdings that are not easy to sell, are among the issues with wealth taxes that experts have long struggled with.

The design of the California proposal was also somewhat unusual. Almost all of its revenue would have been dedicated to funding health care in California, rather than general budget needs. The tax was also a one-time charge and not a continuing revenue source. Proposals for a federal wealth tax typically commit the potential revenue to general government spending needs and collect it on an annual basis.

The hope for Democrats is that the California result is, at most, a setback for wealth taxes specifically — and not a sign that taxing the rich in general is politically unpalatable. Beyond wealth taxes, there are plenty of other ways to raise revenue. Those include seemingly technical tweaks, like changing the tax treatment of assets at death, that could still raise substantial revenue. Other options include simply raising the income tax rates that high-income individuals and corporations pay.

“It’s plausible to me that the voters are more comfortable with a more traditional income tax approach, and that could serve as lesson for policymakers going forward,” Mr. Mitchell of the Washington Center for Equitable Growth said.

It is also always possible that wealth taxes become more popular in the future. Proponents said they always expected a years- or even decades-long fight to put a wealth tax into place in the United States. They compare their campaign to the long, winding process for imposing an income tax, which required adopting a constitutional amendment in the early 20th century.

“It’s always complicated, it always take a little time,” said Gabriel Zucman, an economist at the University of California, Berkeley and a proponent of a wealth tax. “It’s just slowing down what I think is a pretty much inevitable evolution.”

Andrew Duehren covers tax policy for The Times from Washington.

The Eight Articles of Impeachment Against Hegseth, Explained

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Hegseth Faces Impeachment

Advertisement

Supported by

The charges accuse the defense secretary of illegally starting the war with Iran, directing extrajudicial killings and ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces eight articles of impeachment introduced by Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky. They accuse him of violating federal law and the Constitution through military operations against Iran, Venezuela and Yemen, the killing of civilians and retaliation against a sitting U. S. senator.

Three of the charges center on the war with Iran, which Mr. Massie argues was unlawful from the start. The remaining articles focus on decisions Mr. Hegseth has made in overseeing the Pentagon, including his rollback of civilian-casualty protections and military strikes against suspected drug traffickers in the Pacific and Caribbean.

“We’re not indicting him for being bad at his jobs,” Mr. Massie said during a news conference on Capitol Hill on Monday after he read his resolution on the House floor. “In fact, he was very effective at killing schoolchildren in Iran. The argument here is that he has broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”

Mr. Hegseth held a news conference on Tuesday morning in which he cast the articles as a slanderous effort by a “disgruntled and defeated congressman,” and the Pentagon has said that he “will not back down or be deterred.”

President Trump defended Mr. Hegseth on Sunday, saying, “He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars.”

Here is a closer look at the charges, with excerpts from each.

Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation notwithstanding the absence of congressional authorization, an attack upon the United States giving rise to the national emergency contemplated by law, or an imminent threat requiring immediate defensive action, thereby substituting unlawful Executive action for the constitutional and statutory judgment of Congress.

The first charge invokes the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which was enacted over a veto and limits the president’s ability to initiate or escalate military actions abroad without consent from Congress.

It asserts that the war, which began on Feb. 28 when American forces launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, was illegal from the beginning because it did not satisfy any of the conditions laid out in the statute for authorizing a conflict. Those include a declaration of war, congressional approval for the use of military force or an attack on the United States.

The resolution refers to the March 17 resignation of Joe Kent, who at the time served as the director of the National Counterterrorism Center and said Iran posed no imminent threat to the United States.

The administration has maintained that the president has the constitutional authority under his powers as commander in chief to conduct the military campaign without any action by Congress.

Secretary Hegseth carried out unlawful orders, and continues to do so, in contravention of Section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, section 1544(c) of title 50, United States Code.

The House voted on June 3 to direct the withdrawal of American forces from unauthorized hostilities in Iran. On June 23, the Senate approved the same measure, a concurrent resolution that on its own did not have the force of law but was a clear statement of congressional opposition to continuing the conflict.

Mr. Massie argues that the votes satisfied a provision in the War Powers Resolution that requires the withdrawal of American troops if Congress passes a concurrent resolution directing it. By ignoring the measure, Mr. Massie says, Mr. Hegseth acted “in contravention” of the war powers law.

“The law is on the book,” he said on Monday. “Pete Hegseth is obligated to follow the laws on the books, not the laws that he wants to follow.”

There is legal uncertainty about such a charge. A 1983 Supreme Court ruling, I. N. S. v. Chadha, casts doubt on congressional mechanisms that attempt to bind the executive branch without presenting legislation to the president for his signature, which concurrent resolutions do not require.

Directing the Department of Defense to treat the mandatory termination requirement as discretionary.

The third article centers on a 60-day deadline in the war powers law that determines when military action that was not authorized by Congress must end. The statute allows an additional 30 days under limited circumstances if needed to facilitate the safe withdrawal of American forces. Mr. Trump and his administration ignored both deadlines, arguing that they were not bound by the law.

The president and his advisers have at various points claimed that the war was over, including in May, around the 60-day mark, when they declared Operation Epic Fury, the original mission, “concluded” amid a cease-fire, and then classified subsequent attacks as a separate military operation.

“The war was never over,” Mr. Massie said. “There was never a legitimate stop to the war.”

By directing the Department of Defense in a manner that foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives, Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians and abused the trust of the men and women under his command by requiring them to conduct military operations within a targeting and legal-review system that he had deliberately degraded.

The article charges Mr. Hegseth with disregarding congressionally mandated safeguards against civilian deaths and casualties, including by gutting funding for the Army database that tracks them, eliminating a majority of the staff overseeing civilian harm mitigation and firing military lawyers across several branches.

It seeks to tie those moves to the bombing of the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Iran, on the opening day of the war, which Iranian officials have said killed at least 175 people, most of them children.

The resolution quotes Mr. Hegseth’s remarks during a news conference he held days after the war began when he said there would be no “stupid rules of engagement” in the conflict.

It also refers to a statement by the secretary last year boasting of a force focused on “maximum lethality, not tepid legality.”

Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die.

This article challenges the administration’s strikes against boats suspected of trafficking narcotics in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean, which began in September 2025. It accuses Mr. Hegseth of positioning himself as an “executioner” who directed the extrajudicial killings of at least 221 people over the course of more than 60 strikes.

The article singles out a Sept. 2 attack in which American forces launched a so-called “double tap” strike that killed two survivors clinging to wreckage from an initial strike, calling it “contrary to United States law and customary international law.”

The administration has defended the operations as necessary to fight dangerous trafficking organizations, but the resolution declares that the campaign exceeded the Pentagon’s legal authority and endangered American service members by encouraging adversaries to disregard protections for survivors.

Using the powers of his office, Secretary Hegseth retaliated against and sought to intimidate United States Senator Mark Kelly for his statement through a scheme or course of conduct intended to interfere with Congress’ constitutional authority to oversee the Executive Branch.

The sixth charge concerns Mr. Hegseth’s response to a November 2025 video in which Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona and a group of other Democratic lawmakers informed troops that they could refuse illegal orders.

After Mr. Trump accused Mr. Kelly, a retired Navy captain, of sedition and called for him to be hanged for the remarks, Mr. Hegseth echoed the rebukes, censured the senator and initiated a disciplinary procedure that could result in the reduction of his military rank and pension.

Mr. Kelly sued Mr. Hegseth, accusing the defense secretary of violating his free speech rights, and a federal judge agreed and blocked the punishment, though the Justice Department has appealed the ruling.

The resolution calls the actions against Mr. Kelly retaliation against protected speech and a public campaign to intimidate a sitting member of Congress.

An act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement

This article addresses the Jan. 3 military operation that captured President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela and his wife, Cilia Flores.

The operation involved more than 150 aircraft and drones and hundreds of American military personnel. The Trump administration has repeatedly said that the mission was a law enforcement operation tied to federal indictments, but the impeachment charge calls it an unauthorized “act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement.”

Secretary Hegseth initiated and directed Operation Rough Rider without Congressional authority

The final article challenges the administration’s military campaign against the Houthis in Yemen, carried out in the spring of 2025, saying that it, too, was an unauthorized operation launched without congressional approval or an imminent threat to the United States.

The campaign was intended to stop attacks on commercial ships in the Red Sea. It became associated with an early scandal for Mr. Hegseth, in which he and other senior administration officials discussed the planned military strikes in a group chat that inadvertently included a journalist.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

Mamdani Has Been a Fierce Opponent of ICE. A Judge Handed Him a Setback.

The New York Times November 10, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

A federal judge ordered Mayor Zohran Mamdani to comply with a federal subpoena for information about some migrants with serious criminal records.

By Luis Ferré-Sadurní

Over the past year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has fiercely resisted entreaties from the Trump administration to help with its immigration crackdown in New York, even calling for the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency to be abolished.

But last week, a federal judge handed New York City leaders a setback.

A ruling by Judge Lewis A. Kaplan, of Manhattan federal court, would force Mr. Mamdani to comply with a year-old subpoena and help ICE identify immigrants in the city’s last migrant shelter who have serious criminal histories and are in the United States illegally.

The ruling, though narrowly focused on migrants in one shelter, has placed Mr. Mamdani in a legal and political bind.

If he complies, he would be aiding an agency he has rebuked and threatened to sue. If he fights, he would be hailed by his left-wing base but is likely to open himself to further attacks from Republicans for protecting migrants with criminal records who are staying in a taxpayer-funded shelter.

Though Mr. Mamdani has nurtured a surprisingly amicable relationship with President Trump, the mayor’s repudiation of ICE had grown more forceful after a federal immigration officer shot and injured a Dominican migrant in New York last month.

City Hall has not said whether it will appeal the ruling.

“We are evaluating next steps,” said Ivonne Rodriguez, a spokeswoman for Mr. Mamdani.

The Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of ICE, declined to comment on the ruling “due to ongoing litigation.”

The ruling was a victory for the Trump administration in its often-stymied efforts to force sanctuary cities such as New York to work with ICE.

Last year, the courts blocked a plan to allow ICE agents into the Rikers Island jail complex. In October, a judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit that sought to dismantle the city’s sanctuary laws. And over the past year, Mr. Mamdani has sought to uphold sanctuary policies that prohibit the city from helping ICE enforce federal immigration laws.

The legal wrangling over the subpoena had played out quietly in the courts for 11 months until it burst into public view with Judge Kaplan’s ruling, which was first reported by Politico.

It began in 2025, when ICE issued a series of subpoenas during the final months of Eric Adams’s tenure as mayor.

On Aug. 6, 2025, an ICE subpoena demanded that city officials hand over the names and birth dates of men living at two city-run migrant shelters — the Row Hotel in Manhattan and a shelter in the Bronx known as Bruckner.

In a letter attached to the subpoena, Ricky Patel, the New York leader of Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative arm of ICE, said that federal officials believed that an unspecified number of migrants at the shelters had “engaged in criminal behavior” and were in the country illegally.

The city said in court filings that the subpoena amounted to “an improper fishing expedition lacking any legitimate investigatory purpose.”

ICE withdrew that subpoena, issuing another on Aug. 22, 2025, that was narrower. It focused on the Bruckner shelter and demanded information only on migrants who had been charged with or convicted of one of eight serious criminal offenses — including murder, rape, robbery, assault and grand larceny.

The city refused, arguing that it would require officials “to conduct a time-consuming and costly investigation on ICE’s behalf.” ICE filed another slightly narrower subpoena on Sept. 5, 2025, also rejected by the city.

After ICE issued a fourth subpoena on Oct. 6, 2025, the U. S. attorney’s office in Manhattan took the city to court two months later, trying to force it to comply. Mr. Mamdani inherited the court battle when he became mayor and continued to fight the subpoena.

During the court proceedings, federal officials said that they had two goals: gathering information so that migrants who were in the country illegally could be deported and determining whether the city had violated federal laws that prohibit the harboring of undocumented immigrants. Federal officials said in court filings that at least 12 migrants at the shelter had been charged with a serious crime.

City lawyers argued that ICE was trying to undermine New York’s sanctuary city law, adding that ICE’s motive was “more political than investigatory,” according to court filings.

On Friday, Judge Kaplan, who was appointed by President Bill Clinton, sided with the Trump administration and ordered the Mamdani administration to comply with the subpoena, unless the city proved the subpoena was issued “in bad faith or for other improper purposes.”

The judge told the city to hand over the names of migrants at the Bruckner shelter to a special master who would be appointed by the court and would screen the records, giving ICE the names only of migrants with a serious criminal history.

“Although the city and the federal government do not see eye to eye on immigration policy,” Judge Kaplan wrote in the 12-page ruling, “nothing in the record sufficiently suggests that ICE is attempting to identify migrants with serious criminal histories for any reason other than to enforce the immigration laws against them.”

The Bruckner shelter, in a converted warehouse in the Mott Haven neighborhood of the Bronx, is the last city shelter exclusively housing migrants. Most other migrants have been moved to the city’s traditional shelter system for homeless people.

The shelter, which houses single adult men, had 1,600 residents in March, but city officials said on Monday that the population had dwindled to the hundreds. They declined to provide a specific figure.

Mr. Mamdani ordered his administration in February to close the shelter by the end of the year.

Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, called on the city to appeal the ruling, saying it may violate city sanctuary policies.

“ICE is hunting down vulnerable New Yorkers on the streets, at work, in their homes and now in city shelters simply to meet an arbitrary deportation quota,” Mr. Awawdeh said.

Mr. Mamdani’s critics accused the mayor of endangering public safety by not helping ICE go after migrants with criminal records.

“Ask yourself who the city was protecting,” Scott Mechkowski, the former deputy head of the ICE office in New York City, wrote in a post on X. “Grown men with violent charges, sleeping in a shelter New Yorkers pay for, and the city’s lawyers went to war so federal agents couldn’t learn who they are.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

Luis Ferré-Sadurní is an immigration reporter for The New York Times.

Connections Coach

critic’s notebook

If these projects come to fruition, Washingtonians will lose access to sports fields, fishing spots and other tent poles of everyday city life.

Giant images of President Trump have been displayed around Washington. Credit...

Supported by

By Michael Kimmelman

Photographs by Alex Kent

Michael Kimmelman, the architecture critic of The Times, has written about the White House ballroom and biked around Washington to survey some of President Trump’s other redecorating efforts.

Voters left no doubt they are done with President Trump.

But the president is clearly not done with Washington.

Last week he made plain his lame-duck priorities. He gave speeches praising his helipad and ballroom and boasting about the reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which is reportedly still cracked and peeling.

Then he doubled down on his glow-up plans. He issued a proclamation seeking to declare his gilded Oval Office a national monument. And as for the egregious arch, his appointees on a federal planning commission rubber-stamped it before lawsuits tie the project up and Democrats take control of Congress.

A judge lost no time blocking that project. She paused construction to allow the lawsuits by veterans groups, the District of Columbia and the state of Virginia to make their way through the courts.

Inevitably, attention has focused on these obsessions of the redecorator-in-chief. They come across as a strategy to distract Americans from bigger problems and to distract himself. But it’s his plans for other, less gilded places around the capital that make the district makeover story an urban parable of the midterm results and of the nation at large under Trump.

Some efforts have been positive. Plazas have been cleaned up, parks refurbished and fountains repaired.

But like the plaque he put up in the Palm Room of the White House celebrating himself for his “exquisite” choice of crystal chandeliers, the president’s determination to leave his stamp on the capital treats not just Washington but also its full-time occupants as mostly backdrops or impediments to his vainglory.

I biked around the city with Neil Flanagan, an architect and public historian of the district. I wanted to tour some of the sites that link to the daily lives of D. C. residents.

We headed toward West Potomac Park, where Trump is burning to get rid of sports fields used by schools and clubs.

Nearby, contractors for the president’s National Park Service, defying a different judge, chopped down trees in East Potomac Park where Trump pictures a championship golf course replacing low-cost courses that have long served Washingtonians. The new course would take over Hains Point, at the southern end of the park, a tent pole of city life for diverse residents with its bike paths, fishing spot, minigolf and cherry blossom trees.

During Jim Crow, Hains Point became a retreat for Black residents barred from the park’s swimming pool, golf and tennis facilities. Today it is where local teens and families hang out on warm weekend evenings, where Washingtonians run and skate, catch catfish, cook out and picnic.

Trump officials have said they will try to find a different place for residents to fish and picnic, citing West Potomac Park, which is where the president has envisioned losing the sports fields to install hundreds of statues in a Garden of American Heroes that would include Muhammad Ali, Calvin Coolidge and Bob Hope.

“The power that presidents have over D. C. reveals what they’re really about,” Flanagan pointed out. “Most presidents I can think of, like Obama, Clinton, Ford or Eisenhower, were pretty indifferent to the city because their big plans were elsewhere.”

For Trump the city is a mirror of his self-image and grievances. The obvious example is the Kennedy Center, which the president’s handpicked trustees shuttered in September after yet another judge ruled that he couldn’t put his name on a slain predecessor’s Congressional memorial.

The Kennedy Center is not just a national cultural landmark. It’s where generations of families have taken their children to free concerts, dance classes and movies. It is civic bedrock for local arts organizations, building audiences and raising money.

Flanagan and I visited some of the statues, plazas and fountains that federal authorities fixed up before the 250th celebration last summer. The National Columbus Memorial Fountain outside Union Station hadn’t worked for years.

Now the water’s flowing and the grime is gone.

Lafayette Park is refurbished, too, although it’s half gated off. The Secret Service recently widened the security perimeter around the White House, extending it beyond the monument of Andrew Jackson on horseback into the middle of the park. A strongman in a stronghold is how Trump, his administration and his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, view the presidency and the city, an attitude reinforced by the ubiquity of armed National Guardsmen around town and the talk about the need for a sniper’s nest at the arch.

From Lafayette, Flanagan and I checked in on Freedom Plaza along Pennsylvania Avenue, a windswept and never particularly inviting open space from the 1980s, designed by Venturi, Scott Brown, which during recent years was occupied by skateboarders and a homeless encampment. The encampment is now cleared. And for the 250th, the White House scattered around the plaza sculptures from a French foundry depicting Revolutionary-era figures and a “Spirit of Liberty” holding up a sword.

But the plaza remains windswept and little visited.

“Everyone agreed something had to be done with Freedom Plaza,” as Flanagan put it, but the National Park Service “missed an opportunity to do something better.”

By better, Flanagan meant that an area near the White House full of government offices, tourists, students, families and businesses lacks enough amenities like playgrounds, benches and trees for shade.

New York transformed Bryant Park in Midtown from a drug den and pit into a paragon of public space after business leaders in the area called in urban planners, who interviewed New Yorkers and then introduced kiosks for food, movable furniture and Ping-Pong tables.

Something similar happened in the middle of Washington in 2013. Local district officials working with the National Park Service put out requests for proposals to improve Franklin Square and engaged in a similar design process to get public feedback. The $21 million renovation, completed in 2021, added a play area, children’s garden, water features like a splash pad and trees. Franklin Square has changed.

The renovation shows what can happen when authorities collaborate with citizens.

Last week’s manic flurry by Trump on the decorating front suggests that the president’s inner circle may be content for him to retreat further into his district revamp. Better the ballroom than the Strait of Hormuz. But where does that leave Washington for the next two years?

The president’s makeover dream has gotten murkier. Declaring the Oval Office a National Monument can be undone, as he has himself undone National Monument designations. Democrats say they will kill the arch once they run Congress. They can replace a couple of Trump cronies on the federal planning commission, shifting its balance of influence. The District of Columbia’s newly elected Democratic Socialist mayor, Janeese Lewis George, will also send new representatives to the commission. She ran for office saying Washington is not the president’s private property.

There will always be the Roman option. “Damnatio memoriae,” ancient Romans called it: the damnation of memory. After the departure of an unpopular emperor, the Roman Senate issued an official condemnation, followed by a dismantling of monuments and the erasure of his name.

Purges are a costly business, of course. History needs preserving to remind us of our virtues and mistakes. Still, ancient Rome may be a timely reminder.

That city wasn’t built in a day. But an office can be ungilded in one.

Michael Kimmelman is The Times’s architecture critic and founded and was editor at large of Headway, a team of journalists focused on large global challenges and paths to progress. He has reported from more than 40 countries and was previously chief art critic.

My Dog Eats Like a Person Because People Think Dogs Are Better People Than People

The New York Times November 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

I Fed It

What are you really getting when you spend a Chanel handbag’s worth every year on “human grade” dog food?

By Amy X. Wang

For the last six years, I have been harboring in my house a migrant, or a refugee, or possibly a fugitive from justice — I don’t know her history, and who am I to judge? She’s a Wild Thing: a semi-feral, dingo-ish mutt, inexplicably christened Pocahontas and missing a front leg, hailing from either rural Texas or Mexico. An animal shelter near the border picked her up and brought her to New York, and now it’s on me to keep her alive.

Dog ownership has gone on for eons. But in my six years of it, I have witnessed the rise and rise and rise of Big Canine — the industrial complex that tells me I am not being a good-enough (brace your eyeballs to roll like tennis balls off a sloped roof) “pet parent” to my (and your shoulders to judder like those same balls now bouncing down a staircase) “fur baby” unless I thoroughly spoil this creature. Hand-knit sweaters, Starbucks Puppucinos, velvet bedding. There’s an unsubtle message behind all of this — that dogs are surrogate children and ought to be treated as such — and nowhere is it more obvious than in the trazillion-dollar market for high-end dog food.

Sure, you can still buy sacks of bog-standard kibble. And before the invention of commercial pet food, who can even guess what alleyway detritus made up the average dog’s diet. Yet wouldn’t it be the moral choice, whispers Big Canine, to splurge on your beloved’s health, their livelihood?

Enter the fresh-dog-food start-ups. Of which there are so, so many. In the direct-to-consumer space right now are Freshpet, JustFoodforDogs, the Farmer’s Dog, Spot & Tango, Ollie, Nom Nom and a grab bag of other venture-capital-funded empires shipping “human grade” dog meals — several of which I have been guilted into buying by pathos-laden advertising. The ingredients are almost always some combination of meat and peas and rice and berries, and the math averages out to about $68 a week. What you lose in your a) wallet and b) refrigerator space is compensated by the joy of seeing your dog eat food that looks like actual food, instead of the postapocalyptic slabs in “Snowpiercer.”

Poca seemed to really enjoy her “chef formulated” fare. She also once joyously ate a bag of raw flour when my back was turned. Ultimately, $3,536 a year — more than I spend on groceries for my human self — proved too steep for me to keep up a subscription.

A few weeks ago, though, I decided to give upscale dog food another go — this time with Golden Child, a start-up whose very name literalizes this new development in American living. Started this April by Hims & Hers alums, Golden Child has visually arresting branding: luxe neutrals foregrounded by sleek, slim typography, quite brazenly echoing the look of both David Protein bars and the Trump Gold Card. Signing up for a box of 30 meals involved a Myers-Briggs-like questionnaire and the selection of “beef-glazed chicken” or “chicken-glazed beef” for Poca’s prebiotics-filled Longevity Formula. At the end, I was asked to upload a full-body picture of her, which the company promised would yield a “surprise gift.” This turned out to be an A. I.-generated image of my dog wearing sunglasses on a yacht; curiously, her missing leg had been restored.

I opened the delivery of fresh-frozen meals and thawed the first packet out. My dog scarfed it in about 13 seconds flat.

Slow down, I tried to beg her. Savor it! I no longer eat fast-casual slop bowls for lunch so that I can spend the money on yours instead. The least you could do is show some appreciation!

She licked the empty bowl, clambered onto the sofa and went to sleep.

Why was I doing this? Why is anyone? As nicely as Golden Child was marketed, all these premium-dog-food options look more or less the same when they’re scooped out of their packaging; after all, there are not that many human food items that dogs are vet-approved to eat. Everything is chunks of meat buttressed by grains and vegetables, just presented differently. This abundance of minorly differentiated products, sold to people who will not even directly consume it, speaks not to tastiness — but to taste.

Each fresh-dog-food brand has its own look, its own signaling. The Farmer’s Dog is clearly for bohemian outdoorsy types. JustFoodforDogs is for either software engineers or rock climbers or both; Nom Nom appeals to those who still self-identify as “foodies”; Spot & Tango buyers keep the magazines on their coffee tables in neat minimalist snacks. A Golden Child dog is, obviously enough, a David customer: a gym-maxxing, macros-counting, image-conscious bro. Of course, humans have already spent centuries engineering dogs, tailoring them into breeds for specific needs like hunting and herding. Now that we no longer need dogs for practical tasks and instead keep them inside our houses for leisure, they have taken on a new function as class signifiers; through our choice of their diets, they are receptacles for our very own anxieties and desires.

A dog is the perfect recipient of all of this crazed aspirational consumption, too — because she has no such aspirations of her own. You can make a dog anything. She won’t — she can’t — push back with her own aesthetic or moral stances. While a child might flatly reject a parent’s attempt to indoctrinate a taste for Gorgonzola or art-house films and reach instead for Goldfish and Marvel flicks, a dog will never turn up its nose at its caretaker’s values. Perhaps the D. T. C. premium-dog-food companies know a deep and uncomfortable truth about us and our dogs, which is that these furry courtesans are not so much real surrogates for human kids as they are our guilty, utopian, totally fantastical version of children — all of the delight and fine-tuning and consumer control, less of the selfhood, none of the talking back.

My partner, who works from home, texted me copious pictures of Poca chowing down on her ridiculously expensive food: “Look at our golden child!” And: “She does seem to like it. But she also tried to eat the stale half-eaten pizza on the curb this morning, and a dead pigeon.”

Later, another text: “Oh no,” he wrote. “Her farts are diabolical.”

Amy X. Wang is a story editor and writer at The New York Times Magazine.

‘We Have to Take Over’: Far-Right Extremists Want to Seize Control of the GOP

Wired November 10, 2026

On Election Day last week, white nationalist Nick Fuentes urged his supporters on X to “get out and vote Democrat today.” The post racked up over 12 million views. Hours later, in the wake of the Democratic sweep, Fuentes took credit for the victory. “We did it again” he wrote on Telegram, later calling the phenomenon “the Groyper Effect,” a reference to the nickname given to his followers.

In recent days, Fuentes has claimed the election results are an opportunity for him and his allies on the far right.

“Let the Democrats rule; see how that goes,” Fuentes said during a livestream last week. “There will come a time when the far left will terrorize people, and they're going to push all of them into the arms of the right. Who's going to fight the far left? Only the far right. This is why we have to take over the right wing now.”

In another livestream last week, Fuentes added a warning to the GOP leadership: “It’s our party now … You need to cooperate with us… Groypers are open for business. It has [to] be America First—and if it's not, we'll do it again for the enemy.”

A WIRED review of comments from white-supremacist, Christian-nationalist, and other far-right groups in the wake of the midterm results shows much of the same. While the groups are uniformly attacking Donald Trump’s failure to prioritize white, Christian, American values, they also believe that this sudden shift to the left will result in a backlash that will see more people embrace far-right groups and ideologies.

“Many prominent figures in racist, extremist movements have taken to declaring the MAGA movement dead since the midterm elections, claiming that the results validate their previous criticisms of the Trump administration and opens new opportunities for their movements to push disaffected voters toward their ideological beliefs,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED.

While some of the Republican party’s extremist candidates were rejected during the elections last week, many did win their elections.

The Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights tracked 535 candidates running in statewide races who were members of at least one far-right Facebook group. The researchers found that of the 476 races that had been called by last Friday, 338 of those candidates were victorious, representing a 71 percent win rate. (The vast majority of these races saw GOP incumbents retain their seats.) In Florida, for example, 34-year-old citrus farmer Marshall Rawson, who attended the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, in 2017, easily defeated his Democrat opponent in the state’s 10th District State House race.

Many states also passed ballot measures that could further far-right agendas, including anti-transgender rules, onerous voter ID laws, and anti-immigrant measures.

“Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington approved bans on trans athletes in female sports, so girls in Washington state, for instance, will now have to go through a genital exam or pass a DNA test before they can participate in youth sports,” Devin Burghart, executive director with IREHR, said on Friday during a briefing with reporters.

The success of these ballot measures was celebrated by extremist groups as evidence that Americans wanted what the current GOP could not deliver.

The Proud Boys, the street-fighting group that Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations made largely redundant in recent years, were optimistic following the losses. “The ultimate rebuke of the current Republican establishment was citizens voting them out of office, then doing their job for them by passing ballot measures on issues the Republicans should have already handled,” the Cape Fear Proud Boys wrote in their Telegram channel.

“What this signals to me is even in those places where they lost, they're getting 41-47 percent of the vote, [so] there's still a mass base to try to be mobilized,” Chuck Tanner, research director at IREHR, said during the briefing. “That's the lesson that some of these groups are taking out of it, is that there's still that mass base.”

And it is the existence of this base, extremist groups claim, that leaves the Republican Party vulnerable to takeover from the inside.

“Now is the time, if you're a nationalist, to start looking at moving on the Republican Party where you live,” Warren Balogh, a white supremacist from Pittsburgh who attended the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville in 2017, wrote on his Telegram channel. “And by that I mean, organizing your guys and going in to do a hostile takeover.”

“This may be the best thing that has happened to the Republican Party in a half-century,” the Cape Fear Proud Boys declared in a post on Telegram days after the election. “Now you will learn to placate us, or you will continue to fail. Understand this: You’re going to run people we like, and you’re going to do what we say.”

But other extremists appear less inclined to wait until the next general election in 2028, preferring a more direct takeover.

"I'm not saying that we will win through democracy. I'm just saying we'll win,” Joel Webbon, a Christian nationalist pastor said last week in a video posted online after the election. Webbon and fellow far-right pastors, as well as guest speaker and noted conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, are set to meet at a conference in Texas this week where attendees will discuss, in at least one talk, “battle plans” for “Christian nationalists on the right to be able to seize power.”

Experts WIRED spoke to said they have not seen any explicit calls for violence from the far-right groups they are tracking, but some figures are already looking ahead to January 3, when Congress is set to certify the midterm election results.

Far-right activist and pardoned January 6 rioter Jake Lang, however, is planning an event in DC on January 3. It is unclear how many people are planning to attend, but one of the Christian nationalist pastors listed by Lang as an official speaker has said he won’t be speaking.

Lang, who spent last weekend disrupting a cat convention that he thought was a furry convention, did not respond to a request for comment.

4DX Movies Are Entering Their Thirsty Romance Era

Wired November 10, 2026

Following the temporary collapse of the fan fiction website A03, extremely horny millennial women are on the hunt for other ways to get their rocks off—and Regal Cinemas execs are more than happy to help.

On Tuesday, the movie theater chain announced that for one night only, on November 16, it will be screening 4DX versions of episodes 5 and 6 of Heated Rivalry, the smash-hit gay hockey show adapted from the bestselling novels by Rachel Reid that first aired on the Canadian network Crave but blasted into the mainstream when it came to HBO Max. The screenings will be at 59 theaters across the US, as well as a handful of theaters in Canada and the United Kingdom.

The screenings are intended to give fans the opportunity “to go to the cottage and really experience” Hollanov all over again, says Jack Grimes, senior director of alternative business development at Regal.

The 4DX screenings are upping the ante for the fan-favorite Heated Rivalry screenings, which have been selling out in movie theaters across the US for the past month. Though the series is widely available to stream, fans have flocked to theaters to shout along to t. a. T. u’s “All the Things She Said” during the club scene in episode four and post photos of the Heated Rivalry–themed popcorn buckets featuring stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams in a sweaty, shirtless embrace. Thus far, such public displays of down bad-ness have been incredibly lucrative: as of November 8, Regal has earned $1.4 million from its limited theatrical release, per Variety’s reporting.

Still, Heated Rivalry isn’t an obvious candidate for a 4DX release. Originating in South Korea in 2009, 4DX technology provides an immersive experience for the viewer, such as motion-enabled chairs; environmental effects like wind, snow, and rain; or even scents, such as the smell of gunpowder or explosives during battle scenes. It’s mostly been used for big-budget action-adventure movies and thrillers such as The Odyssey and Avatar: The Way of Water.

Recently, however, there’s been increasing demand for 4DX big-screen releases for not just conventional action movies but also straightforward dramas, comedies, and even romances. Put another way, there’s evidence that a not-insubstantial number of the filmgoing public would like nothing more than a two-hour license to hump their seats.

For instance, as the result of what was essentially an extremely online in-joke, last month the film distributor Black Bear hosted 4DX screenings of the romantic black comedy Wicker, starring Olivia Colman as a woman who falls in love with a straw-plaited man (Alexander Skarsgaard). The screening featured such immersive special effects as water splashing in the audience’s faces when Colman’s character empties out her chamber pot, as well as synchronized motion-activated “thrusts” in the audience’s seats during sex scenes.

Grimes tells WIRED that the idea to produce 4DX Heated Rivalry screenings was in part inspired by the intense social media response to Wicker.

“We think the demographic overlap is really significant between the two,” he says. “They’re both very female-driven, in terms of what the viewership looks like.” The sales numbers for the Heated Rivalry screenings “emphasized that we needed to bring this to life,” Grimes says.

In general, filmmakers are increasingly becoming more creative about how they incorporate 4DX effects into their work. According to a Vulture interview with Jaehyun Jeong and Jaesang Yoon, two producers for the special effects company CJ 4DPlex, Paul Thomas Anderson specifically requested “sexual movements” for a scene in One Battle After Another in which Sean Penn’s character masturbates.

When asked about which specific effects will be used for Heated Rivalry, Grimes says CJ 4DPlex is in the process of coding the 4DX version, so he couldn’t say for sure. But he says it will likely “lean a lot into the motion effects,” albeit “where it makes sense to do so and where it's going to be tasteful to do so.”

Does that mean the chairs will thrust during sex scenes, as some randy fans have speculated? “I mean, it's, it's something that we saw in Wicker, so I wouldn't say that it's out of a stretch of imagination to say it's going to happen here,” Grimes says.

Unfortunately, the effects will perhaps not be quite as explicit as they were in Wicker, as it’s worth noting that episodes 5 and 6 are significantly less graphic than those earlier in the season. But it’s still tempting to consider how, exactly, Regal plans to incorporate special effects into the screening. Chirping crickets during the cottage scenes? Ice chips flying around when Kip rushes down to the rink to make out with Scott to the adrenaline-pumping percussive strains of “I’ll Believe in Anything”? An unidentified substance spraying in the audience’s faces when Ilya finishes off Shane while he’s on a call? The mind reels.

This New Linux-Based Desktop Operating System Is Built for AI Nerds

Wired November 10, 2026

Kirt McMaster knows that his new operating system—Kora—won’t be for everyone, and he’s fine with that.

Kora, announced on Tuesday, is designed as a desktop alternative to Windows or macOS for “the AI native, not mass market,” he says. McMaster, the company’s CEO and cofounder—who also cofounded Boost Mobile—likens his strategy to how Steve Jobs targeted creators when overhauling desktop publishing with the Mac.

This “next-generation” desktop OS can integrate context from user interactions across multiple AI tools. Targeted to creators and developers, Kora’s central idea is to bring AI models together at the system level and help power users interact more seamlessly with multiple providers, rather than siloing everything off into desktop apps and browser tabs. It’s scheduled to launch sometime in 2027.

By tapping into your data and context at a machine level, Kora could streamline some of the current speed bumps of using AI tools on a desktop. “All your context, all your memory is on your machine,” says Franck De Girolami, one of Kora’s cofounders. He gives the example of someone designing a project with an OpenAI model inside Kora’s interface, switching to Anthropic’s tools to deploy code, and leaning on a local model to save money on AI tokens.

Kora is a standalone operating system built on the Linux kernel that runs directly on hardware. The startup has partnered with Qualcomm to bring Kora to Snapdragon PCs next year, but it also supports x86-64 architecture, so you can likely install it on current Intel- or AMD-based PCs.

To bridge the software gap, built-in compatibility layers will allow users to run standard Windows apps. The company is also developing its own native apps for basics like contacts, calendar, and email, alongside a software development kit (SDK) for third-party developers. Along the bottom of the home screen is a dock, as you would expect on a desktop OS. This is where users can switch between email, web browsing, and launching games.

The OS is designed around what the startup calls a "neural file system.” Based on example screenshots, the user experience may feel like messaging a chatbot or AI agent. File data is indexed by meaning so you can ask questions about the broad context of files by typing into an OS search bar, without necessarily looking up specific file names. For example, you could search for a business contract saved somewhere on your device based on a small detail you remember.

Kora grew out of McMaster’s startup Playtron, which launched its own gaming OS, GameOS, last year. GameOS is primarily built to run on portable handhelds, like a Steam Deck, with PC support as well. That architecture now lives inside Kora as GameFrame, letting users run PC games—provided their hardware can keep up.

The broader pitch caters to PC gamers and power users. “That’s always our thing—next-generation creators who are using these tools daily to build new applications and services, but they want everything else that they can get from a Windows PC or what’s currently available on macOS,” McMaster says.

Taking on the giants is difficult, especially with a team of under 100 people, but Kora’s leadership knows a thing or two about launching operating systems. Kora’s three founders—McMaster, De Girolami, and John Lagerling—each bring their own expertise. McMaster cofounded and helped lead Cyanogen, an open source Android fork that gained millions of users before shutting down around a decade ago. De Girolami helped develop Playtron’s GameOS. Lagerling previously worked on Android at Google.

Kora isn’t the first to rethink the desktop operating system in the AI age. Google launched its Googlebook OS and compatible laptops in October, designed around Gemini AI. Even so, McMaster doesn’t see that OS and its Android support as satisfying power users who want to run AI models that require serious chip power. The company is optimizing Kora for desktop configurations with at least 64 gigabytes of RAM, which is twice the memory capacity of the top Googlebook.

“We can evolve much faster than macOS and Windows,” McMaster says. “When you’re a billion-user incumbent, it’s impossible to tip the boat, man. It’s just really hard to make big changes. Over time, there’s this event horizon where building a new kind of OS for intelligence can become something very compelling.”

Ring’s Indoor Drone Camera Is Back—and Now Powered by AI

Wired November 10, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

No one's home tonight, but the sensor on your home office window upstairs alerts your phone: “motion detected.” Maybe it's just your cat or a flicker of a passing car’s headlights. Instead of shrugging it off, you ask Alexa to send your Ring Drone Cam to check it out.

The tiny, 165-gram drone lifts out of its charging dock, buzzing loudly, and autonomously flies upstairs, giving you a first-person view on your phone’s screen as it scans the room. Since it's dark in the house, the Drone's spotlights kick in, making it look like someone's physically in the home and moving around—a potential deterrent to would-be thieves. All clear? It heads back to its base to recharge.

That's the peace of mind Ring wants to offer with its latest home security solution, which it announced today for $250, alongside the Ring Rover Cam, a $1,000 roving security robot designed to help businesses monitor warehouses and factories. Both fall under the company's new Ring Robotics brand. The Rover Cam launches first on December 16, followed by the Drone Cam on January 27.

The Ring Drone Cam flies out of its charging station to monitor the home.

This isn't the company's first at-home drone camera. CEO and founder Jamie Siminoff says he had the idea for a flying sentry in 2016 before Amazon bought Ring. The company previously announced an indoor security drone in 2020—the Ring Always Home Cam—and nearly launched it last year. But Siminoff says the team kept running into edge cases that forced them to add more sensors. Those additions required more computing resources and made the drone more power- and battery-hungry, which made it harder to fly. The solution? Move the intelligence off the vehicle and into the cloud.

The Drone Cam has enough smarts to land if it loses internet connectivity, but the rest of its intelligence now sits entirely in the cloud; the drone sends video straight to Ring’s servers, where a custom AI Pilot agent tells it where to go. That lets the drone be lightweight and nimble.

It will avoid people and objects, and if you accidentally stick a finger into the propellers, Siminoff says, you will feel it, but “you'll be fine.” If your cat manages to swat it out of the air, however, that's a different story. A Ring spokesperson tells WIRED customers shouldn't “fly it” if it's damaged and should contact support for help (no word on repairability). The Drone Cam runs a motor health check before take-off every time and won't fly if it detects a problem.

Users can't manually control the drone but can also set up custom flight routes and patrol schedules. It can automatically respond to alerts from security sensors you may have set up in the home, like motion, door, or window sensors. It will not leave your home, as it needs a Wi-Fi network to operate and uses the Alexa Home Map you may have created with existing Echo devices to help it navigate. It can fly five to eight minutes per charge. (The final production model will be black, not white like in the photos.)

“There are times when you do want to just be able to see everywhere around the home, but you don't necessarily want a [fixed] camera," Siminoff says. “That's why we invented Ring Robotics.”

The Ring Drone Cam’s charging base.

Because it doesn't work outdoors and since it's well below the 250-gram threshold, the Drone Cam doesn't need to be registered with the Federal Aviation Administration. Drones have also struggled in the US after the Federal Communications Commission banned DJI from importing foreign-made drones without certification. But Siminoff says the Drone Cam complies with all US regulations and is assembled in Texas.

But what if a bad actor gets access to the Drone Cam? Siminoff points to the company's TAKE technology, or Throw Away the Key Encryption. It encrypts video in transit and rotates keys every few minutes, but Ring temporarily holds the key to run cloud-based AI features before deleting its copy. That brief server-side access window makes it less foolproof than true end-to-end encryption. (Every Ring account requires two-factor authentication to log in.)

Hackers have also invaded smart home devices and peeked through robot vacuum cameras, baby monitors, and other gadgets, so it's not hard to imagine a similar situation with the Drone Cam. To counter the threat of surreptitious surveillance, Siminoff says, the Drone Cam is loud by design—the extremely loud buzz of its propellers means a bad actor couldn't remotely snoop without tipping off people in the home.

Concerns don't just stem from third parties trying to access your devices, though. Amazon's Ring has been accused of normalizing suburban surveillance, partly stemming from the company's cozy relationship with law enforcement, and it has even handed Ring videos to cops without warrants.

Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, says a device like the Drone Cam is a personal choice and that people should “think through” how it will make others in the home—or visitors—feel.

“I think the companies who make these sorts of surveillance products are invested in us feeling less safe at home,” Klosowski says. “If there is a way to sell a product that helps alleviate the problem they are creating, I think they will do it.”

The Rover Cam is designed to patrol warehouses and factories.

The telescoping camera pops out to scan the area.

Ring Robotics' second robot is designed for businesses, not consumers. The Ring Rover Cam might look familiar—it shares many of the same hardware guts as Amazon's Astro, the short-lived home robot that didn't do much. Amazon had even pivoted it as a $2,350 security robot for businesses before eventually bricking them 10 months after launch.

Siminoff says the robot was great, but the software needed polishing, and people largely wanted to use Astro for security—that's why the Rover Cam ditches the cute face seen on the previous bot. It has the same AI Pilot as the Drone Cam, which helps it navigate through spaces and avoid obstacles. A telescoping 4K camera pops up to monitor its surroundings, and the Rover beams a light circle to the ceiling so you can always glance up to see where the short bot is on the factory floor.

It responds to sensor alerts, can automatically check an area, features two-way talk, and has a built-in siren. It covers up to 5,000 square feet and returns to its charging dock after its patrol ends. (It can do about 30 minutes). It's significantly cheaper than Astro was, but buyers still face the lingering risk that Amazon could pull the plug if Ring Robotics doesn't pan out.

The Grindr 1 Percent Is Getting Its Own Gated Community

Wired November 10, 2026

In a reddit AMA on Friday, in between jokes about gay bears and JD Vance’s potential username being CushionCasanova, Grindr CEO George Arison answered a question about the economy. He didn’t hold back.

“Inflation is terrible, and there’s a massive affordability crisis in this country that our government has ignored since at least 2020,” he wrote in the r/wallstreetbets subreddit, where, following the release of the company’s quarterly earnings report, he took questions from users.

It was a startling admission from the man whose company is about to release a subscription offering intended to price out most Grindr users. On November 17, Edge, a “premium tier” with some AI-powered features costing $120 a month, will be available to members worldwide, according to the report. Early access opened today.

The document suggests that Edge will help users find connections “with less effort” and will include a personalized recommendation feature, Insights, to “understand compatibility and the likelihood of a reply,” as well as Reconnect, which “brings past connections back into view.” The app will have an entirely new design, interface, and icon intended to create a different experience for users willing to foot the high price tag.

But even if you can afford it, you may not get in. As with Raya, an invite-only app where some people have been on the wait list for as long as seven years, the company is planning to turn Edge into a digital gated community of sorts: Sign-ups will be limited to 1 percent of global monthly users.

The goal is to “deliberately [manage] the growth of the Edge community to preserve exclusivity” for “a select community” who can pay “meaningfully more,” the report indicated. According to figures from the company, only 1.4 million of its current 16 million users pay to use Grindr.

Edge’s official rollout comes following pilot programs in Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and the US, and a year’s worth of speculation about how much it would cost and what exactly would separate it from other apps that provide comparable features at a lower price.

“These VIP tiers make me think of [it as a] digital version of expensive hustler bars,” one user said on Instagram. “The men who will pay hundreds for access are rarely the hot men you would log on for.”

Grindr is the world’s largest dating app for gay, bi, and trans people, but it has consistently struggled with concerns over data privacy and user safety. And as it unveils its latest upsell, many members say the app’s fundamental infrastructure remains broken.

“Grindr is a top-tier example of enshitification and predatory monetization,” one person wrote in the reddit AMA from last week. “You need to stop with the intrusive ads and start getting in touch with reality,” posted another.

In September, the company agreed to a $35 million class action settlement over allegedly sharing users’ HIV status and testing information with third-party vendors; the details of the settlement included no admission of liability on Grindr’s behalf. That same month, Grindr acquired the telehealth company Freddie, which helps people get access to the HIV-prevention medication PrEP. The purchase builds on Arison’s investment into health care and turning the app into a social network. Currently, Grindr sells erectile dysfunction pills and GLP-1 weight-loss medication through its Woodwork program.

Critics will likely argue that pivoting to luxury dating in an economy where more and more people are struggling isn’t great optics, but Arison is betting that improved features and a “deliberately limited membership” will create opportunity for “substantially higher pricing over time,” the report noted.
